# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L56


# Vulnerability details

In the `writeEntropyBatch1`, `writeEntropyBatch2` and `writeEntropyBatch3`  functions, there's a require statement that checks if pseudoRandomValue is equal to 999999:

```
require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
```

However, `pseudoRandomValue` is a 78-digit number, making it practically impossible for this condition to ever be true.

## Impact
Increased Gas Costs: The unnecessary require statement is executed in a loop, consuming additional gas for each iteration. This leads to higher transaction costs for users.

This is also the reason why setting entropy values cannot be set during contract initialization in a single transaction and has to be done in 3 batches due to contract & block size limits.

## Proof of Concept
The `pseudoRandomValue` is generated as follows:
```
uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, block.timestamp, msg.sender)));
```
This generates a 78-digit number.
The check pseudoRandomValue != 999999 will always be true, as 999999 is only a 6-digit number.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the unnecessary require statement:
``` 
- require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
```


## Assessed type

Loop

raw_row.title: High Likelihood of Zero Performance Factor Due to Inconsistent Entropy Generation

title: High Likelihood of Zero Performance Factor Due to Inconsistent Entropy Generation
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L181-L182
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L154


# Vulnerability details

The entropy generation mechanism in `EntropyGenerator.sol` involves slicing a large pseudo-random number into smaller 6-digit chunks. 
```
    uint256 entropy = (slotValue / (10 ** (72 - position))) % 1000000; // adjust the entropy value based on the number of digits
    uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));
```

If the large number has fewer than 78 digits, the resulting number / 10^72 will give a number with less than 6 digits.

Then the paddedEntropy will add a 0's at the end to get 6 digit number.

Similar thing happens when 1st digit in any of the 6 digit slices is 0. 

Since performanceFactor is calculated as entropy % 10, it has a high chance of being 0.

## Impact
This issue significantly impacts the randomness and distribution of the performance factor. 

A zero performance factor can lead to entities that do not age, creating an imbalance in the game mechanics and potentially leading to unforeseen advantages or disadvantages for certain players. 

This undermines the fairness and unpredictability that are crucial for a competitive game environment.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Using digits 3 or 4 in the 6 digit value returned is much more reliable.


## Assessed type

Other

The listForForging function in EntityForging.sol allows users to list their tokens for forging.

If the listings become outdated, users will have to manually cancel them by calling cancelListingForForging function.

Manual Review

Add an expiration time to each listing. Listings should automatically expire after a certain period.

# Vulnerability details

The `EntropyGenerator` contract uses `block.number` and other on-chain data to generate entropy values. This method of randomness generation is predictable and can be manipulated by miners or other actors who can influence block production.
For example, in the `writeEntropyBatch1` function:


``` solidity

uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, block.timestamp, msg.sender)));

```

Similar patterns are used in `writeEntropyBatch2` and `writeEntropyBatch3`.

## Impact
The predictability of the randomness severely undermines the security and fairness of any system relying on this entropy. Malicious actors could potentially:

Predict future entropy values, giving them an unfair advantage in any randomness-dependent features.
Manipulate the entropy by timing their transactions or colluding with miners.
Exploit this predictability in connected systems like NFT trait generation or forging mechanics.

This vulnerability could lead to significant economic impacts and undermine user trust in the system.

## Proof of Concept
A malicious actor could:

Observe the current block number and timestamp.
Calculate the next block's number and approximate timestamp.
Predict the entropy value that will be generated.
Time their transactions to take advantage of favorable entropy values.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use a verifiable random function (VRF) provided by oracles like Chainlink for true randomness.
Implement a commit-reveal scheme where users submit a hash of their secret and the contract's random value, then reveal it in a separate transaction.
Use multiple sources of entropy and combine them in a way that's difficult to predict or manipulate.
Consider using future block hashes as a source of randomness, although this method still has some limitations.


## Assessed type

Other

The EntropyGenerator contract stores all generated entropy values in private state variables:

These values are visible to anyone who can read the blockchain state.

## Impact
The visibility of entropy values on-chain defeats the purpose of randomness in the system. This could lead to:

Predictability of outcomes in any system relying on this entropy.
Unfair advantages for users who can read and analyze the blockchain data.
Potential for front-running or other exploits in connected systems.

This vulnerability undermines the core functionality of the randomness mechanism and any features dependent on it.

## Proof of Concept
Any user can:

View the entropy values by viewing the state changes for the transactions involving `writeEntropyBatch1`, `writeEntropyBatch2` and `writeEntropyBatch3`.

Use these known values to predict outcomes in any system using this entropy.

eg `writeEntropyBatch1` transaction on testnet:

## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a commit-reveal scheme where the actual entropy values are not stored on-chain.
Use a verifiable random function (VRF) from an oracle service like Chainlink.
If on-chain storage is necessary, consider encrypting the values before storage and implement a secure decryption mechanism.
Redesign the system to use ephemeral, non-stored randomness that cannot be predicted from on-chain data.

Using `transferFrom` instead of `safeTransferFrom` can lead to:

The NFT could become permanently stuck or lost.

Manual review

Replace all instances of `transferFrom` with `safeTransferFrom` for ERC721 transfers.
Ensure that the contract handles the return value of `safeTransferFrom` correctly.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L88-L89


# Vulnerability details

In the `listForForging` function, the comparison for forger tokens uses `<=` instead of `<`:

```
    require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

## Impact
This allows one more forge than intended by the `forgePotential` value increasing the value of the forger tokens.

## Proof of Concept
Assume a forger token with `forgePotential` of 5.

Use the token for forging 5 times, incrementing `forgingCounts[tokenId]` to 5.

Attempt to list the token for forging again.

The transaction will succeed, allowing a 6th forge, despite the intended limit of 5.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the comparison operator from `<=` to `<`:

```
    require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

In the `forgeWithListed` function, the following require statement is used.
```
  require(msg.value >= forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging');
```

and then the dev fee is calculated using a fixed `forgingFee` value instead of the actual `msg.value`:
```
uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
```
This calculation doesn't account for cases where `msg.value` might be greater than `forgingFee`.

## Impact
Incorrect fee distribution: 
If a user sends more ETH than the required `forgingFee`, the excess amount will not be factored into the fee calculation, resulting in a lower percentage going to the dev fund than intended.

## Proof of Concept
Assume `forgingFee` is set to 1 ETH and `taxCut` is 10 (10% fee).

A user calls `forgeWithListed` with `msg.value` of 2 ETH.

The dev fee is calculated as: devFee = 1 ETH / 10 = 0.1 ETH

The forger receives: 2 ETH - 0.1 ETH = 1.9 ETH

The actual fee percentage is: (0.1 ETH / 2 ETH) * 100 = 5%, instead of the intended 10%

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the fee calculation to use `msg.value` instead of `forgingFee`.
```
uint256 devFee = msg.value / taxCut;
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

In the `EntropyGenerator` contract, forge potential is calculated using the first digit of the entropy:
```
 forgePotential = getFirstDigit(entropy);
```
However, in the `EntityForging` contract, it uses the fifth digit
```
uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
```

Similar issue is also found in the nukeFactor calculations
nukeFactor calculation in EntropyGenerator contract (will always be 0):
```
    nukeFactor = entropy / 4000000;
```
nukeFactor calculation in NukeFund contract:
```
    uint256 initialNukeFactor = entropy / 40; // calcualte initalNukeFactor based on entropy, 5 digits
```

## Impact
This inconsistency could lead to several issues:

User Confusion: Players may be confused if the forge potential they expect (based on the EntropyGenerator logic) differs from what they can actually use in the EntityForging contract.

System Integrity: The inconsistency raises questions about which implementation is correct, potentially indicating deeper design or implementation issues.

## Proof of Concept
Generate an entropy value for a new entity: "123456"

In EntropyGenerator, the forge potential would be 1 (first digit)

In EntityForging, the forge potential would be 5 (fifth digit)

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Decide on the correct implementation for forge potential calculation and apply it consistently across all contracts.

Error

require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Looping through every slot of `pseudoRandomValue` to ensure that the entropy is not equal to `999999`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L53-L55
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L73-L75

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In `writeEntropyBatch1`, `writeEntropyBatch2`, and `writeEntropyBatch3`, the calculation for `pseudoRandomValue` is

```solidity
  uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
    keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
  ) % uint256(10) ** 78;
```

Since `uint256` can not hold `10**78`, `10**78` will be overflow to `10**78 % 2**256`. As a result, the largest value of the entropy slot can only be `(10**78 % 2**256) / 10**72 = 73663`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Let an entropy slot hold only a 12 six-digit number.

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L108


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `EntropyGenerator` implementation, there is a function `getNextEntropy()` that's  used by `TraitForgeNft` contract to get the entropy of the next tokenId that's about to be minted to the user. The problem is that the slot index is reassigned to 0 after the final slot is reached and it allows to override and mint the same entropy to several users.

## Proof of Concept

`getNextEntropy()` nullifies the current slot index if the maximum slot is reached which allows to create the same entropy for some users:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L105-109
```
 if (currentNumberIndex >= maxNumberIndex - 1) {
      currentNumberIndex = 0;
      if (currentSlotIndex >= maxSlotIndex - 1) {
        currentSlotIndex = 0;
      }
```



## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Don't update current slot index and just break the counter by changing generation.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L215


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `TraitForgeNft` smart contract, `mintWithBudget()` function is used to mint as many tokens as corresponding provided with the function call `msg.value` allows. The problem is that the only limit is that the tokenIds should be less than maximum tokens per generation. It can result in DoS of the user as the number of repetitions can be very huge if it's some big customer and the gas costs of the loop may significantly increase.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L215-220
```
while (budgetLeft >= mintPrice && _tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen) {
      _mintInternal(msg.sender, mintPrice);
      amountMinted++;
      budgetLeft -= mintPrice;
      mintPrice = calculateMintPrice();
    }
```

User can mint as many tokens as he wants unless it's no greater than maximum tokens per generation. This may result in a huge gas costs for implementing the loop and in potential DoS as `maxTokensPerGen` equals to `100000`.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reduce the bounds for the while loop.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L47
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L30


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `EntropyGenerator` smart contract, the slots with 78 digits number (13 concatenated entropies) should be initialized for each generation (total number of 10). And as there are the total of 10000 tokens per generation, 770 slots are therefore needed. The problem is that there is no any initialization of slots and new entropies for the next generations - it's only done for the first one.

## Proof of Concept

There are 3 functions that fill the 770 slots with entropies:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L47

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L64

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L84

The only thing is called when the generation is incremented inside of `TraitForgeNft` smart contract, it's `initializeAlphaIndices()` which creates a slot index and number index for the special entropy - `999999`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L345-355
```
 function _incrementGeneration() private {
    require(
      generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen,
      'Generation limit not yet reached'
    );
    currentGeneration++;
    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
    priceIncrement = priceIncrement + priceIncrementByGen;
    entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();
    emit GenerationIncremented(currentGeneration);
  }
```

This leaves all the contract with only 10000 entropies initialized and without entropies for the future generations and it can be considered as unexpected behavior.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Check if new entropies are initialized for new generations as well.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L148


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`NukeFund` smart contract allows the user to claim some part of the nuke fund in accordance with his nuke factor value (of the entity). In the documentation it's said that the full maturity should be after 30 days for the fastest entities and for the slowest entities it's 2 years. The problem is that the full maturity basically means that the user's nuke factor make him eligible to claim 50% (maximum  possible value) and the final nuke factor is determined completely random without significant connection to the perfomance factor.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at how `finalNukeFactor` is determined:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L147-148
```
    uint256 finalNukeFactor = ((adjustedAge * defaultNukeFactorIncrease) /
      MAX_DENOMINATOR) + initialNukeFactor;

    return finalNukeFactor;
  }
```

`adjustedAge` value is obtained like this:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L128-131
```
uint256 age = (daysOld *
      perfomanceFactor *
      MAX_DENOMINATOR *
      ageMultiplier) / 365; // add 5 digits for decimals

```

So we get some random number represented as age and then we just add `initialNukeFactor` at the end which is just the addition of two random numbers. It makes it a deviation from the spec as there is no any relation to perfomance factor and actual maturity as it's just used as a value for multiplication. The tokens that can nuke 50% of the funds have completely random nuke factors that does not depend on perfomance factor as described in the spec.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change the way nuke factor is calculated and make it the way it's described in the docs.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L6


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `EntityForging`, the contract inherits OZ  `Pausable` functionality but does not initialize `pause()` and `unpause()` externally as they are internal functions.

## Proof of Concept

OZ implementation:

https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol#L103-106
```
  function _pause() internal virtual whenNotPaused {
        _paused = true;
        emit Paused(_msgSender());
    }
```

https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol#L115-118
```
function _unpause() internal virtual whenPaused {
        _paused = false;
        emit Unpaused(_msgSender());
    }
```

The contract `EntityForging` only implements `whenNotPaused` modifier:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L70

But it cannot be practically used as there are no functions that would pause and unpause the contract.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement external `pause()` and `unpause()`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L116


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `TraitForgeNft` contract, there is a function called `setMaxGeneration()` that allows the owner to set the maximum generation. It  checks whether the new max generation is greater or equal to the current generation. The problem is that the new max generation can be bypassed by forging if it's set to the current generation.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the `setMaxGeneration()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L114-120
```
 function setMaxGeneration(uint maxGeneration_) external onlyOwner {
    require(
      maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration,
      "can't below than current generation"
    );
    maxGeneration = maxGeneration_;
  }

```

The crucial part here is that the function checks whether the new max generation is greater or equal to the current generation. However, if there are tokens that were already created by forging - they would simply be in a disallowed generation:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L166
```
require(newGeneration <= maxGeneration, "can't be over max generation");
```
`forge()` correctly checks for the new max generation but the problem is that there can already be forged tokens in the new generation from the current generation. Even if there are not, users can just front-run setting `setMaxGeneration()` and create tokenIds in a new generation. This would put protocol in an unexpected state where there are existing entities that are effectively above the maximum allowed generation.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reconsider the logic regarding forging and when it's allowed. Or the simplest solution is just to remove `setMaxGeneration()` so the maximum generation would be hardcoded.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L351


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `TraitForgeNft`, users are able to directly mint entities via `mintToken()` and `mintWithBudget()` and by forging two tokenIds (merger's and forger's). So when it's a direct minting, the `generationMintCounts` is increased for current generation. And if the max tokens per generation state is reached, it's incremented to the next generation. In comparison, with forging, the tokenId of the new entity is in the next generation. The problem is that when we update the generation with direct minting via `_incrementGeneration()`, `generationMintCounts` is nullified and it does not account for already existing entities resulted from forging.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at this part of `_mintInternal()` and `incrementGeneration()`:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280-283
```
  function _mintInternal(address to, uint256 mintPrice) internal {
    if (generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen) {
      _incrementGeneration();
    }
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L345-351
```
  function _incrementGeneration() private {
    require(
      generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen,
      'Generation limit not yet reached'
    );
    currentGeneration++;
    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
```

In comparison, when user wants to forge and create a new entity via it, `generationMintCounts` is incremented for the next generation:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L328
```
generationMintCounts[gen]++;
```

So imagine there are already new entities that are derived from forging in the new generation. The `generationMintCounts` is correctly increased for them the first time. But when the generation is changed through direct minting, the variable is simply nullified and it reflects the incorrect value. This would put the contract in an unexpected state where the number of the variable does not correspond to reality.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Check for already existing tokens from forging when updating generation in `_incrementGeneration()`.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L191


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `NukeFund` contract, the token age is determined in `calculateAge()` and `canTokenBeNuked()` functions. However, in both cases different functions are used which should not be the case and can be considered as unexpected behavior and inconsistency.


## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the `calculateAge()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L121-125
```
 uint256 daysOld = (block.timestamp -
      nftContract.getTokenCreationTimestamp(tokenId)) /
      60 /
      60 /
      24;

```

In this case, `getTokenCreationTimestamp()` is used while in `canTokenBeNuked()` it's `getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L190-191
```
 uint256 tokenAgeInSeconds = block.timestamp -
      nftContract.getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp(tokenId)

```

This is a deviation from the expected behavior as `getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp()` would calculate completely different age based on when the token was last transferred and not when it was created

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use `getTokenCreationTimestamp()` when determining the age of a token in `canTokenBeNuked()` function.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L367


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Currently `TraitForgetNft` contract implements ERC721 functionality. In particular, it's `_beforeTokenTransfer()` hook. The problem is that its implementation deviates from the necessary one and deviates from the standard itself as well. 

## Proof of Concept

Take the look at the `_beforeTokenTransfer()` implementation:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L367-373
```
function _beforeTokenTransfer(
    address from,
    address to,
    uint256 firstTokenId,
    uint256 batchSize
  ) internal virtual override {
    super._beforeTokenTransfer(from, to, firstTokenId, batchSize);
```

The problem is that it should override ERC721 `_beforeTokenTransfer()` which is empty by itself and then implement its own functionality. But it provides this function call to the parent contract with parameter that is not present in it that is `batchSize`:

https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/api/token/erc721#IERC721-safeTransferFrom-address-address-uint256-bytes-


```
_beforeTokenTransfer(address from, address to, uint256 tokenId)
```

This would break composability with ERC721 contract.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Remove `batchSize` parameter from the hook. The function should also override ERC721 and ERC721Pausible.





## Assessed type

Other

brief_summary: The current functionality of `TraitForgeNft` allows users to burn their tokenIds. The only requirement is that the caller should be the owner or approved address. The problem is that the hook only checks for `EntityForging` contract and forgets about `EntityTrading` where users can trade their tokens as well. # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The contract `EntropyGenerator` calculates entropies for the tokens and write them in the batches. There is a separate function - `initializeAlphaIndices` that allows to write the special entropy for every generation with parameters `999999`. However, the function currently has `onlyOwner` modifier which is not correct as the caller should be `TraitForgeNft` contract when the generation is incremented.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at `initializeAlphaIndices()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206
```
 function initializeAlphaIndices() public whenNotPaused onlyOwner
```

It currently has `onlyOwner` modifier. The contract has the following modifier as well that checks whether the caller is `TraitForgeNft` contract:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L25-28
```
  modifier onlyAllowedCaller() {
    require(msg.sender == allowedCaller, 'Caller is not allowed');
    _;
  }
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L30-33
```
constructor(address _traitForgetNft) {
    allowedCaller = _traitForgetNft;
    initializeAlphaIndices();
  }
```

The function is called when incrementing generation in `TraitForgeNft`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L353
```
 entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();
```

This would lead to tx revert as the caller is not the one that's expected.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use `onlyAllowedCaller()` modifier instead of `onlyOwner()`.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the current implementation of `EntityTrading` smart contract, there is an operation of transferring NFT token from the user to the owner when listing NFT on sale. The problem is that the contract does not implement onERC721Received() function which makes it unable to receive ERC721 tokens.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the `listNFTForSale()` functionality:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53
```
nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId); // trasnfer NFT to contract
```

The contract transfers the token from `msg.sender` to `address(this)`. The problem is that the contract does not implement `onERC721Received()` that's necessary to obtain NFT tokens in a smart contract. Moreover, the contract uses `transferFrom()` instead of `safeTransferFrom()` which is necessary for safe NFT transfers (it checks if the contract implements `onERC721Received()`):

https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/api/token/erc721#IERC721-safeTransferFrom-address-address-uint256-bytes-
```
If to refers to a smart contract, it must implement IERC721Receiver.onERC721Received, which is called upon a safe transfer.

```

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement onERC721Received() and use `safeTransferFrom()` instead of `transferFrom()` for ERC721 token transfer.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L208


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Currently `EntropyGenerator` uses `blockhash` and `block.number` to generate some pseudo-random entropies. The problem is that it also uses them to generate the best entropy that's possible to obtain with `999999` feature. And as `blockhash` and `block.number` are pretty predictable values and can be gained by validators - it makes the whole process unfair towards other participants.


## Proof of Concept

`initializeAlphaIndices` uses `blockhash` and `block.number` to determine slot index selection and number index selection point of `999999` entropy:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L207-209
```
 uint256 hashValue = uint256(
      keccak256(abi.encodePacked(blockhash(block.number - 1), block.timestamp))
    );
```

The problem is that these values can be known by validators beforehand and hence their slot index selection point and number index selection point can be easily determined:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L211-215
```
  uint256 slotIndexSelection = (hashValue % 258) + 512;
    uint256 numberIndexSelection = hashValue % 13;

    slotIndexSelectionPoint = slotIndexSelection;
    numberIndexSelectionPoint = numberIndexSelection;

```

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use Chainlink VRF services or some alternative source of randomness.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L152


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `EntropyGenerator` smart contract, there is a `nukeFactor` value that determines how much of nuke fund a user can claim after some delay. The problem is that it's not calculated the same way as it's done in the docs and it creates inconsistency as it deviates from the spec.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at `deriveTokenParameters()` functionality:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L152
```
  nukeFactor = entropy / 4000000;
```

From the docs:

```
Entropy /40 = initalNukeFactor
```

So it creates a deviation from the spec and will calculate an incorrect value.

## Tools Used

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L168
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L102


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Inside of `EntropyGenerator` smart contract, there are two functions that are used to get entopies: `getEntropy()` and `getNextEntropy()`. The problem is that they check for incorrect max slot index at the start of the function which may result in an unexpected behavior.

## Proof of Concept

There are only 770 slots designed to store 78 digit numbers (with 13 concatenated entropies in them). And the first slot has always index 0. That basically means that the last slot will have the index of 769. But in the current implementation of `EntropyGenerator`, it checks for 770 instead of 769:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L102
```
  function getNextEntropy() public onlyAllowedCaller returns (uint256) {
    require(currentSlotIndex <= maxSlotIndex, 'Max slot index reached.');
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L168

```
  function getEntropy(
    uint256 slotIndex,
    uint256 numberIndex
  ) private view returns (uint256) {
    require(slotIndex <= maxSlotIndex, 'Slot index out of bounds.');
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L17
```
uint256 private maxSlotIndex = 770;
```

This check basically allows to get entropies for more slots than there are in existence and it can potentially result in an unexpected behavior and DoS.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Replace the check above on this:

```
 require(currentSlotIndex < maxSlotIndex, 'Max slot index reached.');
```


## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L88


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `listForForging` function in the `EntityForging` contract allows the owner of a token, specifically a forger entity, to list it for forging. It [checks](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L88) if the forging counts did not exceed the forge potential. However, the check is incorrect:
```solidity
function listForForging(
  uint256 tokenId,
  uint256 fee
) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
  // ...
  uint256 entropy = nftContract.getTokenEntropy(tokenId); // Retrieve entropy for tokenId
  uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
  require(
    forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential, // @audit Wrong check
    'Entity has reached its forging limit'
  );

  // ...
}
```
The check `forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential` is incorrect because it allows the forger to forge one additional time beyond the forge potential. This happens because the `forgingCounts[tokenId]` is incremented only after the  [the merge occurs in `forgeWithListed` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L133). Therefore, the check does not account for the current forging transaction. This can occur for every token held by the forger.

## Proof Of Concept
Consider the following example:
- Entity `A` with the forger role has a forge potential of `1` and owns tokenId `1`.
- Entity `A` lists its token for forging by calling `listForForging`. Notice that `forgingCounts[1]` is NOT incremented at this stage.
- Entity `B` with the merger role calls `forgeWithListed` to merge the previously listed token. During this transaction, `forgingCounts[1]` [is incremented]((https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L133)). At this point, entity `A` should have consumed all its forge potential.
- Entity `A` attempts to list its tokenId `1` for forging again by calling `listForForging`. The check that verifies if entity `A` has consumed its forge potential will pass, even though it should not:
  ```solidity
  require(forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential, 'Entity has reached its forging limit');
  ```
  This is because `forgingCounts[1]` equals `1`, and `forgePotential` equals to `1`, so `1<=1`.
- Entity `B` with the merger role calls `forgeWithListed` to merge the previously listed token.

Entity `A` could forge its token id one additional time beyond its forge potential.
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider updating the previous check to the following:
```diff
```diff
 require(forgePotential > 0 && 
- forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential
+ forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential
 , 'Entity has reached its forging limit');
```
```








## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L56
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L76


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Entropy is stored in `uint256` slots, with each slot able to contain 13 concatenated entropies. Entropies are generated in three passes, and there is a *golden entropy* value `999999` that should not be generated in the first two passes, [as specified in the documentation](https://github.com/TraitForge/GitBook/blob/main/GamePlay/Entropy.md#entropy):
> There is a certain entropy, “999999” which is referred to as “the Golden God”, since it has perfect parameters and will exceed all other entities if played correctly. **The Golden God is scanned for and is kept out of the first 2 passes**, but is deliberately set in the final pass (at some random point)

The issue is that [writeEntropyBatch1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L56) and [writeEntropyBatch2](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L76) functions do not correctly check for the golden entropy:
```solidity
function writeEntropyBatch1() public {
    require(lastInitializedIndex < batchSize1, 'Batch 1 already initialized.');

    uint256 endIndex = lastInitializedIndex + batchSize1; // calculate the end index for the batch
    unchecked {
      for (uint256 i = lastInitializedIndex; i < endIndex; i++) {
        uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
          keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
        ) % uint256(10) ** 78; // generate a  pseudo-random value using block number and index
        require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.'); // @audit INCORRECT check
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue; // store the value in the slots array
      }
    }
    lastInitializedIndex = endIndex;
  }
```
The function(same for `writeEntropyBatch2`) attempts to ensure that no golden entropy is generated using the following check: `require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');`. However, this check is incorrect because `pseudoRandomValue` does NOT represent a *single* entropy value but **represents the entire slot value, which contains 13 entropies**. For example, if the pseudo-randomly generated slot value is `........999999123345`, the check will pass while it should not because the second entropy is a golden one.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The current check incorrectly validates the entire slot value. Consider updating the check to validate each of the 13 entropies within the slot value.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L182


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Entity holders can claim a part of the `Nuke` fund by *nuking* their entity via [nuke function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L182). The amount claimable depends on the nuke factor of the entity and the funds held by the contract. The issue is that the function does not protect users from slippage between the moment the transaction is created and the moment it is executed. As a result, users might not receive the funds they expected for the NFT they burned.

## Proof Of Concept
Consider the following example:
1. `NukeFund`'s balance is `5 ETH`
2. Alice with entity A of `50%` nuke factor initializes transaction to nuke her entity, expecting to receive `2.5 ETH`
3. At the same time, Bob with entity B of `40%` nuke factor initializes transaction to nuke his entity, expecting to receive `2 ETH`.
4. Bob's transaction is executed first and receives `2 ETH` as expected. The contract's fund becomes `3 ETH`. 
5. Alice's transaction is executed after and receives `1.5 ETH`.

Alice burned her NFT expecting to receive `2.5 ETH` but received `1.5 ETH`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider allowing players to introduce a minimum claimable amount and revert the transaction if the claimable funds are below the minimum. Below is a suggestion for updated code for the `nuke` function:
```diff
function nuke(
  uint256 tokenId
+ uint256 minimumClaim
) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    require(
      nftContract.isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId),
      'ERC721: caller is not token owner or approved'
    );
    require(
      nftContract.getApproved(tokenId) == address(this) ||
        nftContract.isApprovedForAll(msg.sender, address(this)),
      'Contract must be approved to transfer the NFT.'
    );
    require(canTokenBeNuked(tokenId), 'Token is not mature yet');

    uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
    uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
    uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size

    // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
    uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
      : potentialClaimAmount;
+   require(claimAmount >= minimumClaim, "Claimable amount is below the minimum);
    fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund

    nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
    (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
    require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');

    emit Nuked(msg.sender, tokenId, claimAmount); // Emit the event with the actual claim amount
    emit FundBalanceUpdated(fund); // Update the fund balance
  }
```


## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The following contracts in scope: `DevFund`, `EntityForging`, `EntityTrading`, `EntropyGenerator`, `NukeFund`, `TraitForgeNft` are supposed to be pausable (as they all inherit from `Pausable`), but they don't implement the external pause/unpause functionalities which means it will never be possible to pause them.

The OpenZeppelin `Pausable` contract contains internal functions (`_pause` and `_unpause`) to manage the paused state of the contract. Any contract inheriting Pausable **MUST** implement external functions that call these internal functions to enable pausing and unpausing.

## Tools used
Manual Review

Add public/external pause and unpause functions in the mentioned contracts to enable their pausable functionality. This can be done as shown in the example below:
```solidity
function pause() external onlyOwner {
  _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
  _unpause();
}
```

// EntityForgin::forgeWithListed

uint256 nukeFundContribution = (msg.value * taxCut) / 100; // EntityTrading::buyNFT

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L345-L355


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- `_incrementGeneration` function is called when maximum token per generation is minted and need to start minting new generation token.
- Here `maxTokensPerGen` is 10000 that means every generation has 10000 NFTs to mint and after that new generation is start.
- But when user forge the NFT of 1st generation then user will get NFT of 2nd generation.
- That means when 1st generation NFTs are minted in normal mint at the same time there will be some NFTs of 2nd generation by forging of NFT of 1st gen.
- Now, when 1st gen's 10000 NFTs will be minted, `_incrementGeneration` function will be called which sets `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0`.
- That means 2nd gen count will start from 0 but in actual case there are already other NFTs are minted by forging 1st gen NFTs.
- Due to which every gen has 10000 NFTs to mint statement will be proven wrong and every gen can have more NFTs than 10000.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
 function _incrementGeneration() private {
    require(
      generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen,
      'Generation limit not yet reached'
    );
    currentGeneration++;
@>    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
    priceIncrement = priceIncrement + priceIncrementByGen;
    entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();
    emit GenerationIncremented(currentGeneration);
  }
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L193-L197
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L67-L73


# Vulnerability details


## Description

The `EntityForging` contract manages the listing and forging of tokens. It utilizes two key mappings: `listings` to store listing information and `listedTokenIds` to track which tokens are listed. The `listForForging()` function allows users to list their tokens for forging, while `_cancelListingForForging()` is used to cancel listings.

The issue arises in the `_cancelListingForForging()` function. When a listing is cancelled, the function correctly removes the listing from the `listings` mapping:

[EntityForging.sol#L193-L197](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L193-L197)
```solidity
File: EntityForging.sol
193:   function _cancelListingForForging(uint256 tokenId) internal {
194:     delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];
195: 
196:     emit CancelledListingForForging(tokenId); // Emitting with 0 fee to denote cancellation
197:   }

```

However, it fails to update the `listedTokenIds` mapping. This creates an inconsistent state where `listedTokenIds[tokenId]` still points to a now-deleted listing.

The problem manifests when a user attempts to re-list a previously cancelled token. The `listForForging()` function checks if a token is already listed:

[EntityForging.sol#L67-L73](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L67-L73)
```solidity
File: EntityForging.sol
67:   function listForForging(
68:     uint256 tokenId,
69:     uint256 fee
70:   ) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
71:     Listing memory _listingInfo = listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];
72: 
73:     require(!_listingInfo.isListed, 'Token is already listed for forging');

         // ... rest of the function
}
```

Due to the inconsistent state, this check will incorrectly identify the token as still listed, preventing the user from re-listing their token.

## Impact
The inconsistent state caused by not updating `listedTokenIds` can prevent users from re-listing their tokens after cancellation, leading to a poor user experience and potential loss of functionality. It can also create confusion in the contract state, making it difficult to track active listings accurately.


## Proof of Concept
1. Alice lists her token (ID: 1) for forging:
   - `listForForging(1, 1 ether)` is called
   - `listings[1]` is set with Alice's listing info
   - `listedTokenIds[1]` is set to 1

2. Alice decides to cancel her listing:
   - `cancelListingForForging(1)` is called, which internally calls `_cancelListingForForging(1)`
   - `listings[1]` is deleted
   - `listedTokenIds[1]` remains set to 1

3. Alice tries to re-list her token:
   - `listForForging(1, 2 ether)` is called
   - The function checks `listings[listedTokenIds[1]]`
   - Despite the listing being deleted, `listedTokenIds[1]` still points to index 1
   - The function incorrectly determines the token is already listed and reverts

4. Alice is now unable to re-list her token for forging

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the `_cancelListingForForging()` function to also reset the `listedTokenIds` mapping:

```diff
function _cancelListingForForging(uint256 tokenId) internal {
    delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];
+   delete listedTokenIds[tokenId];
    emit CancelledListingForForging(tokenId);
}
```

This change ensures that both `listings` and `listedTokenIds` are consistently updated when a listing is cancelled, allowing users to re-list their tokens as intended.


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L184-L194


# Vulnerability details

## Description

The `NukeFund` contract implements a mechanism to prevent premature "nuking" (burning for a claim) of tokens through the `canTokenBeNuked()` function. This function is designed to ensure that a token has been held for a minimum period before it can be nuked. However, the current implementation has a flaw that allows users to bypass this restriction.

The `canTokenBeNuked()` function relies on the `getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp()` method from the `nftContract` to determine the token's holding period. It calculates the token's age by subtracting this timestamp from the current block timestamp:

[NukeFund.sol#L184-L194](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L184-L194)
```solidity
File: NukeFund.sol
184:   function canTokenBeNuked(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (bool) {
185:     // Ensure the token exists
186:     require(
187:       nftContract.ownerOf(tokenId) != address(0),
188:       'ERC721: operator query for nonexistent token'
189:     );
190:     uint256 tokenAgeInSeconds = block.timestamp -
191:       nftContract.getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp(tokenId);
192:     // Assuming tokenAgeInSeconds is the age of the token since it's holding the nft, check if it's over minimum days held
193:     return tokenAgeInSeconds >= minimumDaysHeld;
194:   }

```

The issue lies in the fact that this method only considers the most recent transfer, rather than the cumulative holding period. As a result, users can reset the holding period by transferring the token to another address and then back to themselves, effectively bypassing the minimum holding period requirement.

## Impact
Users can bypass the minimum holding period by transferring the token multiple times within a short period. This allows them to "nuke" the token and claim funds from the contract without adhering to the required holding period. This undermines the intended functionality of the contract and can lead to unfair advantages and potential financial losses for the protocol.


## Proof of Concept
1. Alice mints or acquires a token.
2. Alice waits for a period shorter than `minimumDaysHeld`.
3. Alice transfers the token to Bob (who could be a separate account controlled by Alice).
4. Bob immediately transfers the token back to Alice.
5. The `getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp()` is now updated to the time of the last transfer.
6. Alice can now successfully call `canTokenBeNuked()`, as the function will only consider the time since the last transfer.
7. Alice can proceed to nuke the token, bypassing the intended holding period.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To address this issue, the contract should track the cumulative holding time for each token, rather than relying solely on the last transfer timestamp. 


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L64-L81
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L14-L15


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The`writeEntropyBatch2` function uses an incorrect calculation for the `endIndex`, which could lead to the function not being able to initialize all intended slots in the second batch or the function may attempt to initialize more slots than necessary, leading to higher gas consumption.


## Proof of Concept
The `endIndex` in the [`writeEntropyBatch2` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L64-L81) is calculated like this`:

```solidity
uint256 endIndex = lastInitializedIndex + batchSize1;
```

This calculation is incorrect because `lastInitializedIndex` is already at 256 after the first batch and `batchSize1` is 256. While this would result in a correct `endIndex` being set to 512 in this context, but let's assume `batchSize1` is changed to 128 change, only 256 would be initialized in `writeEntropyBatch2` instead of the intended 512 slots.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace the current line:

```solidity
uint256 endIndex = lastInitializedIndex + batchSize1;
```

with:

```solidity
uint256 endIndex = batchSize2;
```

This will ensure that the second batch correctly initializes slots up to the 512th slot (index 511), regardless of the value of `lastInitializedIndex`.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L64-L66

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Executing the `claim` function, by a developer, completely depletes the contract's funds each time, resulting in significant financial losses and disruption of intended fund distribution among developers.

## Proof of Concept
In the `DevFund` contract, the `claim` function improperly calculates the distribution of funds by multiplying the weight value by the total amount of funds raised, instead of dividing it. This leads to the entire contract balance being transferred to the caller on each execution.

Scenario illustrating the issue:
1. The owner calls `addDev` with userA and weight of 100.
2. The owner calls `addDev` with userB and weight of 300.
3. The contract receives 1 ETH, updating `totalRewardDebt` to 1 ETH.
4. userA calls `claim` with weight 100, resulting in:
    
`pending = info.pendingRewards +
          (totalRewardDebt - info.rewardDebt) *
          info.weight;
 `

Calculation: 

`pending = 0 + (1 ETH - 0) * 100 = 100 ETH`

This results in an attempted transfer of 100 ETH to userA, depleting the contract’s 1 ETH balance.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Adjust the `claim` function to divide the amount by `info.weight` instead of multiplying, ensuring proportional distribution of funds.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L158-L159

# Vulnerability details

##Impact

A potential vulnerability exists where malicious contracts set as `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller` can disrupt the intended functionality of the `forgeWithListed` and `buyNFT` functions. This can lead to significant financial and operational impacts for users.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Malicious Contract Assignment:** A malicious contract is intentionally set as the `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller`.
2. **Transaction Manipulation:** The malicious contract has custom logic in its fallback or receive function to specifically revert transactions. This occurs when certain game conditions aren't met from the malicious contract's perspective.
3. **User Transaction Interception:** A user attempts to utilize the `forgeWithListed` or `buyNFT` functions, leading to the transfer of funds to the malicious contract.
4. **Conditional Transaction Reversion:** The malicious contract evaluates the game state. If the conditions it seeks is at its advantage by not accepting the trade, it can deliberately reverts the transaction it receives.
5. **Function Failure:** Due to the reverted transaction, the `.call` method used within `forgeWithListed` or `buyNFT` fails. The subsequent `require` statement encounters this failure, causing the entire user transaction to revert.

This chain of events effectively prevents the execution of `forgeWithListed` and `buyNFT` functions under these circumstances, hindering the game's intended flow. This situation can lead to financial losses (as user lose funds for gas) and diminished user trust in the platform's reliability.

The vulnerability arises from the reliance on the `.call` method, which requires successful execution by the recipient contract. If the recipient is malicious, it has the ability to disrupt the transaction flow by reverting.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this risk, it's recommended to enhance the contract's ability to handle potential reverts from the receiving contracts. This can be achieved through two methods:

1. **Try/Catch Mechanism:** Implementing a try/catch block around the `.call` method allows for graceful handling of reverts by the recipient.
2. **Revert Handling Logic:** Modifying the core contract logic to manage reverts in a way that doesn't automatically revert the entire user transaction.

By implementing one or both of these recommendations, the contract can become more resilient against malicious `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller` contracts, ensuring a smoother user experience.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A vulnerability exists in the `forgeWithListed` function within the `EntityForging.sol` contract. The function fails to handle situations where the user sends additional `msg.value` (ether) exceeding the required amount for forging. This leads to user funds becoming locked indefinitely within the contract, inaccessible by the user, other entities, or even the contract owner. This can result in permanent financial loss for users as retrieving the excess funds becomes impossible.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Forging Listing:** A forger is listed with a price of 0.1 ETH.
2. **Excess Payment:** A user selects this forger to forge with but sends 0.3 ETH instead of the required 0.1 ETH.
3. **Unhandled Excess:** The `forgeWithListed` function only processes the necessary 0.1 ETH for forging. However, the remaining 0.2 ETH remains trapped within the contract.


The `forgeWithListed` function lacks the logic to manage excess `msg.value` provided by users. This additional value isn't refunded or returned to the user, leading to their funds being locked indefinitely.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this risk, it's imperative to implement logic within the `forgeWithListed` function that handles potential excess `msg.value`. This can be achieved by:

1. **Calculating Excess:** Determine the difference between the received `msg.value` and the actual forging cost.
2. **Refunding Excess:** Utilize a mechanism like `.call` or a secure alternative to transfer the calculated excess amount back to the user's address.

By implementing this solution, the `forgeWithListed` function ensures that only the required amount for forging is used, while any additional funds are safely returned to the user, preventing unintended fund locking.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L211-L212


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

An issue exists where the "The Golden God" entropy value (999,999) might be inadvertently excluded from a specific generation. This could alter the intended rarity and value distribution within the game mechanics, potentially affecting user motivation to mint NFTs from that generation.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Entropy Generation Misalignment:** The `maxSlotIndex` and `currentNumberIndex` configuration generates 10,010 entropies (770 x 13) as opposed to the intended 10,000 for a generation.
2. **Excess Entropy Generation:** This results in the `getNextEntropy` function providing 10,010 entropies before resetting to a new generation instead of the expected 10,000.
3. **"The Golden God" Exclusion:** The `initializeAlphaIndices` function assigns the slot for the "The Golden God" value (999,999) potentially beyond the 10,000th index of the `entropySlots` array.
4. **Misplaced Storage:** If the chosen slot falls within the last 10 indices (10,001 to 10,010), the "The Golden God" value gets stored for the following generation, effectively excluding it from the current one.


The discrepancy between the number of generated entropies (10,010) and the intended generation size (10,000) combined with the storage location selection for the "The Golden God" value leads to its potential omission from a generation.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
**Adjust Slot Selection:** Refine the `initializeAlphaIndices` function to ensure the slot chosen for "The Golden God" value falls within the valid range for the current generation (maximum of 10,000 index).

By implementing this recommendations, the "The Golden God" entropy value gets correctly included in each generation, maintaining the intended rarity and value distribution within the game's mechanics.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A vulnerability exists in the `TraitForgeNft` contract. Forging NFTs with the same parent ID can be exploited by malicious users to trigger multiple invocations of the `nuke` function, leading to repeated withdrawals from the `NukeFund.sol` contract. This poses a significant risk of draining the `NukeFund` and disrupting the game's economic balance.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Preparation for Exploit:** A malicious user acquires multiple NFTs using different accounts.
2. **Repeated Forging:** The attacker uses these NFTs to forge new ones repeatedly across their accounts until reaching the maximum `ForgePotential`.
3. **Shared Nuke Factor:** Since the forgings utilize the same parent IDs, the resulting NFTs share the same `NukeFactor`.
4. **Exploiting Cooldown:** After the minimum holding period for the NFTs passes, the attacker can "nuke" (withdraw funds) from all NFTs concurrently due to their identical `NukeFactor`.

This coordinated action triggers numerous withdrawals from the `NukeFund.sol` contract. Depending on the number of forged NFTs, this exploit can potentially deplete the entire `NukeFund`.


The current system allows forging NFTs with identical parent IDs. This enables attackers to exploit the shared `NukeFactor` and trigger repeated withdrawals, jeopardizing the financial stability of the `NukeFund.sol` contract.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this risk, it's essential to implement one or both of the following measures:

1. **Prevent Duplicate Forging:** Implement a mechanism to prevent the forging of NFTs with the same parent IDs. This ensures variation and prevents malicious exploitation of shared `NukeFactor` values.
2. **Cooldown on Parent IDs:** Introduce a cooldown period after forging an NFT with a specific parent ID. This cooldown restricts the ability to re-forge using that parent ID within a designated timeframe, making it harder for attackers to rapidly exploit the system.

By implementing these recommendations, the vulnerability is addressed, and the risk of draining the `NukeFund.sol` contract through repetitive forging with the same parent IDs is mitigated.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A critical vulnerability exists that allows the creation of more NFTs per generation than intended. The current system fails to enforce the 10,000 NFT cap per generation, potentially leading to an oversupply of NFTs. This can significantly disrupt the game's economic balance and devalue individual NFTs due to exceeding the planned scarcity.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Initial Minting:** Minting begins for generation 1, and the `generationMintCounts[1]` variable keeps track of minted NFTs for this generation.
2. **Forging NFTs:** The `forgeWithListed` function is used with two generation 1 NFTs, resulting in a generation 2 NFT. The `generationMintCounts[2]` variable is incremented accordingly.
3. **Generation Cap Reached:** After 10,000 generation 1 NFTs are minted, the `_incrementGeneration` function is triggered.
4. **Unintended Reset:** This function performs the following actions:

   `
   currentGeneration++;`
   `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
   `

   Crucially, it resets `generationMintCounts` for generation 2 to zero, effectively disregarding all previously minted generation 2 NFTs.

The issue arises from the way the `_incrementGeneration` function resets the `generationMintCounts` array. It doesn't account for the existing mints in the current generation, leading to an inaccurate representation of the total minted NFTs. This allows for the creation of more NFTs than intended in subsequent generations. 

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To address this vulnerability and enforce the 10,000 NFT cap per generation, the `_incrementGeneration` function needs modification:

1. **Track Total Mints:** Instead of resetting the current generation's `generationMintCounts` to zero, accumulate the total mints from the previous generation. This can be achieved by adding the value of `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration]` to the corresponding entry for the new generation.
2. **Enforce Cap:** Implement a check within the minting logic to ensure the total number of minted NFTs (including forged ones) doesn't exceed the 10,000 cap before allowing further minting for the current generation.

By implementing these recommendations, the intended 10,000 NFT cap per generation is enforced. This ensures a balanced NFT economy within the game and maintains the perceived value of individual NFTs by adhering to the planned scarcity.

Manual Review

  }

  }

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
As per current implementation of `TraitForgeNft` contract, 
each generation is only supposed to hold a maximum of 10000 NFTs.

`generationMintCounts[]` is the critical mapping 
used to track the number of NFTs minted in a particular generation 


This mapping is designed to be incremented parallelly
by two different functions as follows

1. Minting via `_mintInternal`

		Only mints NFTs in the currentGeneration.

2. Minting via _mintNewEntity:

		Can mint NFTs in subsequent generations as well, 
		even when the currentGeneration is still lower.

The issue arises from the following statement in the `_incrementGeneration` function, 

```
generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;

```
which resets this count to 0, 
potentially overwriting a non-zero count.


## Impact

Number of NFTs minted in subsequent generations 
will exceed the intended maximum limit per generation.

## Proof of Concept

Example Scenario

1. Generation 1 (currentGeneration = 1) has maxTokensPerGen = 10000.

2. `_mintNewEntity` mints some NFTs for generation 2 thru forging, 
		incrementing generationMintCounts[2].

3. When generationMintCounts[1] reaches 10000 through `_mintInternal`, 
		`_incrementGeneration` is called.

4. `_incrementGeneration` resets generationMintCounts[2] to 0, 
		losing the count of NFTs already minted in generation 2.

The same loss of count could happen for subsequent generations as well.

## Tools Used

Foundry, Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One possible mitigaton is to remove the redundant reset statement
```
 generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
```
there's no need to explicitly set it. 
This solution maintains the integrity of the mint counts across generations, 
even when forging occurs in subsequent generations.

# Vulnerability details

## vulnerability summary
Forging potential determines the number of times 
a token can forge in an year.

When forging new NFTs thru `forgeWithListed` function,
It is required that both parents belong to the same generation.

```
require(
      nftContract.getTokenGeneration(mergerTokenId) ==
        nftContract.getTokenGeneration(forgerTokenId),
      'Invalid token generation'
      );
```
The following statement calculates the generation of the new entity, 
which is one more than the generation of the parent1 (forger).

```
uint256 newGeneration = getTokenGeneration(parent1Id) + 1;
```

After which the `_mintNewEntity` function has the following condition 
to restrict minting new entities 
beyond the allowed `maxTokensPerGen` which is set to 10000.

```

require(
      generationMintCounts[gen] < maxTokensPerGen,
      'Exceeds maxTokensPerGen'
       );
```
However, when the calculated `newGeneration` is less than the `currentGeneration`,   
the `newGeneration` would already be at full capacity of 10000 tokens.

In such cases, Even if the parentIDs have Forging potential, 
all forging attempts will be reverted forever.

## Impact

Further forging attempts from parent IDs of older generations 
could be blocked even if they have forging potential.

## Proof of Concept

1. Initial State
```
currentGeneration = 3
Generation 1 has 10,000 tokens (at max capacity)
Generation 2 has 10,000 tokens (at max capacity)
Generation 3 has 5,000 tokens.
```
2. Forging Scenario

Assume an attempt to forge a new entity thru `forgeWithListed`
using `forgerTokenId` and `mergerTokenId`, both of which belong to Generation 1.

The function attempts to mint a new NFT in Generation 2. 

Since `generationMintCounts[2] = 10000`, 
which is already at the maximum token limit for Generation 2, 
the require statement in `_mintNewEntity` reverts 
```

require(
      generationMintCounts[gen] < maxTokensPerGen,
      'Exceeds maxTokensPerGen'
       );
```

## Tools Used

Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To address this, 
we need to ensure that forging can occur 
without hitting the token limit of intermediate generations. 

```
while (generationMintCounts[newGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen) {       
	        newGeneration++;
	}
    
require(newGeneration <= maxGeneration, "can't be over max generation");    
```

One approach is to modify the `newGeneration` calculation inside the `forge` function
to ensure that if the `newGeneration` is already full, 
it increments the `newGeneration` until it finds 
an available slot in subsequent generations without exceeding the `maxGeneration`.

According to the docs

```
TraitForge has a unique visual Entity system. 
It consists of generational progression, 
colour variation through maturity

### entropy: 123456
Entropy[1] = varOptions1 && Role
Entropy[2] = varOptions2
Entropy[3] = varOptions3 && colorOptions3
Entropy[4] = varOptions4 && colorOptions4
Entropy[5] = colorOptions5 && color2

Entropy = initalNukeFactor
Entropy % 10 = performanceFactor
Entropy % 3 ? 0 == Role
```
This means,
Entropies decide the traits and visual attributes of an Entity.
Same entropy values results in same NFTs.

Entropy value is obtained in 2 ways 
1. During direct minting thru a randomized process from `EntropyGenerator` 
2. During forging by taking the average of the parentIDs' Entropies

```
    uint256 newEntropy = (forgerEntropy + mergerEntropy) / 2;

```


So its important that every new entropy is unique.

However, due to the design of the forging mechanism 
and the way newEntropy is calculated as an average of 2 ParentIDs.

It is easier for users to deterministically mint the offspring entropies.
Some desirable entropies will be forged multiple times 
resulting in batches of several entities having 
the same parents, same traits & visual attribiutes. 


## Impact

Multiple Entities could be minted with same entropies while forging. 
This results in several entities having same traits and visuals.

## Proof of Concept

1. Lets assume Alice holds a Forger Entity and a merger Entity in 2 different addresess.
```
Forger Entropy = 100035 (forgePotential = 3)
Merger Entropy = 500141 (forgePotential = 4)
```
2. When forged 
```
the resulting Child's Entropy = ( 100005 + 898163 ) / 2 = 300088
(forgePotential = 8)
(Performance factor = 8)
```
3. Now Alice could forge 3 times using the same parents every year
   producing 3 similar entities.

4. Consider the fact that the same entropy could also be obtained 
   by different combination of parentIDs. 
```
for example 
ForgerEntropy = 100002
MergerEntropy = 500174

also results in ChildEntropy = 300088
```

Manual Analysis

                            parentEntropy2,

                     ));

## Vulnerability details

Even though the airdrop contract itself is out of scope for this audit,
the fairness of airdrop distribution still relies on the

```
if (!airdropContract.airdropStarted()) {
      airdropContract.addUserAmount(to, entropyValue);
}
```
Similarly, in the context of airdrops,
when NFTs are transferred / bought thru secondary sales,
it is important to ensure that the current owners are added to the airdrop contract.

It could be argued that every current owner is an active partcipant of the protocol, 
and is more entitled to the governance token (aka airdrop) than the previous owner. 
 
By not updating the latest owners to the airdrop contract, 
new owners might miss out on their rewards, 
and previous owners might receive rewards they are no longer eligible for.

## Impact

Mishandled ownership updates to Airdrop contract results in 
1. current NFT owners are left with no airdrop rewards.
2. Initial minters are unfairly allocated airdrop rewards even after selling their NFTs.

Manual Review

Although the airdrop distribution logic is out of scope, 
considering fairness of distribution,
Either of the following 2 methods could be adapted.

Method 1 :
   Time-weighted distributed based on the time an user held an NFT.

Method 2 :
    Add the current NFT owners to the airdrop allocation 
	  and remove previous owners during transfers.

Considering the later method is simpler to adapt based on the current implementation,
the following changes could be made.

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

Even though the issue is listed as a 'Low' severity in the 4naly3er report, 
it doesnt mention the scenario by which `taxCut` could be set to 0.

The `taxCut` state variable is used to set the percentage share in the following 3 contracts

1. EntityForging
2. EntityTrading
3. NukeFund

Currently 'taxCut' is set to 10%.
However all 3 contracts have a function to change the 'taxCut' if required
```
function setTaxCut(uint256 _taxCut) external onlyOwner {
    taxCut = _taxCut;
}
```

When the protocol eventually goes into DAO governance in the future,
the community could propose 'taxCut' of 0 in certain contracts.

It is common for projects to operate at 0% royalties in some circumstances. 

But the current implementation is not designed to handle a 'taxCut' value of 0,
as it will cause a panic revert.


## Impact

When the DAO proposes to set the `taxCut` to 0, in the above mentioned contracts
the calculations will cause a panic revert due to division by zero.

## Proof of Concept

   taxCut = 10

Similar logic could be added for the EntityForging & EntityTrading contracts as well.

if (taxCut > 0) {

    remainingFund = msg.value - devShare ;
} else {
    devShare = 0;
    remainingFund = msg.value;
}

fund += remainingFund;
