# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L87-L90
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L133


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
As per the docs
https://github.com/TraitForge/GitBook/blob/main/TraitForger%20Entity/Forge%20Potential%20.md

```
Entities' Forge Potential is determined by the [5] digit in entropy
Each entity may have the ability to forge 0-9 times depending on its Forge Potential.

```
This means an entity with forgePotential of 0 is infertile,
an entity with forgePotential = 1 can forge 1 time an year,
an entity with forgePotential = 2 can forge 2 times an year and so on.

The number of times an enitity forges is tracked in the `forgingCounts` mapping.

This mapping is incremented for both the `forgerTokenId` and `mergerTokenId`
everytime a succesful forging happens thru `forgeWithListed`.

The `forgingCounts[]` of 'mergerTokenIds' is handled correctly.
The increment of `forgingCounts[]` preceeds the condition check.
```
forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++;
    require(mergerForgePotential > 0 &&
		        forgingCounts[mergerTokenId] <= mergerForgePotential,
			      'forgePotential insufficient'
);
```

However, Forger Entities 'forgerTokenId' are able to exceed the forging limit 
due to increment of `forgingCounts[]` happening after the condition check.

The check is made during the `listForForging` call.
But the `forgingCounts[]` mapping is only incremented during `forgeWithListed` call.

This allows the 'Forger Entities' to list one more time than intended.

This results in,
Each Forger entity with non-zero forgingPotential,
having the ability to forge 2-10 times, 
instead of 1-9 times intended by the protocol.


## Impact

As long as Forger Entities have a non-zero forgingPotential, 
the Entity is able to exceed the limit intended by forgingPotential.


## Proof of Concept


Assume a Forger Entity of 
```
   _tokenIds = 123 
   forgingPotential = 1 (extracted from the 5th digit of entropy).
   Initial forgingCounts for tokenId 1 is 0.
```

1. First Listing:

During listing : forgingCounts[123] = 0 
Check: forgingCounts[123] <= forgePotential (0 <= 1) => Pass
During forging :  forgingCounts[123]++ => 1 (during forging)

2. Second Listing:

During listing : forgingCounts[123] = 1 
Check: forgingCounts[123] <= forgePotential (1 <= 1) => Pass
During forging : forgingCounts[123]++ => 2 

3. Third Listing: (Reverts only at the third attempt)

During listing : forgingCounts[123] = 2 (during listing)
Check: forgingCounts[123] < forgePotential (2 <= 1) => Fail
During forging : forging does not proceed.


This shows, 
a forger entity with a forgingPotential of 1 can forge 2 times.
similarly a forger entity with forgingPotential of 9 can forge 10 times.

## Tools Used

Foundry, Manual Analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

This can be fixed in different ways.
The simplest way is to use the '<' instead of the '<=' in the 
`listForForging` condition check.

`forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential`

```
require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
      );
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L199-L206


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

According to the docs
```
 The game has a timestamp from mint 
 that will reset the mapping count back to the [5] digit entropy number 
 once 1 year has been passed in blocks.
```
`_resetForgingCountIfNeeded` is the function used to handle the reset logic.

However , The reset is only calculated from the last time an user listed for forging.
instead of being reset every year

```
function _resetForgingCountIfNeeded(uint256 tokenId) private {
    uint256 oneYear = oneYearInDays;
    if (lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] == 0) {
      lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] = block.timestamp;
    } else if (block.timestamp >= lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] + oneYear) {
      forgingCounts[tokenId] = 0; // Reset to the forge potential
      lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] = block.timestamp;
    }
}
```

An user who owns a merger NFT listsForForging after 300 days day for example 
has to wait for another year before the count is reset

## Impact

Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

## Proof of Concept

1. MINT DATE
	 Bob mints a merger entity on Jan 1st 2024 (with a forgingPotential = 1)

2. Bob waits, so he can forge with an appropriate listing from a forger entity.

3. FIRST FORGE
   Bob finally finds a good listing and proceeds to forge 
   on Dec 26th 2024 (360 days after minting)

This is the timestamp his `lastForgeResetTimestamp[bob]` mapping 
gets updated for the first time.

```
    if (lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] == 0) {
      lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] = block.timestamp;
    }
```
   
4. Now instead of the `forgingCounts[Bob] ` resetting after an year from mint (i.e, Dec 31st 2025), 
   Bob now has to wait another 365 days (till Dec 26th 2025) from the day of his first forge,
   before he could forge again.

   
5. Hence the `forgingCount` doesnt reset every year as the protocol intends. 
   but only resets after an year has passed from the time of every subsequent forging.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reset the forging count every year from the `tokenCreationTimestamps` 
obtained from the `TraitForgeNft` contract.

Math

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L215-L215


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details 

In the `TraitForgeNft` contract, 
the `mintWithBudget` function allows users to mint multiple tokens within a budget.

```
maxGeneration =  10.
maxTokensPerGen = 10,000.
Thus the maximum possible value for `tokenIds` currently is 10000 ×10 = 100,000
```

However, there is an issue with the implementation that restricts the `mintWithBudget` function
to only mint `_tokenIds` upto 10000.

```
 while (budgetLeft >= mintPrice && _tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen) {
```

This condition `_tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen` ensures that 
the minting loop stops once `_tokenIds` reaches 10,000. 

However, `_tokenIds` is a cumulative counter across all generations, 
not just within the current generation.

## Impact

`mintWithBudget` function becomes unusable and 
basically enters a state of DOS beyond `_tokenIds` 10000.

## Proof of Concept


Insert the following test case in a foundry setup 

```
    function testMintWithBudgetRevertsAfter9999() public {
        vm.startPrank(user);
        
        // Initial minting to reach the limit of 9999 tokens
        for (uint i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
            nftContract.mintWithBudget{value: nftContract.calculateMintPrice()}('');
        }
        
        uint256 initialBalance = user.balance;

        // Attempt to mint the 10001st tokenID   
        nftContract.mintWithBudget{value: 1 ether}('');
				
				uint256 finalBalance = user.balance;

				assertEq(finalBalance, initialBalance, 'user refunded');															
				assertEq(nftContract._tokenIds(), 10000, "10001st tokenID not minted") 
    }

```
At this point, 
due to the condition `_tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen`, 
the minting process will stop, 
even though subsequent generations (2 to 10) can still have 10,000 tokens each.

Manual Review, Foundry

Since the following logic is already present in the `_mintInternal` function.
```
    if (generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen) {
      _incrementGeneration();
    }
```
We could ignore the 'mint count per generation' check 
from the while loop condition and modify it as below

```
while (budgetLeft >= mintPrice) {
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The document the forge potential as the 5th digit of entropy: Entropy[4] = colour1 && forgePotential. But in EntropyGenerator::deriveTokenParameters the forge potential was calculated as the first digit of entropy.
According to the document, 10% of the population is infertile from birth, which means 10% of the forgePotential should be zero. Owing to the padding strategy below, if the first digit was chosen as forgePotential, the probability of getting a zero is 0, which was wrong. Still if the fifth digit was chosen, the probability of it being zero is actually (90%+9%)*10%+(1-99%)=10.9% (90% for not having to pad, 9% for having to pad one digit).

```solidity
// EntropyGenerator.sol : 52
        uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
          keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
        ) % uint256(10) ** 78; // generate a  pseudo-random value using block number and index
        require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue; // store the value in the slots array

// EntropyGenerator.sol : 180
    uint256 slotValue = entropySlots[slotIndex]; // slice the required [art of the entropy value
    uint256 entropy = (slotValue / (10 ** (72 - position))) % 1000000; // adjust the entropy value based on the number of digits
    uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));
```

Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct the calculation of forgePotential in deriveTokenParameters

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L19


# Vulnerability details


## Impact
Impact: High, as methods include the whenNotPaused modifier but the contract cannot be paused.

Likelihood: High, as the contracts lack the necessary external functions to pause and unpause, making it certain that the contract can't be paused at all.

## Description
All relevant smart contracts inherit from OpenZeppelin's Pausable contract. However, the _pause and _unpause methods are not exposed externally and thus cannot be called. This results in a situation where methods that use the whenNotPaused modifier cannot actually be paused. This misapplication of the Pausable contract could lead to a false sense of security, as it appears the contracts can be paused, but they cannot.

The affected contracts and their functions are as follows:

`TraitForgeNft.sol` - `startAirdrop()`, `burn()`, `forge()`, `mintToken()`, `mintWithBudget()`

`EntrophyGenerator.sol` - `initializeAlphaIndices()`

`EntityForging.sol` - `listForForging()`, `forgeWithListed()`, `cancelListingForForging()`

`EntityTrading.sol` - `listNFTForSale()`, `buyNFT()`, `cancelListing()`

`DevFund.sol` - `claim()`

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add simple external functions for pausing and unpausing in these contracts, callable by the owner. Below is an example implementation:

```solidity

function pause() external onlyOwner {
    _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
    _unpause();
}

```

By implementing these changes, the contracts can properly utilize the Pausable functionality provided by OpenZeppelin, allowing the owner to pause and unpause contract operations as needed.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L102


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept

Protocol is to deploy on Base network

Protocol allows forging via [Forging.sol#L102](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L102)

When forging there is a need to get the listed NFT's by their Ids.

This then means that this scenario is possible.

- Two different integrators mint & list their NFTs for forging
- NFT A is very rare, as such the owner sets the forge fee to be `1.5 `Ether.
- NFT B is not too rare so the fee is `0.1` Ether.
- They both list their NFTs for forging.
- The forger seeing this attempts to forge NFT A so as to own it.
- A chain reorg happens and the order of transactions is swapped.
- The forger ends up forging the wrong NFT _less rare_, and they end up losing `1.4 ETH` in the process.

## Impact

A chain re-org would make a forger forge the wrong NFT and could even lose funds due to this, since they pay too much for forging and end up forging the wrong NFT.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

When forging the listed tokens consider the forger to indicate the fees of the NFTs they would like to forge, so in our case here even if the re-org happens the tx would revert since the fees wouldn't match.



## Assessed type

Timing

in `forgeWithListed()` and `_distributeFunds()` add a require statement that make sure the `nukeFundAddress != address(0)`.
similar to this check:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`TraitForgeNft.mintWithBudget()` cannot mint new NFTs after `_tokenIds` reaches `maxTokensPerGen`.

## Proof of Concept
The while loop in `mintWithBudget()` checks that `_tokenIds` is less than `maxTokensPerGen`.

```
    while (budgetLeft >= mintPrice && _tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen) {
      _mintInternal(msg.sender, mintPrice);
      amountMinted++;
      budgetLeft -= mintPrice;
      mintPrice = calculateMintPrice();
    }
```
[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L215-L220)

The problem with this is that `_tokenIds` is incremented on every mint [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L285), and `maxTokensPerGen` is a constant declared [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L22).

So, after some time this function will stop being able to mint new NFTs.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`_mintInternal()` already deals with `maxTokensPerGen` limit correctly. So, it should be safe to remove `_tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen` check.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L104


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The use of `transferFrom` method for ERC721 transfer is discouraged and recommended to use safeTransferFrom whenever possible by OpenZeppelin.
This is because transferFrom() cannot check whether the receiving address know how to handle ERC721 tokens.

In the function shown at below, ERC721 token is sent to `msg.sender` with the transferFrom method.

```
function cancelListing(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
  Listing storage listing = listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];

  // check if caller is the seller and listing is acivte
  require(
    listing.seller == msg.sender,
    'Only the seller can canel the listing.'
  );
  require(listing.isActive, 'Listing is not active.');

  nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer the nft back to seller

  delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]]; // mark the listing as inactive or delete it

  emit ListingCanceled(tokenId, msg.sender);
}
```

If this `msg.sender` is a contract and is not aware of incoming `ERC721` tokens, the sent token could be locked up in the contract forever.

Reference: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/api/token/erc721

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

I recommend to call the  `safeTransferFrom()` method instead of `transferFrom()` for NFT transfers.





## Assessed type

ERC721

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L182


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The function `nuke` in the `NukeFund` claims a share of the Nuke Fund by nuking an entity, removing it from the game infinitely.

```
function nuke(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
  require(
    nftContract.isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId),
    'ERC721: caller is not token owner or approved'
  );
  require(
    nftContract.getApproved(tokenId) == address(this) ||
      nftContract.isApprovedForAll(msg.sender, address(this)),
    'Contract must be approved to transfer the NFT.'
  );
  require(canTokenBeNuked(tokenId), 'Token is not mature yet');

  uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
  uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
  uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size

  // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
  uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
    ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
    : potentialClaimAmount;

  fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund

  nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
  (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
  require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');   // @audit does remove the owner control??

  emit Nuked(msg.sender, tokenId, claimAmount); // Emit the event with the actual claim amount
  emit FundBalanceUpdated(fund); // Update the fund balance
}
```

However, after burning the entity and transferring the funds the owner isn't zeroed this allows for unexpected behaviour, like being able to call approve() and call() functions on non-existent tokens.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Reset the approval on transfer.


## Assessed type

ERC721

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L14-L19


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Multiple contracts are using Openzeppelin's `Pausable` module via inheritance, and in those contracts the relevant modifiers like `whenNotPaused` are used, indicating that the dev planned to implement an emergency stop mechanism by using this `Pausable` module. However, the inherited `Pausable` module itself only contains `_pause` and `unpause` internal functions which need to be called by a public/external function (with access control, of course) defined in the child contract. The contracts in this protocol didn't define such functions, so that the whole `Pausable` functionality will not work. Such a discrepancy in the design makes it an Medium severity issue.

## Proof of Concept
Openzeppelin contracts added warnings regarding how to use the `Pausable` module correctly in this [PR#4007](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/pull/4007/files). 

The mistake in this protocol is exactly what those warnings are referring to. Quoted as below:
```
 * IMPORTANT: This contract does not include public pause and unpause functions. In
 * addition to inheriting this contract, you must define both functions, invoking the
 * {Pausable-_pause} and {Pausable-_unpause} internal functions, with appropriate
 * access control, e.g. using {AccessControl} or {Ownable}. Not doing so will
 * make the contract unpausable.
```

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Define a public/external callable function with access control to correctly use the `Pausable` module.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L64-L66
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L45
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This can lead to the complete drain of the contract's funds with each execution of the `claim` function, resulting in significant financial losses for the rest of the developers. Each developer will withdraw the entire contract balance, disrupting the intended distribution of funds and leading to inequities among developers.

In the `DevFund` contract, the owner sets the weight value for each dev to claim their corresponding amount of funds. However, the contract incorrectly multiplies the weight value by the total amount of funds raised in the `claim` function, instead of dividing it. Consequently, each execution of the claim function transfers all the contract's funds to the caller.


## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this, consider the following scenario:
1. The owner calls the addDev function passing userA, and weight equal to 50. 
2. The owner calls the addDev function passing userB, and weight equal to 200. 
3. The contract receives 1 ETH of funds, updating the `totalRewardDebt` to 1 ETH.
4. userA, with a weight of 50, calls the `claim` function. The pending reward is calculated as follows:

`
pending = info.pendingRewards +
      (totalRewardDebt - info.rewardDebt) *
      info.weight;
`

Resulting in `pending = 0 + ( 1 ETH - 0 ) * 50 = 50 ETH`.

As a result, the contract attempts to transfer 100 ETH to userA, which would drain the contract's total funds of 1 ETH.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The contract should divide the amount by `info.weight` instead of multiplying by `info.weight`. This change will ensure that the distribution of funds represents a proportionate share of the total funds.



## Assessed type

ETH-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L158-L159
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L77-L80


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The inability to execute the `forgeWithListed` and `buyNFT` functions can disrupt the normal flow of the game, leading to financial and operational impacts for users. This vulnerability can result in loss of funds, as users are unable to complete transactions, and it can also undermine the trust and reliability of the platform.

## Proof of Concept
Both the `forgeWithListed` function in the `EntityForging.sol` contract and the `buyNFT` function in the `EntityTrading.sol` contract send funds to the `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller` using the `.call` method and require the success result to be true. However, there is the possibility that the `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller` is a malicious contract that will revert the transaction when the funds are sent, in case the resulting output of the forge or sale is not to its advantage based on the current state of the game. This behavior effectively blocks legitimate transactions, causing financial loss and frustration for users.

To illustrate this issue, consider the following scenario:

1. A malicious contract is set as the `forgerOwner` or `listing.seller`.
2. This malicious contract overrides the fallback or receive function to revert any transaction unless certain game conditions are met.
3. When a user calls the `forgeWithListed` or `buyNFT` functions, the funds are sent to this malicious contract.
4. The malicious contract checks the state of the game. If the conditions are not favorable, it reverts the transaction.
5. The `.call` method fails, and the `require` statement in the `forgeWithListed` or `buyNFT` function causes the entire transaction to revert.

This behavior effectively makes it impossible to execute the `forgeWithListed` or `buyNFT` functions under these conditions, disrupting the normal flow of the game.
## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps


The contract should tolerate potential reverts from the underlying contracts since this interaction is part of the main transfer flow. This can be achieved by implementing a try/catch mechanism or by handling the revert gracefully within the main contract logic.



## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User funds remain locked within the `EntityForging.sol` contract without the ability to be withdrawn by the user, any other entity, or the owner of the contract. Users will lose their funds without the possibility of a refund. This occurs because the `forgeWithListed` function does not handle the potential additional `msg.value` that may be provided during the execution of the `forgeWithListed` function.



## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this issue, consider the following scenario:

1.  A forger is listed with ID: 587 for 0.1 ETH, transaction:
https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x2288f0c78c289468be4b2285409b11759622fc6324a76e8164456a4425172ced

https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x26a20263f7648d393e4a88cc67876317f62fd6f0e0d0e54454e19a4a1100f0cf

3. 0.05 ETH remains transferred and locked in the `EntityForging.sol` contract.




## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Handle the potential extra `msg.value` by implementing logic within the `forgeWithListed` function to refund any excess ETH provided during the transaction. This ensures that only the required amount for the forging process is utilized, and any additional funds are returned to the user.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L211-L212


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Missing the “the Golden God” entropy value of a generation could undermine the goal of the game and fail to prompt users to mint out the generation. As a result, a generation of 10,000 NFTs might mint out without including an NFT that contains the entropy value of 999,999. This would affect the rarity and value distribution intended by the game mechanics.


## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this issue, consider the following:

1. The total number of `maxSlotIndex` is equal to 770, and the `currentNumberIndex` is equal to 13. This produces a total of `770 x 13 = 10,010` total number of entropies.
2. This means that the `getNextEntropy` will produce 10,010 entropies before resetting instead of 10,000.
3. Since the `initializeAlphaIndices` function sets the slot of the 999,999 value, if that slot is set to the last 10 indices, then that entropy will never be utilized within the generation.
4. `initializeAlphaIndices` is called, which sets the `slotIndexSelection` equal to 769 and `numberIndexSelection` equal to 12.
5. The entropy is stored in the last element in the index 10,010 of the `entropySlots` array. As a result, it will be set to the next generation since each generation can have a maximum of 10,000 mints.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to utilize a total of 10,000 slots instead of 10,010 to ensure that each entropy value accurately reflects the minting of the current generation. Additionally, modify the slot that stores the 999,999 value so that it is not greater than the 10,000th index of the entropies array.




## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L153-L179


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Repetitive executions of the same nuke factor tokenId can result in multiple withdrawals from the `NukeFund.sol` contract, potentially depleting its funds. This exploit allows a malicious user to almost drain the contract, leading to financial loss and disruption of the intended game mechanics.

## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this issue, consider the following scenario:

1. A malicious user utilizes multiple accounts that possess different NFTs.
2. The malicious user forges the same NFTs multiple times using different accounts until their ForgePotential reaches its maximum.
3. The resulting forgedId NFTs have the same NukeFactor since they are produced using the same parentIds.
4. The cooldown period for the minimum days held of the NFTs passes, allowing the malicious user to nuke multiple NFTs with the same NukeFactor simultaneously.

This results in multiple withdrawals of funds from the `NukeFund.sol` contract. Depending on the number of NFTs produced, this exploit can nearly empty the contract.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Prevent the forging of the same parentIds or implement a cooldown period during which the same parentId cannot be forged again. This will limit the ability of malicious users to exploit the system and drain huge amounts of the contract's funds.



## Assessed type

ETH-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L169-L176


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The same NFTs with identical images and entropy can exist within the same generation. As a result, duplicate NFTs will exist, undermining the game objectives and goals. This can affect the rarity and uniqueness of NFTs, which are essential for maintaining user interest and the value of the game assets.

## Proof of Concept
Each time two NFTs are forged, the resulting NFTs get an entropy value which is the average entropy from its parentIds:

`
uint256 newEntropy = (forgerEntropy + mergerEntropy) / 2;
`

As a result, if the `forgeWithListed` function is executed multiple times using the same parentIds, the same NFTs will be produced.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `newEntropy` that is produced when using the same parentIds should be checked and modified to ensure it results in an entropy value that does not already exist. This will prevent the creation of duplicate NFTs within the same generation and maintain the uniqueness and value of each NFT.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L350-L351


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If more than 10,000 NFTs are generated per generation, there will be an oversupply of NFTs, which exceeds the intended cap for each generation. This undermines the game's intended functionality and the value of NFTs by allowing an uncapped number of NFTs to be minted per generation.

## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this issue, consider the following scenario:

1. Minting starts and `generationMintCounts[1]` is incremented as the mints of generation 1 occur.
2. The `forgeWithListed` function is called using two NFTs of generation 1, producing an NFT of generation 2. As a result, `generationMintCounts[2]` is incremented to track the total mints of generation 2.
3. 10,000 NFTs of generation 1 are minted, and the `_incrementGeneration` function is called. This function performs the following changes:

   `
   currentGeneration++;
   generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
   `
4. This resets the `generationMintCounts` of generation 2 to zero, effectively ignoring all previously minted NFTs of generation 2.

As a result, all NFTs that were forged and minted as generation 2 are not taken into consideration, leading to an oversupply of NFTs beyond the intended 10,000 cap per generation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
When resetting to the next generation, the code should take into consideration the total mints that have already occurred in the current generation. Ensure that the `generationMintCounts` accurately reflect the number of NFTs minted and forged to prevent oversupply.



## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L87-L90


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

Entities minted to every user have some set of properties and included is the forgePotential which determines how many times a forger's entity can forge with any merger's entity to mint an entity in the next generation with even stronger properties. In simple terms, if an entity's forge potential is 2, then it can forge with another entity at most 2 times but if the forger is able to forge more than 2 times, this becomes a vulnerability.

In [`EntityForging::listForForging()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L87C5-L90C7), the check as to whether the forgePotential is not 0 and hasn't been exceeded precedes incrementing the forgingCounts which enables the forger to list one more time than he should be allowed to. The increment happened much later when a merger has initiated the merging. The proper way is found in [`EntityForging::forgeWithListed()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L139C5-L144C7) but on the merging side. A forgePotential of 2 will be able to forge 3 times and a forgePotential of 4 will be able to forge 5 times.

## Impact
Forger is able to game the protocol into earning extra which the merger has to pay for.

## Proof of Concept
Assume that there is a forger, BOB with a forge potential of 2 and 2 mergers, ALICE and KEN.

```solidity
  function listForForging(
    uint256 tokenId,
    uint256 fee
  ) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    ..........
    require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
    ..........
  }
```
1. BOB lists his entity when forgingCounts is 0. `listForForging()` checks if 0 <= 2.
2. ALICE merges which increases the forgingCount to 1.
3. BOB lists again when forgingCounts is 1. `listForForging()` checks if 1 <= 2.
3. KEN merges to increase the forgingCounts to 2.
4. At forgingCounts = 2, BOB lists his entity once more when he shouldnt be able to. `listForForging()` checks if 2 <= 2. and allows the listing.
5. ALICE merges again and forgingCount increases to 3.

From the Proof of Concept above, it is clear that BOB is able to list 3 times, one more time than he should be able to.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Increment the forgingCount for the forger tokenID before checking if the forge potential has been exceeded.





## Assessed type

Error

## Impact
With current impementation of calculating `claimAmount` the `NukeFund::nuke()` is vulnerable to MEV attacks. Malicious user can front-run other user to gain more share from `fund`

## Proof of Concept
When performing `NukeFund::nuke()` user take percent of total funds accumulated in contract. Current good strategy would be waiting as long as they can to receive percentage share of bigger value.

Take a look at scenario with 2 users that waits for funds to accumulate:
UserA - has NFT with `nukeFactor` that has maximum possible claimAmount = 50%
MaliciousUserB - has NFT with `nukeFactor` that has claimAmount = 20% 
Current funds accumulated in contract is 1 ether


1. UserA decides to nuke his NFT. His expected share should be 0.5 ether
2. UserB front-run UsersA transaction and take his 20% share = 0.2 ether
3. Current funds at contract `1-0.2=0.8 ether`
4. UsersA transaction goes through and he claims 50% of the remaining 0.8 ether
`0.8*0.5=0.4 ether`
5. UserA end up with lower claimed amount than he expected

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider changing calculations for `claimAmount`. For example use fixed value in wei instead of percentage of total funds

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L128-L133

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

According to the documentation, aging factor is related with the entropy values of the entities. The best entity's entropy is 999999, it's performance factor is 9 which is fastest and it has biggest initial nuke factor. According to the documentation, if an entity reach 50% nuke factor level it's fully mature. 

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pihtkKyyxobFWdaNU4YfAy56Q7WIMbFJjSHUAfRm6BA/edit

And the best entity should be mature in 30 days based on the documentation but the current implementation doesn't fit with this statement with current parameters.

## Impact
Much slower aging for every entity

## Proof of Concept
In order to prove this claim. I will show the calculations in reverse order using 999999 entity. According to the documents 999999 should be mature in 30 days.

Note: calculation codes are mentioned in affected code part

Calculation:

Initial parameters: 
MAX_DENOMINATOR = 100000
performanceFactor = 9 ( in 999999 entity )
ageMultiplier = 1
initialNukeFactor = 25000 ( 999999 / 40 )
defaultNukeFactorIncrease = 250

In order to reach 50% level final nuke factor should be 25000 + initialNukeFactor ( 25000 )

25000 * MAX_DENOMINATOR = 2500000000
2500000000 / defaultNukeFactorIncrease = 10000000 ( It's adjusted age right now)
10000000 * 365 = 3650000000
3650000000 / MAX_DENOMINATOR = 36500
skip ageMultiplier because it's 1
36500 / performanceFactor = 4055 days

Which means 999999 entity should wait 4055 days in order to be fully mature.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In order to reach 30 days level, defaultNukeFactorIncrease should be at least 33750

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L47-L61


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
Entropy values should be random values and it needs to be hard to predict. The current implementation calculates the slot values using block number which is public for everyone. 

```solidity
uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
          keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
        ) % uint256(10) ** 78;
        require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue;
```

## Impact
Slots will be really easy to predict, so people easily compute their entropy values.
These slots are really important in the game mechanism because it defines the value of minted NFTs.

## Proof of Concept
Scenario:

After deployment and initializing the slots, Alice takes the block number of the transaction and she executes the same code for this block number. Now, she know all the slot values. She always tracks the minted NFT numbers using token id and calculates the position of best entropy values in the slots and she mints new NFTs and she always gets really valuable NFTs. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Random number generation was always a big consideration in blockchain. There are many approaches which generate good results. VRF ( Verifiable Random Function ) is one of them. It provides a off-chain solution for it. Chainlink has a service for VRF but it has costs. Some other methods can also appliable but using block number is definitely worst way to do that.





## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L12
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L13
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L53


# Vulnerability details

### [H-03] Entropy Of Every Entity Can Be Predicted

**Description:**
To get the next entropy for a direct mint, the function **getNextEntropy()** of EntropyGenerator is called inside **mintToken()**. 
It then calls **getEntropy(currentSlotIndex, currentNumberIndex)** to determine the value of the next entropy to be retrieved.
Initially both **currentSlotIndex** and **currentNumberIndex** start from 0 and are being incremented inside each iteration or possibly reset to 0 after some time to then start over again. 
The core issue is that even though both vars are private, their value is still visible on the blockchain.

It is also notable that the block producer can easily pre-calculate all **entropySlots[i]** values when confirming the **writeEntropy{1,2,3}** transactions.
This is due to the fact that the validator has control of all arguments (block.number and i which is in the range [0;770]) used in the generation formula: 
```solidity
uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
) % uint256(10) ** 78;
```

**Impact:** The entropy for every token id can be predicted (pre-calculated). 
This implies that the moment the NFT Golden God is going to be mint for a particular generation can also be predicted and then possibly this transaction can be front run by the malicious actor.

**Proof of Concept:**
To read the private variables **currentSlotIndex** and **currentNumberIndex**, one just needs to know their corresponding storage slot number.
Then knowing the current values of those variables, the malicious user can calculate the entropy of the next tokenId himself using the maths in **getEntropy()**
or even easier - call **getPublicEntropy()** by just passing the next indices.

**Recommended Mitigation:** The way the randomization algorithm is used should be redesigned, possibly considering the usage of Chainlink VRF.
It should at no cost rely on some publicly visible parameters in order to generate an entropy. 


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206-L216


# Vulnerability details

Using block.number and block.timestamp together creates a predictable final number. A predictable number is not a good random number. Malicious users can manipulate these values to choose the correct moment for minting with 'The Golden God' entropy.

## Impact
Any user can predict the exact moment to mint with 'The Golden God' entropy since the weak randomization logic.

## Proof of Concept

The issue starts from this function:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206-L216

Since the randomness of those two variables is weak attacker is able to wait for the right time to mint.

1. The minting process initiates through the mint():
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L181-L200

2. The mint() function calls the internal _mintInternal() function:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280-L298

3. During the minting process, the entropyGenerator.getNextEntropy() function is called to generate entropy:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L101-L120

4. The getEntropy function is invoked to derive these entropy values. Due to the weak randomness, an attacker like Bob can predict these values and strategically choose the optimal time to mint. For instance, Bob can mint with a known entropy value such as 999999 (The Golden God) because of:

Malicious users can read EntropyGenerator::entropySlots, EntropyGenerator::currentSlotIndex, and EntropyGenerator::currentNumberIndex private variables by analyzing the deployed contract's storage slots and effectively cherry-pick NFTs during the minting process to guarantee desirable entropies.

1 - Deploy the contract
```

```

2 - Analyze the contract's storage to read `entropySlots` (the same commands can be run for `currentSlotIndex` and `currentNumberIndex`  
```
cast storage 0x77c7E3905c21177Be97956c6620567596492C497 0
# output -> 0x000000000000000000000000976ea74026e726554db657fa54763abd0c3a0aa9

cast storage 0x77c7E3905c21177Be97956c6620567596492C497 1
# output -> 0x2b232c97452f0950c94e2539fdc7e69d21166113cf7a9bcb99b220a3fe5d720a

cast --to-dec 0x2b232c97452f0950c94e2539fdc7e69d21166113cf7a9bcb99b220a3fe5d720a 

#output -> 19511599891424801449367108142964227787403202039135897967463264740723690140170
```
3 - We can split this into 13 groups of 6 digits each:
195115 998914 248014 493671 081429 642277 874032 020391 358979 674632 647407 236901 401700 (add padding)

4. So, the 13 entropies stored in this slot are:
    - 195115
    - 998914
    - 248014
    - ...

5. Perform the same steps to read `currentSlotIndex` and `currentNumberIndex`
6. With the entropies, currentSlotIndex, and currentNumberIndex, malicious users can call/front-run `TraitForgeNft::mintToken` on entropies next up in `EntropyGenerator::entropySlots` guaranteeing they get the best: nuke factor, forge potential, performance factor, a forger NFT over a merger, or “the Golden God.” 
7. This effectively makes the game a gas competition for who can call `TraitForgeNft::mintToken` with the most gas and at the right time to get a desirable entropy score, effectively making the game unplayable.

Manual Review, Foundry (cast)

Refactor the sequential nature of `EntropyGenerator::getNextEntropy` and randomly select from `EntropyGenerator::entropySlots` using Chainlinks VRF.

In the `forgeWithListed()` function of EntityForging.sol, users can potentially pay more than required - `require(msg.value >= forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging')` . uint256 excessPayment = msg.value - forgingFee;

## Impact
The receive() function in the NukeFund contract is vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack through the flooding of small Ether transactions. The issue stems from the fact that each transaction triggers the receive() function, which may become clogged with the high volume of transactions, causing delays and increasing the gas costs for processing legitimate transactions.

Attack Scenario:
Step 1: An attacker sends 100 Wei in each of 10,000 transactions to the NukeFund contract.
Step 2: Each transaction triggers the receive() function, leading to a substantial amount of processing.
Step 3: The high volume of small transactions can clog the contract’s processing, leading to delays for legitimate users who may struggle to send Ether or perform other actions efficiently.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A potential reentrancy vulnerability arises in this smart contract. In the `claim` function, there is a state modification after external calls.

Reentrancy attacks can occur when a contract calls external contracts and then proceeds to make changes to its state. An attacker can recursively call back into the vulnerable function, leading to the condition that the state changes apply to outdated data.

```solidity
uint256 claimedAmount = safeRewardTransfer(msg.sender, pending);  // external call

```

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To avoid potential reentrancy attacks, checks-effects-interactions (CEI) pattern should always be followed. This pattern suggests to first make all the internal work (checks and state changes) and eventually call the external functions and transfer ethers (interactions).

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/TraitForge/traitforge-contracts/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L128-L129


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The contract allows resetting of the forge potential (limit) arbitrarily within its `forgeWithListed` function. This can lead to potential abuse of the system.

The `_resetForgingCountIfNeeded` function is intended to reset a NFT's forge potential if a year has passed since the last reset. However, this function is called in the `listForForging` and `forgeWithListed` functions for both the forger token and merger token. 

This can lead to an unintended resetting of the forge potential if these functions are called within the `forgeWithListed` function.

## Proof of Concept

Here is a code snippet from the `forgeWithListed` function where it calls the `_resetForgingCountIfNeeded` function:

```solidity
_resetForgingCountIfNeeded(forgerTokenId); // Reset for forger if needed
_resetForgingCountIfNeeded(mergerTokenId); // Reset for merger if needed
```

And here is the `_resetForgingCountIfNeeded` function itself:

```solidity
function _resetForgingCountIfNeeded(uint256 tokenId) private {
    uint256 oneYear = oneYearInDays;
    if (lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] == 0) {
        lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] = block.timestamp;
    } else if (block.timestamp >= lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] + oneYear) {
        forgingCounts[tokenId] = 0; // Reset to the forge potential
        lastForgeResetTimestamp[tokenId] = block.timestamp;
    }
}
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To prevent unintended resetting of the forge potential, the call to `_resetForgingCountIfNeeded` in the `forgeWithListed` function could be removed or carefully controlled. Analyse the code and decide the suitable function that needs the call to `_resetForgingCountIfNeeded`. 
As a suggestion, it can be best to reset the forge potential when owners list their tokens for forging by using the `listForForging` method.


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/TraitForge/traitforge-contracts/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The smart contract makes use of integer division that may not provide the expected results. In Solidity, integer division truncates the fraction. As such, any integer division operation can drop significant digits that could lead to monetary loss or manipulation of the system.

In the forgeWithListed() function, devFee is calculated as forgingFee / taxCut. Given the integer division, it could round down and miscalculate the fees. This can either lead to a smaller fee being extracted than expected or a larger forgerShare being credited.

## Proof of Concept

Affected code in the forgeWithListed() function:
```solidity
uint256 forgingFee = _forgerListingInfo.fee;
uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
uint256 forgerShare = forgingFee - devFee;
```


## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

A Right logic would be to calculate forgerShare and then subtract it from forgingFee on the go rather than dividing forgingFee again.
```solidity
uint256 forgingFee = _forgerListingInfo.fee;
uint256 forgerShare = forgingFee * (100 - taxCut)/100;
uint256 devFee = forgingFee - forgerShare;
``` 
However, the above code has hardcoded percentage (100) and that should be calculated from taxCut itself. If all these parameters (forgingFee, taxCut, etc.) are stored in contract using a decimal standard like wei, you can perform the calculation safely and then convert back to the original unit.

The suggested changes will make sure the contract calculates devFee and forgerShare accurately and prevent any potential loss or manipulation.



## Assessed type

Math

https://github.com/TraitForge/traitforge-contracts/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the contract EntityTrading.sol, there exists a vulnerability that could be exploited to perform a reentrancy attack. 

A reentrancy attack occurs when an external contract hijacks the control flow, during a pending payment or state change, and reenters the calling contract before the said change has been completed.

In this case, the vulnerability lies with the `buyNFT` function. The contract first calls an external contract (`transferToNukeFund(nukeFundContribution);`), and then later, it changes the state of the contract. 

This allows the called contract to make calls back into the original contract and alter the state in unexpected ways before it's settled.


## Proof of Concept

Reentrancy Attack code can be identified in the `buyNFT` function:

```solidity
function buyNFT(uint256 tokenId) external payable whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
  ...
  transferToNukeFund(nukeFundContribution); // Facilitates potential for reentrancy attack
  ...
  nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer NFT to the buyer
  delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]]; // remove listing
  ...
}
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The quick fix would be to follow the "Checks-Effects-Interactions" pattern in Solidity. 

This means to first make all of the state changes in the contract before calling external contracts. 




## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/TraitForge/traitforge-contracts/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L53-L54


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The contract uses block.number and timestamps as inputs for the `keccak256` function to generate pseudo-random numbers, which is a weak implementation of random number generation in Ethereum.

This can lead to vulnerabilities where an attacker could, in theory, influence the outcome of these "random" numbers.

## Proof of Concept

The pseudo-random numbers are generated in the following method:
``` solidity
function writeEntropyBatch1() public {
    ...
    uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))) % uint256(10) ** 78;
    ...
}
```
It uses `block.number` to generate what's supposed to be a random value. Similar pseudo-random number generation is found in other parts of the code such as 'writeEntropyBatch2' function, 'writeEntropyBatch3', and 'initializeAlphaIndices' functions.

## Tools Used

Manual Review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

As best practice, a contract should never use `block.number`, `block.timestamp` or any other block variables to create randomness because smart contracts run on an environment where miners can manipulate those values. 

A reliable mechanism to generate pseudo-random numbers in solidity hasn't been standardized yet. However, possible alternatives could be to use oracle services like Chainlink VRF (Verifiable Random Function) which provides provably-fair and verifiable randomness, or alternatively, build or use an on-chain commit-reveal scheme, or generate the random number off-chain and provide a proof on-chain (like a VDF or zkProof).

In addition to that, if randomness is not required to be on-chain, it would be better to move it off-chain, where it is easier to generate random numbers securely. In this case, an off-chain server generates the random number, and interactions between the smart contract and the server are done using signatures or oracle services. 

The chosen solution would depend on the specifics of the dapp and the level of trust, decentralization, and verifiable fairness required by the specific use case.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/TraitForge/traitforge-contracts/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L182


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The "nuke" function of the NukeFund contract is vulnerable to re-entrancy attacks. 
Whilst there is nonReentrant modifier in place, it is possible to perform potential re-entrancy attacks due to external calls, specifically the call which sends Ether to the msg.sender.

A re-entrancy attack can occur when a contract calls external contracts and makes state changes after the external call. If the called contract is malicious and implements a fallback function, it can re-enter the caller contract before the state changes have been committed, leading to potential exploits. 

In this function, an amount of fund is deducted and a token is burnt after making an external call to transfer Ether. If the payable external address is a contract that has a fallback function, it could re-enter the "nuke" function and repeatedly claim funds, before the state changes (i.e., token burn and fund deduction) of the initial call are actually committed to the blockchain.

## Proof of Concept

In the "nuke" function, the following code snippet is especially vulnerable:

```solidity
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');
fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund
nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
```

A malicious contract with the payable fallback function can re-enter the "nuke" function in the line where Ether is being transferred to `msg.sender`.


## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this, you should follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern which recommends performing any external calls as the very last operation in your function. Additionally, you can use the OpenZeppelin library's `SafeMath` module for state-changing operations to mitigate re-entrancy vulnerabilities. The `nonReentrant` modifier from OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard` can also be used to prevent recursive calls. 

So, moving state changes before external interaction would look like:

```solidity
fund -= claimAmount;
nftContract.burn(tokenId);
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');
```

Note that even though the contract already employs a `nonReentrant` modifier, it wouldn't be effective in its current placement. It is best practice to place the `nonReentrant` modifier where re-entrance could happen, in this case, it should be placed at the function with the external payable call. 


## Assessed type

Reentrancy

brief_summary: Blockchains have a block gas limit to prevent DoS attacks, and in Solidity, loops consume gas. Specifically in Ethereum, if a function's gas usage exceeds the transaction's gas limit, it will fail to execute, and the gas is lost. The `mintWithBudget` function uses a loop to continuously mint tokens until the budget is exhausted or the max token limit per generation reached. However, it's not considering the worst-case scenario where the function execution could be halted due to the exceeding Ethereum block gas limit, leading to potential Denial of Service (DoS).

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L166
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L167
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L170
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L174


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

The nuke functionality burn the Entity and send ether base on the nukeFactor of the Entity and the balance of the nuke fund, the problem is that the person that nukes their token first get's more reward than the next and subsequent persons to nuke their token.

This because the first person to nuke get a percent of the total nuke `fund`, that percentage is subtracted from the total nuke fund `fund -= claimAmount`, so for subsequent users the nuke fund reduces so they get less even with thesame or more nuke factor.


```sol
  function nuke(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    ...
    uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
@->    uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
    uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size

    // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
@->    uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
      : potentialClaimAmount;

@->    fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund
    ...
  }
```


## Proof of Concept

1. Bob and Alice both have a nuke factor of 20000
2. The current nuke fund balance is 100 ether
3. Bob nukes his token, he will claim 100 * 20000 / 100000 = 20 ether
4. The current nuke fund is now 100 - 20 = 80 ether
5. Alice nukes her token, she will get 80 * 20000 / 100000 =  16 ether

Alice got 4 ether less than Bob despite having the same nuke factor because Bob nuked first


## Impact

1. Loss of funds to subsequent nukers, which is unfair to them
2. This will encourage people to nuke on time thus making the game not enjoyable


## Tool Used 

Manual Analysis

## Recommendation

Create a form of ERC4626 vault that share rewards base on nuke factor.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L103
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L193
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L288


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

Entities have unique characteristics based on their entropy when they are minted, this entropy is based on pseudo-random numbers that are generated on-chain the `entropyGenerator.getNextEntropy()` function generates the entropy. The problem is that the blockchain is a deterministic environment and the entropy can be predicted before the Entity is minted.

The generated entropy is based on `currentSlotIndex` and `currentNumberIndex` though these variables are private they can be read directly from the blockchain.

```sol
uint256 private currentSlotIndex = 0;
uint256 private currentNumberIndex = 0;
```

Using the `deriveTokenParameters()` function a user can easily get the traits of the Entity they want and if it is not desirable they won't simply mint the Entity. If this becomes common knowledge people will be reluctant to mint Entities when they know that it doesn't have the desired traits that they want.

## Proof of Concepts

Add the following test to the `EntropyGenerator.test.ts` file

```javascript

  it('POC entropy', async function () {

    await entropyGenerator.writeEntropyBatch1();
    await entropyGenerator.writeEntropyBatch2();
    await entropyGenerator.writeEntropyBatch3();

    for (let slotIndex = 1; slotIndex < 40; slotIndex++) {

      for (let numberIndex = 1; numberIndex < 10; numberIndex++) {
        const [nukeFactor, breedPotential, performanceFactor, isSire] = await entropyGenerator.deriveTokenParameters(slotIndex, numberIndex);
        if (breedPotential > 7n && performanceFactor > 7n && isSire) {
          console.log("Most Desired:  ","slotIndex: " + slotIndex, "numberIndex: " + numberIndex, nukeFactor, breedPotential, performanceFactor, isSire);
        }

        if (breedPotential < 3n && performanceFactor < 3n && !isSire) {
          console.log("Least Desired: ","slotIndex: " + slotIndex, "numberIndex: " + numberIndex, nukeFactor, breedPotential, performanceFactor, isSire);
        }
      }

    }
    
  });
```

Output
```
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 3 numberIndex: 1 0n 1n 2n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 6 numberIndex: 1 0n 2n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 7 numberIndex: 8 0n 1n 0n false
Most Desired:   slotIndex: 8 numberIndex: 4 0n 9n 8n true
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 10 numberIndex: 5 0n 1n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 12 numberIndex: 7 0n 1n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 14 numberIndex: 7 0n 2n 2n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 19 numberIndex: 7 0n 2n 1n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 20 numberIndex: 3 0n 1n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 20 numberIndex: 6 0n 2n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 20 numberIndex: 9 0n 1n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 24 numberIndex: 7 0n 2n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 25 numberIndex: 1 0n 1n 2n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 28 numberIndex: 8 0n 1n 0n false
Most Desired:   slotIndex: 30 numberIndex: 9 0n 9n 8n true
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 31 numberIndex: 2 0n 2n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 32 numberIndex: 7 0n 2n 1n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 34 numberIndex: 1 0n 2n 2n false
Most Desired:   slotIndex: 36 numberIndex: 1 0n 9n 8n true
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 36 numberIndex: 2 0n 2n 2n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 36 numberIndex: 3 0n 2n 0n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 36 numberIndex: 4 0n 1n 2n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 37 numberIndex: 6 0n 2n 1n false
Least Desired:  slotIndex: 39 numberIndex: 8 0n 2n 0n false
```

From the above output we can see the position of the most desired and list desired Entities and choose to mint or not depending on the `currentSlotIndex` and `currentNumberIndex` values.


## Impact

1. Because entropy is not truly random users will know the properties of the token before minting them.
2. A user who is looking for a forger will knowingly wait for two other people to mint before they will mint to get the forger token.
3. Since some Entities have traits that are more desirable than others it will lead to users not willing to mint the less desirable Entity. Making the protocol to be unused.

## Tool Used

Manual Analysis


## Recommendation

Because the blockchain is deterministic, randomness cannot be generated on-chain, but services like Chainlink and Gelato provide VRF (Verified Random Function) that can be generated through randomness on-chain.

The following are two approaches that I recommend.

1. When someone mints a new Entity the Gelato VRF should determine the entropy. This might be more expensive since users have to pay for the cost of randomness with each Entity mint.
2. Batch the minting of Entities so whenever a user mints an Entity it gets sent to a queue that can be called by a keeper that delivers the random numbers from a VRF provider. So, the minting of entities can be done every 1 to 24hrs.





## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- Rounding Errors
- Predictability
- Incorrect Age Calculation
- Fund Exploitation
- Potential Exploits

## Proof of Concept
`EntropyGenerator`
1. Deploy the Contract:
```
// Assume the contract is deployed and initialized
```
2. Trigger the Vulnerability:
```
// Call getPublicEntropy with specific slotIndex and numberIndex
uint256 faultyEntropy = entropyGenerator.getPublicEntropy(0, 0);
```
3. Observe the Rounding Error:
```
// Check the returned entropy value for precision loss
console.log(faultyEntropy);
```

`NukeFund`
1. Deploy the NukeFund Contract:
- Ensure the contract is deployed with the necessary addresses and initial parameters.
2. Mint an NFT:
- Mint an NFT using the `nftContract` and note its creation timestamp.
3. Manipulate Time:
- Fast forward the blockchain time to simulate the passage of days (e.g., using a testing framework like Hardhat or Ganache).
4. Calculate Age Manually:
- Manually calculate the expected age of the token in days.
5. Call `calculateAge`:
- Call the `calculateAge` function with the token ID and compare the result with the manually calculated age.
- Observe the precision loss due to integer division.
6. Exploit the Fund:
- Use the nuke function to claim funds based on the inaccurately calculated age, demonstrating the potential for exploitation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`EntropyGenerator`
- Ensure the divisor does not cause overflow.
- Utilize OpenZeppelin's SafeMath for safer arithmetic operations.
```
// Import SafeMath library
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/math/SafeMath.sol";

function getEntropy(uint256 slotIndex, uint256 numberIndex) private view returns (uint256) {
    require(slotIndex <= maxSlotIndex, 'Slot index out of bounds.');

    if (slotIndex == slotIndexSelectionPoint && numberIndex == numberIndexSelectionPoint) {
        return 999999;
    }

    uint256 position = numberIndex * 6; // calculate the position for slicing the entropy value
    require(position <= 72, 'Position calculation error');

    uint256 slotValue = entropySlots[slotIndex]; // slice the required part of the entropy value
    uint256 divisor = 10 ** (72 - position);
    require(divisor > 0, "Divisor overflow");
    
    uint256 entropy = (slotValue / divisor) % 1000000; // adjust the entropy value based on the number of digits
    uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));

    return paddedEntropy; // return the calculated entropy value
}
```

`NukeFund`
- Modify the age calculation to use a single division operation to minimize precision loss.
```
uint256 daysOld = (block.timestamp - nftContract.getTokenCreationTimestamp(tokenId)) / 86400; // 86400 seconds in a day
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L125-L126
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146-L147


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `EntityForging::forgeWithListed()` requires that user sends msg.value >= forgingFee

The `EntityForging::forgeWithListed()` function requires that the user sends `msg.value greater than or equal to the forgingFee`. However, the function only uses forgingFee for calculations and does not refund any excess amount sent. This can result in users unintentionally losing funds if they send more than the required fee.

Refer to impacted line(s) of code here:

- Requires that msg.sender sends `msg.value >= forgingFee`

  - [EntityForging.sol#L125-L126](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L125-L126)

- The calculations are made using the `forgingFee` and not `msg.value`, which does not take into account any excess amount sent to the function, in which case the user won't be getting any refund.
  - [EntityForging.sol#L146-L147](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146-L147)

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

### One of the two of the following mitigations can be made

- Mitigation 1: Modify the check to accept exact value from `msg.sender`.

[EntityForging.sol#L126](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L126)

```diff
L126:
-   require(msg.value >= forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging');
+   require(msg.value == forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging');
```

- Mitigation 2 : Calculate `devFee` and `forgerShare` with `msg.value` instead of `forgingFee` and refund the remaining funds

[EntityForging.sol#L146-L147](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146-L147)

```diff
L146-L147 :
-    uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
-    uint256 forgerShare = forgingFee - devFee;
+    uint256 devFee = msg.value / taxCut;
+    uint256 forgerShare = msg.value - devFee;
+    uint256 excess = msg.value - devFee - forgerShare
+    if(excess > 0){
+       (bool success_refund, ) = msg.sender.call{ value: excess }('');
+       require(success_refund, 'Failed to refund excess amount');
+    }
```

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L47
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L64
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L84


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
`writeEntropyBatch1()`, `writeEntropyBatch2()`, `writeEntropyBatch3()` functions are used for initalizing entropy values inbatches to spread gas cost over multiple transcations. The main problem is in the `unchecked` block of code in the functions:

```javascript
unchecked {
    for (uint256 i = lastInitializedIndex; i < endIndex; i++) {
@>      uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))) % uint256(10) ** 78; // generate a  pseudo-random value using block number and index
        require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, "Invalid value, retry.");
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue; // store the value in the slots array
    }
}
```

Here is how the value of `pseudoRandomValue` is calculated:
1. `Keccak256` the value of the `block.number` and the index from the for-loop and cast it to `uint256`.
2. Modulo by `uint256(10)`, so we can get the last digit.
3. Bring the value to the power of 78.

However, this line of code will always overflow, because the first in the order of calculation is the power and `uint256(10) ** 78` will always overflow.

## Impact
Breaking core functionality of contract in three functions.

## Proof of Concept
You can test this line of code by substituting `i` with any number, which is casted to `uint256` and it will always overflow.

```javascript
uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))) % uint256(10) ** 78;
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
What you can do is to add parentheses in the equation like this:

```diff
-   uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))) % uint256(10) ** 78;
+   uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i)))) % uint256(10) ** 78;
```





## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Vulnerability details

## Description
The entire EntropyGenerator uses prng that decides how much the user will gain when calling `nuke()`, for this reason, the users will be able to predict how much they will gain for minting and wait until `currentNumberIndex` and `currentSlotIndex` are good enough to output an entropy that will result in better gains, and then send the transaction or even frontrun to get the NFT in the desired entropy.

## Impact
High, users can predict the entropy and get the better NFTs.

## Proof of Concept
1. Bob wants to mint an NFT from the TraitForgeNFT
2. Bob has an idea and clones the contract in his machine, inputing the block.number that was deployed, and also using future `currentNumberIndex` and `currentSlotIndex`
3. Bob decides to wait a little until `currentNumberIndex` and `currentSlotIndex` outputs a good entropy
4. After a some mintings, Bob sees that he will gain a good NFT if he mints now, he sends a transaction with high priority getting that NFT

## Tools Used
Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use chainlink VRF in the `EntropyGenerator` to make the numbers more random and unable to predicted

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When users list their Forger NFTs or Mergers NFTs, if they do not delist their NFTs, they may accidentally repurchase their own listed NFTs in subsequent purchase operations and incur a `nukeFundContribution` fee.

In addition to the absence of `buyer` and `seller` address verification in the `buyNFT` function of `EntityTrading.sol`, I noticed that on https://traitforge.game/trading, there is no clear indication of short address display for users, such as 0x1abc...abc or 0x2bde...fg. Additionally, there is no feature to hide NFTs listed by the user's connected wallet address. As a result, users are very likely to make the mistake of purchasing NFTs they have already listed, resulting in the loss of a portion of their `msg.value`.

Let's consider the following scenario:

Regular User:
1. Suppose the buyer lists a tokenId 1 NFT at a price of 1 ETH and transfers the NFT authorization to the `EntityTrading.sol` contract.
   
2. In a subsequent purchase, the user mistakenly buys their own listed tokenId 1 NFT.
   
3. The user pays 1 ETH as msg.value during the purchase, and according to the initialized `uint256 public taxCut = 10;`, a certain percentage of the fee is sent to the `NukeFund.sol` contract.

4. Based on `uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;`，the calculation is nukeFundContribution = (1 ETH / 10) = 0.1 ETH.

5. According to `uint256 sellerProceeds = msg.value - nukeFundContribution;`, the calculation is sellerProceeds = (1 ETH - 0.1 ETH) = 0.9 ETH.

6. `EntityTrading.sol` sends the tokenId 1 NFT back to the user, completing all purchase operations.
7. Buyer lost 0.1eth of `msg.value`


Batch Purchase NFT Bot:
1. Since batch purchase NFT bots may lack verification of the actual seller of the NFT, suppose it includes the functionality of listing NFTs and lists 10 NFTs [TokenId: 0...10], repeating the above operation, the loss of `msg.value` would be nukeFundContribution * 10 or nukeFundContribution * x.
2. EntityTrading.sol sends the tokenId[0...10] NFT back to the bot, completing all purchase operations.
3. bot lost total 0.1eth * 10 or 0.1eth * x eth of `msg.value`


## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L65-L69

The buyNFT function only validates the `listing.price` and seller being an empty address, lacking the verification of `msg.sender == listing.seller`, allowing buyers to purchase their own listed NFTs
```
require(
    msg.value == listing.price,
    'ETH sent does not match the listing price'
);
require(listing.seller != address(0), 'NFT is not listed for sale.');
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L72-L74
```
//transfer eth to seller (distribute to nukefund)
uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;
uint256 sellerProceeds = msg.value - nukeFundContribution;
transferToNukeFund(nukeFundContribution); // transfer contribution to nukeFund
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review and VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to add a check to ensure the NFT buyer is not the same person as the seller
```
require(msg.sender != listing.seller, "Seller cannot buy operation");
```





## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

priceIncrement in each generations is not handled properly , which makes minting towards the end of each generations highly unfeasible and unfair for the users.

## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L227-L232

```Solidity
 function calculateMintPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 currentGenMintCount = generationMintCounts[currentGeneration];
    uint256 priceIncrease = priceIncrement * currentGenMintCount;
    uint256 price = startPrice + priceIncrease;
    return price;
  }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L24

```Solidity
  uint256 public startPrice = 0.005 ether;
  uint256 public priceIncrement = 0.0000245 ether;
  uint256 public priceIncrementByGen = 0.000005 ether;
```

The priceIncrement in each generation is set as 0.0000245 ether and priceIncrease calculated by :
`uint256 priceIncrease = priceIncrement * currentGenMintCount;`

Towards, the end of the generation, say generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 9999 , priceIncrease will be 0.0000245 * 9999 = 0.2449 ether 
price = 0.005+0.2449 =0.2499 ether

This is a very high mint price and the user can just wait till the start of the next generation to mint as then the price will be:

price = 0.005 + (0.0000245 + 0.000005) * generationMintCounts[nextGeneration]

say generationMintCounts[nextGeneration] =1

then price = 0.0050295 ether 

This is approx 50 times lesser mint price

So minting towards the end of each generations is highly unfeasible and unfair for the users


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Handle the priceIncrease in each generations so that the user wont suffer huge loss . Make the priceIncrement much smaller.

Context
