# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `EntityTrading` contract allows users to list NFTs for sale and takes a 10% tax on each sale to contribute to the `NukeFund`. However, if a user lists an NFT for a very low value (e.g., 19 wei or 59 wei), the calculation for the tax cut suffers from precision loss due to Solidity's integer division, resulting in the `NukeFund` receiving less than 10% or even zero contribution.


## Impact
Precision loss in the tax calculation can lead to the protocol not receiving the intended 10% contribution for low-value NFT sales. This reduces the funds available in the NukeFund and can be exploited by malicious users who list NFTs for very low prices to avoid paying the correct tax amount.

## Proof of Concept
EXAMPLES

Price = 19 wei, TaxCut = 10:

`NukeFund contribution: 19 / 10 = 1 wei` (should be 1.9 wei)
`NukeFund receives: 1 wei` (which is approximately 5.26%)
`User receives: 18 wei` (which is approximately 94.74%)

Price = 59 wei, TaxCut = 10:

`NukeFund contribution: 59 / 10 = 5 wei` (should be 5.9 wei)
`NukeFund receives: 5 wei` (which is approximately 8.47%)
`User receives: 54 wei` (which is approximately 91.53%)

code - https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63C3-L92C4

## Tools Used
Manual code review and calculations
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Implement a minimum listing price to ensure the tax cut calculation does not suffer from precision loss
2. Alternatively, round up the tax cut calculation to ensure the NukeFund receives at least the minimum expected amount.
3. Add a check to ensure the NukeFund receives the correct contribution, even for low-value sales. This can be done by ensuring the minimum tax amount is enforced

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L88


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `EntityForging` contract allows users to `forge` tokens based on their `Forge Potential`, which is set randomly on Gen 1 mint. According to the protocol documentation, "the Forge Potential determines the number of times an entity can forge before becoming infertile." However, there is an off-by-one error in the `listForForging` function due to the use of the `<=` operator instead of `<`. This allows users to forge one additional time beyond their stated `Forge Potential`.

## Impact
Users can exploit this off-by-one error to forge one additional time per entity than intended. This results in entities being able to forge one more time than their Forge Potential, potentially leading to an imbalance in the game's mechanics and the overall token economy.

## Proof of Concept
Consider an entity with a Forge Potential of 5. According to the protocol documentation, this entity should be able to forge exactly 5 times within a year. However, the current implementation allows it to forge 6 times due to the <= operator.

Iterations to illustrate the bug:
`forgePotential = 5`
Forge 1st time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 0 (Check: 0 <= 5, passes)` 

Forge 2nd time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 1 (Check: 1 <= 5, passes)`

Forge 3rd time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 2 (Check: 2 <= 5, passes)`

Forge 4th time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 3 (Check: 3 <= 5, passes)`

Forge 5th time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 4 (Check: 4 <= 5, passes)`

Forge 6th time: `forgingCounts[tokenId] = 5 (Check: 5 <= 5, passes)`

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace the `<=` operator with the `<` operator to correctly enforce the Forge Potential limit
```solidity
require(
  forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
  'Entity has reached its forging limit'
);
```

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206-L216


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A user can mint the “the Golden God” NFT with 999999 entropy without any difficulty.

## Proof of Concept

Whenever a new NFT is minted, the [next available](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L288) entropy is assigned to it, from which its traits and parameters are derived. There are `10000` entropies created per generation, 13 of which get concatenated and stored in a single storage slot. The entire process revolves around the users getting a random entropy for their NFT, in order for the protocol’s fairness to remain consistent across all generations, for all users. The best entropy a user’s NFT can get assigned is `999999`, which would mean that all of its stats are the highest that one could get. It can be achieved only when the specific slot and index within that slot are matched with the parameters [slotIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L19) and [numberIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L20) (assigned upon deployment of [EntropyGenerator](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol) by calling [initializeAlphaIndices](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206-L216))

A problem arises when a user can mint “the Golden God” without going through any hurdles. As the selected slot index and number index are stored in state variables in [EntropyGenerator](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol), a user can read the current values of [slotIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L19) and [numberIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L20) and then call the function [getPublicEntropy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L123-L128) with them passed as an argument. The returned result from the function will confirm that the user can get their NFT minted with 999999 entropy, if they mint an NFT at that specific slot and number.

An additional source that can help with their timing, are the parameters [currentSlotIndex](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L12) and [currentNumberIndex](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L13) which can be read using the function [getStorage](https://web3js.readthedocs.io/en/v1.2.11/web3-eth.html#getstorageat) at from web3js (an [example](https://solidity-by-example.org/hacks/accessing-private-data/) of how that works). Using the information stated so far, a malicious user can time their mint perfectly, ensuring that they receive “the Golden God” NFT, or they can front-run any other user who would’ve got “the Golden God” using pure luck.

<details>
<summary>Coded PoC (foundry)</summary>

In order to setup Foundry run the commands:

- `foundryup`
- `forge install`
- `forge install foundry-rs/forge-std --no-commit`
- Add `forge-std/=lib/forge-std/src/` to `remappings.txt`

Within the `test` folder, create a new file `FoundryTests.t.sol` and paste the following:
https://gist.github.com/Vancelott/8be01402db0c498f29b20e85943a9991

You can run the test with: `forge test —mt testEasyGolden -vvvv`
</details>

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One possible reccomendation may be instead of setting the `slotIndexSelection` and `numberIndexSelection` variables in the [`initializeAlphaIndices()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206) function, remove it and let the user randomly get the "Golden God” NFT using pure luck.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Lost NFTs due to the contract [EntityTrading](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol) not implementing the interface [IERC721Receiver](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721Receiver.sol).

## Proof of Concept

The current implementation of the contract has just one function [listNFTForSale](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L38-L60), in which a NFT is being transferred from the user to the contract. However, the contract doesn’t implement neither [onERC721Received](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721Receiver.sol#L22-L27), nor does it inherit the interface [ERC721TokenReceiver](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721Receiver.sol). This will lead to all NFTs transferred to the contract via [safeTransferFrom](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721.sol#L55-L73) by the users, to revert. The likelihood of this happening is very high, because the suggested way of transferring tokens is to use the safe version of transfer and the receiver has to implement [IERC721Receiver and onERC721Received](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721.sol#L50-L51), which in this case is the `EntityTrading` contract, otherwise the transfer will never succeed.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The issue can be mitigated by implementing [OpenZeppelin’s IERC721Receiver](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721Receiver.sol)

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L19

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L9


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

All of the contracts in scope inherit from the Pausable contract, but as that’s not enough, none of the contracts can be paused, consequently all functions with the modifier whenNotPaused won’t be paused as well.  

## Proof of Concept

The following contracts are in scope for this audit: `TraitForgeNft, NukeFund, EntropyGenerator, EntityTrading, EntityForging and DevFund` - all of which inherit from the [Pausable](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol) contract. Its primary purpose is to allow the inheriting contract to pause/unpause functions that have the modifiers [whenNotPaused/whenPaused](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol#L54-L69).

However, one important step was missed, and that is making an external function for both the internal [pause/unpause](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol#L103-L118) functions. Without them, the contracts can’t take advantage of the functionality of `Pausable`, therefore none of the functions with the modifier `whenNotPaused` can be paused.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To address the issue, two external functions must be implemented in all inheriting contracts:

```solidity
function pause() external onlyOwner {
 _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
 _unpause();
}
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L86-L90


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A forger with a `forgePotential` of `x` should be able to forge only `x` times within a year. The required condition to list a forger in `EntityForging::listForForging` is incorrect and allows a forger to list for forging even if they have already forged x times:

```javascript
    uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
    require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

## Proof of Concept

`forgingCounts[tokenId]` starts at 0 and increments when the forging is completed. If the `forgingCounts[tokenId]` reaches `forgePotential`, it shouldn't be able to forge anymore. However this incorrect check allows it to be listed one more time to forge.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change `<=` to a strict `<`:
```diff
    uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
    require(
-     forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
+     forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```




## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L181-L225


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`TraitForgeNft::mintToken` and `TraitForgeNft::mintWithBudget` can be front-ran and all NFTs with more favourable traits can be minted by malicious actors while leaving NFTs with less favourable traits to other users, allowing them a bigger share at the Nuke Fund.

## Proof of Concept
Each NFT is assigned an entropy. Entropy determines the traits of the NFT. Based on the entropy value, a user is allocated a share in the Nuke Fund.
Since this entropy value is fetched from the storage slots which are public, any malicious user can read the favourable entropy values and front-run any mint transactions to these specific NFTs.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Supplement bit stuffing with Chainlink VRF to randomise entropy and make it unpredictable.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L51
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L202
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L188


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When using [MerkleProof.sol](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/cryptography/MerkleProof.sol)  avoid using leaf values that are 64 bytes long prior to hashing. However proof in `onlyWhitelisted` modifier in  `TraitForgeNft` contract uses leaf values that are exactly 64 bytes long. An attacker can bypass the merkle-tree proof  and exploit  the `onlyWhitelisted` modifier to mint tokens.


## Proof of Concept
As stated in the [Natspec](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/e3786e63e6def6f3b71ce7b4b30906123bffe67c/contracts/utils/cryptography/MerkleProof.sol#L16) of [MerkleProof.sol](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/cryptography/MerkleProof.sol) :

```console
 * WARNING: You should avoid using leaf values that are 64 bytes long prior to
 * hashing, or use a hash function other than keccak256 for hashing leaves.
 * This is because the concatenation of a sorted pair of internal nodes in
 * the Merkle tree could be reinterpreted as a leaf value.
            //                 //             //
```
The leaf value in `onlyWhitelisted` modifier are exactly 64 bytes long (uint256 + uint256 = 32 bytes + 32 bytes = 64 bytes).


The merkle-tree proof could be bypassed when the leaf values are 64 bytes long. The following links can help you understand the details.
https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/issues/3091
https://blog.openzeppelin.com/zksync-layer-1-audit/#merkle-library-verifies-intermediate-inputs

The modifier  [TraitForgeNft.sol#L51](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L51) :


```
  modifier onlyWhitelisted(bytes32[] calldata proof, bytes32 leaf) {
    if (block.timestamp <= whitelistEndTime) {
      require(
        MerkleProof.verify(proof, rootHash, leaf),
        'Not whitelisted user'
      );
    }
    _;
  }

```


How its been used in the functions  [mintToken()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L188) 

```solidty
 function mintToken(
    bytes32[] calldata proof
  )
    public
    payable
    whenNotPaused
    nonReentrant
    64 bytes before hashing allows collisions with internal nodes
@audit-issue @-> onlyWhitelisted(proof, keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender)))
  {
```
And [mintWithBudget()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L202) 

```solidity
  function mintWithBudget(
    bytes32[] calldata proof
  )
    public
    payable
    whenNotPaused
    nonReentrant
  64 bytes before hashing allows collisions with internal nodes
@audit-issue @-> onlyWhitelisted(proof, keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender)))
  {
```


Attacker can abuse merkle tree collisions to bypass the `onlyWhitelisted` modifier and mint tokens. 

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Don’t use leaf values that are 64 bytes long
2. Use [@openzeppelin/merkle-tree](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/merkle-tree) instead.










## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L139
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L140


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
From  [forgeWithListed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L102) function, the line `forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++` increases the forging count for the merger token before the check `require(forgingCounts[mergerTokenId] <= mergerForgePotential, 'forgePotential insufficient');`. This sequence can cause a situation where the incremented count exceeds the token's forge potential, even if it was valid before the increment. As a result, a valid operation might inadvertently trigger an error, preventing users from forging merger tokens.

## Proof of Concept
Suppose the `mergerForgePotential` is 3, and the `forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]` is currently 2. 
If the function increments the count first, it becomes 3, which is within the limit. 
However, if the function were called again, the count would increment to 4, now exceeding the potential, and the function would revert.

Below [EntityForging.sol:forgeWithListed#139](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L139)

```solidity
 function forgeWithListed(
    uint256 forgerTokenId,
    uint256 mergerTokenId
  ) external payable whenNotPaused nonReentrant returns (uint256) {
         //        //          //       
// @audit-issue  The count is incremented before checking if it exceeds the potential    
  forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++;
       require(
      mergerForgePotential > 0 &&
        forgingCounts[mergerTokenId] <= mergerForgePotential,
      'forgePotential insufficient'

     //       //     //

  }

```

Users  will not be able to forge merger tokens.
## Tools Used
Manual Review 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

increment operation should occur only after confirming that the count is within the allowed limits.
```diff
 -- forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++;
require(
  mergerForgePotential > 0 &&
  forgingCounts[mergerTokenId] < mergerForgePotential,
  'forgePotential insufficient'
);
 ++ forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++;

```





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L7-L9
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L10
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L7-L11
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L6-L11
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L7-L20


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The functions which are wanted to pause  or un-pause can not be paused or un-paused.

## Proof of Concept

The contracts **DevFund**, **EntityForging**, **EntityTrading**, **NukeFund** inherits the abstract contract `Pausable` which will be used to pause or un-pause some of the functions such as [claim](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L61), [nuke](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L154) and other function where the pause or un-pause is used.

We think that pause or un-pause is needed whenever the owner want to update certain set of parameters. when doing so, these function would be paused temporarily and un-paused once the operation is done.

The problem here is, just inheriting the Pausible module will not ensure the calling of the below function as they are internally protected. 

#L89-L104 : https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/security/Pausable.sol#L89-L104

```solidity
    function _pause() internal virtual whenNotPaused {
        _paused = true;
        emit Paused(_msgSender());
    }

    /**
     * @dev Returns to normal state.
     *
     * Requirements:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
EntityForging - forgeWithListed : excess ETH neither utilized not refunded.
over a period of time, the accumulated ETH will be locked inside the contract.

## Proof of Concept

`forgeWithListed` function does the following.

- Retrieve forger listing information.
- Check if forger's entity is listed for forging.
- Verify that the caller owns the merger token.
- Verify that the caller does not own the forger token.
- Ensure both tokens are of the same generation.
- Validate sufficient fee for forging.
- Reset forging counts for forger and merger tokens if needed.
- Increment forger's forging count.
- Validate and increment merger's forging count and forge potential.
- Calculate and distribute the developer fee and forger owner's share.
- Forge a new token with the given forger and merger tokens.
- Send developer fee to the specified address.
- Send forger's share to the forger owner.
- Cancel the forger token's listing for forging.
- Emit the EntityForged event with relevant details.
- Return the new token ID.

when checking the msg.value, below check is seen.

[EntityForging.sol#L125-L126](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L125-L126)

```solidity
    uint256 forgingFee = _forgerListingInfo.fee;
    require(msg.value >= forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging');
```

But, the share calculation is using the forginFee value as shown below. it is not using the msg.value.

[EntityForging.sol#L145-L159](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L145-L159)

```solidity

    uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
    uint256 forgerShare = forgingFee - devFee;
    address payable forgerOwner = payable(nftContract.ownerOf(forgerTokenId));

    uint256 newTokenId = nftContract.forge(
      msg.sender,
      forgerTokenId,
      mergerTokenId,

    require(success, 'Failed to send to NukeFund');
    (bool success_forge, ) = forgerOwner.call{ value: forgerShare }('');
    require(success_forge, 'Failed to send to Forge Owner');
```

So, if the msg.value is > forgeFee, some portion of ETH will be left inside the contract itself. This neither refunded not recovered.

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

We would see the following solutions for this.

- Refund the excess ETH to the caller.
- Use the total msg.value for fee and dev share calculation.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L76-L79


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Seller can control the NFT selling by using the function `buyNFT` when the ETH is transferred to the seller.

## Proof of Concept

NFT can be traded by using the function `listNFTForSale - buyNFT ` Seller can fix the selling price and list it for sale. 

This NFT can not be bought smoothly since it is controlled by the seller in various method.

The issue arise due to the nature of the implementation `listNFTForSale` , `buyNFT` or `cancelListing`.

These functions can be executed in any time. There is no freeze time between the `listNFTForSale` and `cancelListing`.

once the NFT is listed, it can be canceled at any time.

The other point to note, the `buyNFT` function which can be reverted when the seller receive the ETH.

- The issue we observe here is,

 -- Alice list the NFT

 -- After some time Alice notices, the demand for NFT increase, they can immediately call the `cancelListing` to cancel the selling.

- The other issue is,

 -- Alice list the NFT

 -- Alice would be smart contract which would have custom function to revert when it receive the ETH.

 -- Alice would use this block the selling of their NFT when they observe that the NFT price will be increasing.

In above both cases, the buyer would be unfairly affected as they can not buy the NFT as listed.

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

We would suggest to implement the freeze time between `listNFTForSale` and `cancelListing` functions.
when the seller list their NFT, they have to pass through this freeze duration to cancel.

Regarding forcefully revert, instead of push based fund transfer, implement, pull based fund transfer. so that the seller can call and withdraw the ETH.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The vulnerability lies in the minting function of the contract, where the mint price is calculated based on the current generation. However, if the minting of the current generation reaches its maximum limit `(generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen)`, the function proceeds to mint a new generation token without recalculating the mint price for the new generation. This discrepancy can cause users to overpay for their tokens, as they are charged the mint price for the previous generation while receiving a token from the new generation. 

## Proof of Concept

In this scenario, if the condition `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen` is true, the `_incrementGeneration()` function is called, which mints new generation token. However, the mintPrice is calculated for previous generation token, leading to a mismatch in the expected and actual mint prices.

```solidity
function mintToken( bytes32[] calldata proof)
    public
    payable
    whenNotPaused
    nonReentrant
    onlyWhitelisted(proof, keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender)))
  {
    //@audit price calculated before mint
    uint256 mintPrice = calculateMintPrice();
    require(msg.value >= mintPrice, 'Insufficient ETH send for minting.');
    _mintInternal(msg.sender, mintPrice);
```
```
  function _mintInternal(address to, uint256 mintPrice) internal {
    if (generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen) {
      _incrementGeneration();
    }
```

manual review

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L126


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`EntityForging::forgeWithListed` function allows users to forge with a listed Forger and pay a fee. However, the function includes the following requirement:
```
    require(msg.value >= forgingFee, 'Insufficient fee for forging');
```
This can result in any extra Ether sent via msg.value being locked in the smart contract indefinitely.


## Proof of Concept
Consider a scenario where a Forger is listed with a fee of 0.1 ETH. If a user calls the forgeWithListed function with a value exceeding 0.1 ETH:

2. a user call `forgeWithListed` function with value of 1ETH (which is just an additional 0 in wei).

        uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;

To prevent the loss of funds, replace the requirement with:

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153-L182


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `Nuke` function allows users to burn their NFTs and receive up to 50% of the `NukeFund` contract balance. However, a malicious user can front-run large `Nuke` function calls by others, causing them to receive up to 50% less than expected.

## Proof of Concept

Consider a scenario with two users, Alice and Bob, both eligible to claim up to 50% of the `NukeFund` balance, which is 100 ETH (for simplicity):

1. Alice has been waiting for the balance to reach 100 ETH for long time! Once it does, she calls the `Nuke` function to burn her NFT and receive 50 ETH.
2. Bob is monitoring the situation and can also claim 50% of the balance but is not doing so as long as nobody else does, waiting for the balance to go up. He sees Alice's transaction in the mempool, calling `Nuke` to get 50 ETH.
3. Bob front-runs Alice's transaction, and since there's no slippage mechanism or delay between `Nuke` calls, both transactions proceed.
4. Bob nukes the 100 ETH balance and receives 50 ETH.
5. Alice nukes the remaining 50 ETH balance and receives 25 ETH, burning her NFT for 50% less than she intended.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider implementing a slippage mechanism where users specify a minimum amount of ETH they expect to receive from burning their NFT or minimum amount of ETH balance in the contract. Alternatively, introduce a delay between `Nuke` calls to prevent front-running.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L46-L98
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L288-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `EntropyGenerator` contract is responsible for generating entropy, which determines the traits and attributes of the minted tokens.

*Taken from the [whitepaper](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pihtkKyyxobFWdaNU4YfAy56Q7WIMbFJjSHUAfRm6BA/edit)*:
"The traits and parameters per Entity are derived from “Entropy” a 6-digit random number associated with each Gen 1 Entity. The entropy is established at the genesis of the game and cannot be changed.
Entropy is set into uint256 slots, with each slot able to contain a 78 digit number - or 13 concatenated entropies. Thus 770 slots are needed to contain 10,000 entropies. Genesis entropy is seeded using blockhash. Setting all 770 uint256 slots cost 15m gas, and due to contract & block size limits, this cannot be set in contract initialisation. Instead a function writes in entropy in 3 passes after the contract is deployed.
There is a certain entropy, “999999” which is referred to as “the Golden God”, since it has perfect parameters and will exceed all other entities if played correctly. The Golden God is scanned for and is kept out of the first 2 passes, but is deliberately set in the final pass (at some random point). The Golden God should be the most valuable entity."

It doing so by three functions, `writeEntropyBatch1`, `writeEntropyBatch2` and `writeEntropyBatch3`.
However, since all the data is stored on-chain, this source of randomness is very weak. This weakness can lead to front-running on NFTs with better traits and result in severe gas wars.

## Proof of Concept
Consider a scenario where the next token to be minted is the "Golden God", "999999" entropy with perfect parameters. Every user in the game can easily know that the next token will be the best in the game. This knowledge might lead to significant front-running, causing severe gas wars, and potentially resulting in users losing substantial amounts of ETH due to higher gas fees.
the same scenario can happen to any other token with good parameters.

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this issue, consider implementing a different source of randomness, that will not store the traits onchain. A robust solution might be utilizing [Chainlink VRF](https://docs.chain.link/vrf), which provides verifiable randomness and can prevent the predictability and subsequent front-running issues observed with the current on-chain entropy generation method.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L353
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L205-L216


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `initializeAlphaIndices` is responsilbe to set the "Golden God" entropy of the next gen. it is being called from `TraitForgeNft` in `TraitForgeNft::_incrementGeneration` function. 
```
  function _incrementGeneration() private {
    require(
      generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen,
      'Generation limit not yet reached'
    );
    currentGeneration++;
    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] = 0;
    priceIncrement = priceIncrement + priceIncrementByGen;
    @> entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();
    emit GenerationIncremented(currentGeneration);
  }
```
however, the the `initializeAlphaIndices` has `onlyOwner` modifier, which only allow the owner of the contract call this function, thus, the next Generations can not be ever minted, and this might cause DoS of the entire protocol.

## Proof of Concept
when GEN1 is sold out, and `mintToken` is being called in `TraitForgeNft` contract, it will call the `_incrementGeneration` function.
this function will call `initializeAlphaIndices` in the entropyGenerator, which allows only the owner of the contract to call this function.
the NFT contract is not the contract owner, and therefore, this function will always revert, rendering the minting functions unusable.

* one might say, that we can just transfer ownership of the contract to the NFT contract, and therefore it is not a high. however, since the NFT contract is NOT the owner and can not call `onlyOwner` functions, and there's the `allowedCaller`, `modifier onlyAllowedCaller` which is set to the `TraitForgeNft` address, it is a wrong access control.

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
use `onlyAllowedCaller` modifier instead.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L49
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280-L288
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L163-L185
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L100-L120


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
One of the core features of TraitForge is the pseudo-random generation of NFTs ad their traits. As it turns out, these traits are predictable before minting, allowing an attacker to simulate the NFT minting locally and maximizing the value of their minted NFTs by carefully timing their minting.

## Proof of Concept
The entropy value of each token in generated by [EntropyGenerator.getNextEntropy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L100-L120) calling [EntropyGenerator.getEntropy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L163-L185). While fairly complex, it is predictable. The returned entropy value is calculated based on the following values, which if known by an attacker would allow them to predict the next values:
- currentNumberIndex
- currentSlotIndex
- entropySlots

All of these values are known. These state variables are declared private, but as with any smart contract deployed to a public blockchain this merely means that the compiler will not create a getter function.

These values can be obtained by anyone in two different ways. Firstly, by inspecting the `EntropyGenerator`'s storage. Since the contract's code is public, deploying it and debugging it locally to obtain the storage layout is trivial.
Secondly, by monitoring all transactions calling the `EntropyGenerator` contract and keeping track of the counters and the `writeEntropyBatch*` calldata.

## Tools Used
Unreleased AI tool

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use a secure and unpredictable method for entropy generation, such as Chainlink VRF or a similar oracle-based solution. Alternatively, one could implement a commit-reveal scheme, forcing the user to commit to some seed value, but delaying the minting by at least one block time, incorporating data from the latest block that the user could not have predicted at the time they were committing.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/69f64a4fe82f1ebcdf52307cee232de59ec48355/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L154-L157
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/69f64a4fe82f1ebcdf52307cee232de59ec48355/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L177-L178


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the current `nuke` function logic, the ETH reward after nuking the NFT is sent to `msg.sender` (the owner or the approved operator of this NFT). In case the ETH recipient is the approved operator, if the owner has no way to contact (on-chain or off-chain) that approved operator, he will not be able to get his ETH reward.

## Proof of Concept
Observe the `nuke` function:
```solidity
function nuke(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    require(
      nftContract.isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId),
      'ERC721: caller is not token owner or approved'
    );

    // ...

    nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
    (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
    require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');

    // ...
}

```
In the above function, `claimAmount` is sent to `msg.sender` after the NFT is burned. But `msg.sender` is not necessarily the owner of that NFT, so that `claimAmount` ETH is not guaranteed to be sent to that owner.

## Tools Used
Manually Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Solution 1: Force the `msg.sender` must be the owner of the NFT with the given `tokenId`
Fix the conditional in the require statement as:

```solidity
    require(
      nftContract.ownerOf(tokenId) == msg.sender,
      'Sender must be the NFT owner.'
    );
```

Solution 2: If the NFT's approved operator is still allowed to nuke it by the project business logic, the `claimAmount` (ETH) should be transferred directly to the NFT's owner, not the `msg.sender`

```solidity
    (bool success, ) = payable(nftContract.ownerOf(tokenId)).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Entropy sequence can be predicted and bad actors can monitor the contract to know when is the right time to mint given the entropy sequence reference that was generated. It will deny fairness and allow others to take advantage.


## Proof of Concept
From the whitepaper, the following was stated:
```
Genesis entropy is seeded using blockhash. Setting all 770 uint256 slots cost 15m gas, and due to contract & block size limits, this cannot be set in contract initialisation. Instead a function writes in entropy in 3 passes after the contract is deployed. 
```

On each of the `writeEntropyBatch` functions, the following code for generating entropy is:
```
     for (uint256 i = lastInitializedIndex; i < maxSlotIndex; i++) {
        uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
          keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
        ) % uint256(10) ** 78;
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue;
      }
    }
```

This uses the block number. Given the block after it was triggered, the batch entropies can be inferred when we run the calculation of pseudoRandomValue on own. These functions are also public and can be triggered by anyone so it might mess up the genesis functions.

After we can recreate the entropies written during the `writeEntropyBatch` calls, we can determine when is the right time to mint by listening to `Minted` events. The entropy is assigned when the nft contract calls `entropyGenerator.getNextEntropy()` assigning the next predetermined entropy.

A bot can monitor these and check for the following:
- the current number of mints using `totalSupply()`
- the next entropy to be assigned through `entropyGenerator.getNextEntropy()` 
- refer to the sequence of all the entropies generated and predict the `tokenId` given an entropy value.




## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Add access control on `writeEntropyBatch` functions
- Use solutions like Chainlink VRF to securely generate random

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Lets look at how this might happen, currently in the nuke function there is a check that for nuke to be called you have to be approved or owner if a malicious user was to approve themselves this check will pass even if during selling the owner is now the contract since they approved themselves they will still be able to nuke the NFT even if it is later after the NFT is bought as they are already in approve list .


The current implementation of the nuke function allows an NFT to be burned and claim its associated funds without checking if the NFT is listed for sale. This means that if an NFT is listed for sale and a user decides to nuke it, the NFT could be removed from the marketplace, and the user could potentially claim funds that were intended for the sale, disrupting the market and causing financial losses. The lack of this check could result in inconsistent state management and a poor user experience.

```javascript
function nuke(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    require(
      nftContract.isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId),
      'ERC721: caller is not token owner or approved'
    );
    require(
      nftContract.getApproved(tokenId) == address(this) ||
        nftContract.isApprovedForAll(msg.sender, address(this)),
      'Contract must be approved to transfer the NFT.'
    );
    require(canTokenBeNuked(tokenId), 'Token is not mature yet');

    uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
    uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
    uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size

    // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
    uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
      : potentialClaimAmount;

    fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund

    nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
    (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
    require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');

    emit Nuked(msg.sender, tokenId, claimAmount); // Emit the event with the actual claim amount
    emit FundBalanceUpdated(fund); // Update the fund balance
  }
```

## Proof of Concept
Listing an NFT for Sale:

A user first approves themselves and lists an NFT for sale, transferring ownership to the contract and creating a listing entry in the contract's listings mapping.
Nuking the Listed NFT:

user can then call the nuke function on the listed NFT, this will pass because they are still approved successfully burning the NFT and claiming the associated funds from the contract.
Since the nuke function does not verify the listing status of the NFT, the process completes without any errors, even though the NFT is still listed for sale.
Financial Consequences:

The sale proceeds of the NFT are forfeited as the NFT is no longer available for purchase.
Funds intended for the sale may be claimed by the user nuking the NFT, resulting in financial discrepancies.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
implement a check in the nuke function to ensure that an NFT cannot be nuked if it is currently listed for sale.

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
All contracts in scope (`NukeFund.sol`, `TraitForgeNft.sol`, `EntityForging.sol`, `EntityTrading.sol`, `EntropyGenerator.sol`, `DevFund.sol`) implement the Pausable interface from OpenZeppelin, and they all use the `whenNotPaused` modifier in different functions.

VS Code, Manual Review

Create external functions to pause / unpause the contracts that can only be called by the owner. These functions should then call `_pause() / _unpause()` from the Pausable interface.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L190
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280-L294
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L350-L352


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This is an edge case that happens every time there is a generation increment when minting a token. As we can see in the `mintToken()` function in `TraitForgeNft.sol` there is a mint price calculation after which the calculated `mintPrice` is passed to the `_mintInternal()` function. 
In the `_mintInternal()` function we first check if there is a need to increment generation, before minting the token and setting all the storage variables (e.g., `tokenGenerations[newItemId] = currentGeneration;`). 
The problem arises when it is time to increment generation (`_incrementGeneration()`) where the current generation is incremented by one, generation mint count is set to 0 and price increment is also recalculated, but there is no update to `mintPrice`. 

This means two things: 

1. The protocol incurs a loss as the user does not pay the correct price for the intended generation. Currently, this loss is 0.05 ETH, which is the price difference between two generations. Although this may not seem significant initially, if the protocol adjusts prices in the future, the loss could be greater. Additionally, since this occurs with every generation change, the loss will multiply by the number of generations.
2. The user is able to acquire a more valuable NFT for the price of a less valuable one, giving them an immediate advantage and the opportunity to sell it at a higher price. 

## Proof of Concept
Imagine following scenario: 

1. We have currently minted 10,000 NFTs of Gen1
2. User A is calling `mintToken` to mint another token
3. The mint price is calculated by using properties from the Gen1 since the `currentGeneration` is still 1 
4. We check `msg.value` and it is equal to the calculated mint price. All good so far. 
5. In the `_mintInternal()` function, we see that `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen` is satisfied since `10_000 >= 10_000`, so we go to `_incrementGeneration()`
6. In the `_incrementGeneration()` we do `currentGeneration++` setting it to 2. We reset the `generationMintCount[currentGeneration]` to 0, and we add `priceIncrementByGen` to the previous `priceIncrement`. The function is done.
7. The function `_mintInternal()` continues its execution where we actually mint the token and set following storage variables
```
    tokenGenerations[newItemId] = currentGeneration; // currentGeneration = 2
    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration]++;
    initialOwners[newItemId] = to;
```
8. We incremented generation and minted a new token, however after doing that, we forgot to recheck if the `msg.value >= newMintPrice`. This is necessary because we also increased `priceIncrement` which is part of the mint price calculation. 
9. User got Gen2 NFT but paid for GEN1.

## Tools Used
Manual Review, VS Code

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Considering the `calculateMintPrice()` function, the first NFT of the new generation has to be minted (so that `generationMintCounts[currentGeneration]` is not 0, which will cause `priceIncrement` to be 0 as well). 
Therefore, after minting a new token and setting all the variables in `_mintInternal()`, recalculate the price again and check if the `msg.value` will be enough for the new mint price. It would look like this: 

```
    tokenCreationTimestamps[newItemId] = block.timestamp;
    tokenEntropy[newItemId] = entropyValue;
    tokenGenerations[newItemId] = currentGeneration;
    generationMintCounts[currentGeneration]++;
    initialOwners[newItemId] = to;

    uint256 newMintPrice = calculateMintPrice();
    require(msg.value == newMintPrice, 'Insufficient ETH for the new generation');
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L353


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`EntropyGenerator.sol` contract sets the allowed caller variable at the time of deployment. This is supposed to be `TraitForgeNft.sol` contract so that different functions can be called from it. However, the function `initializeAlphaIndices()` has `onlyOwner` modifier from Ownable, unlike other functions which have `onlyAllowedCaller` modifier. This will cause many functions in `TraitForgeNft.sol` to revert when the function `_incrementGeneration()` is called (such as `mintToken()`, `mintWithBudget()` or `forge()`) causing a denial of service. The `_incrementGeneration()` will get called always when there is a need to switch from one generation to another, i.e. when the maximum number of tokens per generation is minted. This means, that users will be able to mint only the first generation. 

It is confirmed by the sponsor that the Multisig wallet is supposed to be the owner of all contracts, except from the `Airdrop.sol` contract (this one is supposed to be owned by `TraitForgeNft.sol` contract). 

## Proof of Concept
For the sake of simplicity add this function to the `TraitForgeNft.sol` contract
``` solidity 
 function _testCall() public {
    entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();
  }
```
And add this test to the TraitForgeNft.test.ts
``` solidity 
it('should not be possible to initializeAlphaIndices() if not owner', async() => {
      await expect(nft._testCall()).to.be.reverted;
    });
```

## Tools Used
VS Code, Hardhat, Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `onlyAllowedCaller` modifier instead of `onlyOwner` on `initializeAlphaIndices()` so that `TraitForgeNft.sol` is allowed to call it.

DoS

**Impact**
* Minting process will be halted after reaching the maximum tokens for the initial generation, also The protocol will be unable to progress beyond the first generation.

The [setWhitelistEndTime function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L126) does not validate if the provided end time is in the future. function setWhitelistEndTime(uint256 endTime_) external onlyOwner {

Manual Review

```solidity
function setWhitelistEndTime(uint256 endTime_) external onlyOwner {
+   require(endTime_ > block.timestamp, "End time must be in the future");
    whitelistEndTime = endTime_;
}
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L40


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [EntityForging contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L40) allows the owner to modify critical parameters, such as oneYearInDays, taxCut, and minimumListFee, after deployment. Although the setter functions in the contract is regulated by the onlyOwner modifier, which implies a level of trust in the owner, the ability to change these parameters can lead to significant disruptions if not properly managed.

The primary concern is the setOneYearInDays function, which allows the owner to reset the annual reset period for forging counts. If set to an unreasonably low value, this can lead to frequent resets, causing tokens to reset their forging counts too often and disrupting the intended functionality of the contract.

## Proof of Concept

While the onlyOwner modifier in the associated function provides a layer of trust, the potential for human error or malicious actions cannot be ignored. Implementing reasonable bounds will enhance the security and reliability of the contract, ensuring it operates as intended without unexpected disruptions. This approach aligns with best practices in smart contract development, promoting trustless systems and minimizing risks.

```solidity
  uint256 public oneYearInDays = 365 days;

  function setOneYearInDays(uint256 value) external onlyOwner {
    oneYearInDays = value;
  }
```

- The setOneYearInDays function allows the owner to set the duration for one year in days.
- This parameter is critical for managing the forging counts reset logic.
- The owner sets oneYearInDays to an unreasonably low value (e.g., 10 days).
- Tokens' forging counts reset too frequently, allowing potentially unlimited forging or disrupting the expected forging cycle.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement upper/lower or a fixed range of [365,366] days bounds for oneYearInDays to ensure it stays within a reasonable range. This minimizes the risk of setting the parameter to an unintended value.


## Assessed type

Context

- The contract developers have effectively stolen the seller's proceeds.

Manual review.

In all instances of the `setTaxCut` function, enforce a requirement that `_taxCut` be greater than `1`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When calling the `forgeWithListed` function, if `msg.value` is greater than the listing `fee`, the remaining amount of ETH will become trapped in the `EntityForging` contract with no way to recover it.

## Proof of Concept
- Alice calls `listForForging(1, 100)` on the `EntityForging` contract. This transaction is mined.
- Bob calls `forgeWithListed(1,2)` on the `EntityForging` contract, and sends a `msg.value` of `100` for the `fee`. This transaction is in the mempool.
- Alice calls `cancelListingForForging(1)` and `listForForging(1, 50)` to reduce the `fee` amount. These two transactions are mined (sequentially) in front of Bob's transaction.
- Bob's transaction is executed, but the fee for that token is now only 50, not 100 like he initially thought. Bob's 50 wei is now locked in the contract.

*I chose this scenario instead of the more obvious one where `msg.value > fee`, because this is a case where no one did anything "wrong" and no one made a mistake.*

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
At the end of the `forgeWithListed` function, calculate the remaining ETH and send it back to the caller.

Payable

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L24
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L128-L132
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L143-L150
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L165-L176


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When the contract NukeFund.sol is deployed, the `ageMultiplier` state variable is automatically initialized to 0. 
This variable is used to calculate the age of an entity, which is a part of the formula that calculates the total amount that can be nuked/claimed from the total pot. If `ageMultiplier` is not set to a non-null value, the total amount to be claimed will always be 0, and the NFT is also destroyed in the claiming process, creating a loss of funds for the users.

## Proof of Concept

The age multiplier is used when computing the age of an Entity in the `calculateAge` function:
```solidity
uint256 age = (daysOld *
  perfomanceFactor *
  MAX_DENOMINATOR *
  ageMultiplier) / 365; // add 5 digits for decimals
return age;
```
As `ageMultiplier` is 0, this function will also return 0.

The age is used in `calculateNukeFactor` to produce the nuke factor:
```solidity
uint256 adjustedAge = calculateAge(tokenId);

uint256 initialNukeFactor = entropy / 40;

uint256 finalNukeFactor = ((adjustedAge * defaultNukeFactorIncrease) /
      MAX_DENOMINATOR) + initialNukeFactor;

return finalNukeFactor;
```
This function will also return 0. This function is called inside `nuke`, to find out the amount to be claimed:

```solidity
uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId);
uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR;

..    

uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
      : potentialClaimAmount; 

fund -= claimAmount; 

nftContract.burn(tokenId); // Burn the token
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: claimAmount }('');
require(success, 'Failed to send Ether');
```

Since `finalNukeFactor` is 0, the claimAmount will also be 0; The function ends by burning the NFT and sending 0 ETH to the user. Sending 0 ETH is possible, so the next state will not cause a revert; The NFT will be burned and the user will not be able to recover his assets.


## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The issue can be mitigated by assigning the variable a non-zero value at construction, just as for the other `public uint256` vars in the contract:
`uint256 public ageMultiplier = 1;`

The issue can also be mitigated by ensuring that the `setAgeMultiplier` function is called after deploying the contract, but before the first `nuke` call. However, it's not safe to assume that this will be done. By looking in the `scripts` directory in the repository (`deployTasks.ts`), it seems that this function is not called anywhere. Doing a `grep -r setAgeMultiplier` call in the entire repository indicates that currently, there is no planned intention to perform this call post deployment, and severity rules instruct not to speculate on future actions or code changes. Consequently, within the current context, I'll label this issue as a high severity.



## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A user can maximize his profits by front-running other nuke transactions

## Proof of Concept

Let's assume that there are currently 1000 active entities, out of which a portion can be nuked. Until time T, all users are waiting for their entities to mature more and produce better profits. At time T, a user X decides to nuke his entity and withdraw a part of the honeypot. With an average nuke factor of ~14% (calculated from the average entropy, 555555), this nuke would eliminate the contribution of the last 86 minted entities, and would require 79 new ones to bring back the pot to the same value.

A malicious user can decide to front-run the transaction of user X and withdraw first, therefore getting a bigger chunk of the reward pool. Two average entities nuking - user X and the malicious user - would remove ~4 out of ~15.5 ETH from the pot. If a second malicious user attempts the same thing, it would already remove ~5.5 out of the 15.5 ETH.

If more than one user shares the same strategy, this could potentially hurt the protocol. If this triggers around 4% of the player base to nuke their entities, a nuke would not even be profitable anymore and would most likely cause all users to attempt to recover what they can from the investment and kill the game.

## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use flashbots to hide user intentions and prevent front-running.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L394


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [TraitForgeNft contract inherits OpenZeppelin's Pausable](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L19), and defines various functions which cannot be called while the contract is paused (for example: [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L141), and [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L394)). Yet it does not define a function that can actually trigger the pausing of the contract (by calling the _pause function available from the OpenZeppelin Pausable inherited). This means the contract can never be paused, and the entire logic for pausing the contract can never be reached - so in an emergency, or cases when the owner would find it appropriate or necessary to pause the contract, it will be impossible to do so.

Note that I have mentioned here only the instances where pausablity is expected in TraitForgeNft, but the same issue exists also in Airdrop, DevFund, EntityForging, EntityTrading, EntropyGenerator, NukeFund, and Trait (the latter inherits ERC20Pausable which inherits Pauseable, but none have a externally exposed function that could trigger the paused state of the contract).

## Proof of Concept
You can see that there is no function that changes the state of the defined _paused state variable, except the _pause and _unpause functions defined by OpenZeppelin, but these are internal and not used in the contract, so cannot be used by the owner (or anyone for that matter).

## Tools Used
Code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add externally callable pause() and unpause() functions which have an onlyOwner modifier for their access control, like so:

```
function pause() external onlyOwner {
  _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
  _unpause();
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L61


# Vulnerability details

### Description
The `claim()` function in the DevFund contract is vulnerable to a form of slippage where the amount of rewards a developer receives can be less than expected due to changes in the contract's balance between the time of calculation and the time of transfer.

### Details
1. The `claim()` function calculates pending rewards based on the current `totalRewardDebt`:

```solidity
uint256 pending = info.pendingRewards + (totalRewardDebt - info.rewardDebt) * info.weight;
```

2. The actual transfer is performed by the `safeRewardTransfer()` function:
```solidity
uint256 claimedAmount = safeRewardTransfer(msg.sender, pending);
```

3. The `safeRewardTransfer()` function checks the current balance before transfer:
```solidity
uint256 _rewardBalance = payable(address(this)).balance;
 if (amount > *rewardBalance) amount = *rewardBalance;
```

### Slippage Scenario
1. A developer calls `claim()`, and `pending` is calculated based on the current `totalRewardDebt`.
2. Before `safeRewardTransfer()` is called, the contract's balance decreases (e.g., due to another claim or an external transfer).
3. `safeRewardTransfer()` checks the new, lower balance and reduces the `amount` to be transferred.
4. The developer receives less than the calculated `pending` amount.

### Impact
- Developers may receive fewer rewards than initially calculated.
- This discrepancy is not accounted for in the contract's state, potentially leading to lost rewards.
- The issue can create an incentive for developers to "race" to claim rewards, potentially increasing gas costs.

### Proof of Concept
1. Contract has 100 ETH, `totalRewardDebt` is 2, and a developer has a weight of 50.
2. Developer calls `claim()`, `pending` is calculated as 50 * (2 - 0) = 100 ETH.
3. Before `safeRewardTransfer()` executes, another transaction reduces the contract balance to 80 ETH.
4. `safeRewardTransfer()` only sends 80 ETH instead of 100 ETH.
5. The developer loses 20 ETH of rewards, and this loss is not recorded in the contract state.

### Fix
Implement an atomic update and transfer mechanism in the `claim()` function:

```solidity
function claim() external whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    DevInfo storage info = devInfo[msg.sender];
    
    uint256 currentBalance = address(this).balance;
    uint256 pending = info.pendingRewards + (totalRewardDebt - info.rewardDebt) * info.weight;
    
    uint256 claimableAmount = pending > currentBalance ? currentBalance : pending;
    
    if (claimableAmount > 0) {
        (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: claimableAmount}("");
        require(success, "Transfer failed");
        
        info.pendingRewards = pending - claimableAmount;
        emit Claim(msg.sender, claimableAmount);
    }
    
    info.rewardDebt = totalRewardDebt;
}
```

This fix ensures that:
1. The claimable amount is based on the current balance at the time of calculation.
2. The transfer is made within the same atomic transaction as the calculation.
3. Any discrepancy between `pending` and `claimableAmount` is stored in `pendingRewards` for future claims.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L123-L128


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A user can mint the “the Golden God” NFT with 999999 entropy without any difficulty.

## Proof of Concept

Whenever a new NFT is minted, the [next available](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L288) entropy is assigned to it, from which its traits and parameters are derived. There are `10000` entropies created per generation, 13 of which get concatenated and stored in a single storage slot. The entire process revolves around the users getting a random entropy for their NFT, in order for the protocol’s fairness to remain consistent across all generations, for all users. The best entropy a user’s NFT can get assigned is `999999`, which would mean that all of its stats are the highest that one could get. It can be achieved only when the specific slot and index within that slot are matched with the parameters [slotIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L19) and [numberIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L20) (assigned upon deployment of [EntropyGenerator](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol) by calling [initializeAlphaIndices](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206-L216))

A problem arises when a user can mint “the Golden God” without going through any hurdles. As the selected slot index and number index are stored in state variables in [EntropyGenerator](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol), a user can read the current values of [slotIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L19) and [numberIndexSelection](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L20) and then call the function [getPublicEntropy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L123-L128) with them passed as an argument. The returned result from the function will confirm that the user can get their NFT minted with 999999 entropy, if they mint an NFT at that specific slot and number.

An additional source that can help with their timing, are the parameters [currentSlotIndex](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L12) and [currentNumberIndex](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L13) which can be read using the function [getStorage](https://web3js.readthedocs.io/en/v1.2.11/web3-eth.html#getstorageat) at from web3js (an [example](https://solidity-by-example.org/hacks/accessing-private-data/) of how that works). Using the information stated so far, a malicious user can time their mint perfectly, ensuring that they receive “the Golden God” NFT, or they can front-run any other user who would’ve got “the Golden God” using pure luck.

<details>
    <summary>Coded PoC (foundry)</summary>

In order to setup Foundry run the commands:

- `foundryup`
- `forge install`
- `forge install foundry-rs/forge-std --no-commit`
- Add `forge-std/=lib/forge-std/src/` to `remappings.txt`

Within the `test` folder, create a new file `FoundryTests.t.sol` and paste the following:
https://gist.github.com/Vancelott/8be01402db0c498f29b20e85943a9991

You can run the test with: `forge test —mt testEasyGolden -vvvv`
</details>

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

One possible reccomendation may be instead of setting the `slotIndexSelection` and `numberIndexSelection` variables in the [`initializeAlphaIndices()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206) function, remove it and let the user randomly get the "Golden God” NFT using pure luck.


## Assessed type

Other

* Due to above mint, `_tokenIds` will be `10000` now.
* call `mintWithBudget` by passing 2 ether. No entities will be minted and all eth will be refunded to the caller.

The problametic condition can be removed since it doesn't serve any purpose in current implementation and blocks the functionality.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L328


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The project has defined "Golden God" which is the most valuable entity. From the documentation,
``
There is a certain entropy, “999999” which is referred to as “the Golden God”, since it has perfect parameters and will exceed all other entities if played correctly. The Golden God is scanned for and is kept out of the first 2 passes, but is deliberately set in the final pass (at some random point). The Golden God should be the most valuable entity. 
``

As confirmed with the sponsor, the game requires to have one "Golden God" in each generation. However, due to inclusion of forged entity in generation count, it is very possible case that there may not be any "Golden God" in some generation. 


## Proof of Concept
* Let's assume 10000 entities are minted in first generation. 
* 3000 entities of second generation are minted via forging from two first generation entities.
* Due to this, only `7000` can be minted now in second generation. If `slotIndexSelectionPoint` for second generation is more than `(7000/13 = 539)`, then minting in second generation won't reach at that `slotIndexSelectionPoint` and no golden god entity will be minted in second generation.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Don't have any easy fix for this. May be design of code should be changed

## Impact
The `_incrementGeneration` function overwrites the `generationMintCounts` of new generation to `0`. However, the new generation may have mint counts due to forging done by previous generation entities. `calculateMintPrice` is also affected since it relies on `generationMintCounts`

* 10000 entities are minted in first generation.
* due to forging, let's assume 5000 entities are produced in generation 2.
* on calling `mintToken`, generationMintCounts[1] will be 0 but should be 5000.
* 10000 entities can be minted in second generation again. But due to forging which is not considered, it can exceed `maxTokensPerGen`

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Do not overwrite next generation mint count to 0

`maxAllowedClaimDivisor` is used to determine the portion of nuke fund that can be claimed by entity holder. It can be updated by owner by calling `setMaxAllowedClaimDivisor`. However, the update to it may cause the issues to user and incentives.

Since `nukeFactor` of user increases as days passes, it may be possible that user is not nuking his entity in hope that he can receive higher portion of nuke fund at later stage. But if `maxAllowedClaimDivisor` is updated(ex: from `2` to `3`), the user was earlier hoping for 50% of nuke fund will now only get `33%` of nuke fund. Due to this, all their incentives for waiting can be useless because of decrease in incentive. It may be the case that user could have gotten similar reward even if they had nuked earlier when `maxAllowedClaimDivisor` was `2`. 

## Tools Used
Manual review

Not a simple solution. Maybe add a timelock with sufficient time for an update to `maxAllowedClaimDivisor` parameter or make it fixed.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L145-L148
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L165-L178


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It seems like formula used in `calculateNukeFactor` is wrong. Users doesn't have much incentive to hold the entity instead of directly nuking the entity and claiming the portion of nuke funds. 

First reason is inconsistency with docs. The docs say that fastest mature will be in 30 days. When the entity is matured, it's `nukeFactor` should be more than or equal to `nukeFactorMaxParam`. However, even if we consider `golden god` entity which has the best performance factor, it is not maturing in 30 days. 
Let's run the calculation for golden god whose entropy = 999999.
```solidity
his performance factor = 9
his adjusted after 30 days is 
age = (30 * 9 * MAX_DENOMINATOR) / 365; 
his fiinal nukeFactor is  finalNukeFactor = (( (30 * 9 * MAX_DENOMINATOR) / 365 * 250) /MAX_DENOMINATOR) + 999999/40; 
= 184 + 24999 = 25183
```

The other reason is incentive mechanism of calculating `nukeFactor`. The `nukeFactor` is calculated as following:
```solidity
 uint256 initialNukeFactor = entropy / 40;
 uint256 finalNukeFactor = ((adjustedAge * defaultNukeFactorIncrease) /
      MAX_DENOMINATOR) + initialNukeFactor; 
```
`performanceFactor` ranges from `0` to `9`.

The `nukeFactor` heavily depends upon `initialNukeFactor` which depends on `entropy`. `defaultNukeFactorIncrease` is only `250` so `nukeFactor` only increases by maximum `performanceFactor / 365` per day which is comparably very small value compared to `entropy / 40`.  Due to this, users don't have any incentive to wait for their increase in nuke factor but directly claiming the nuke fund. 


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The formula to calculate `nukeFactor` should be designed better by considering incentives.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L84-L98


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In `writeEntropyBatch1` and `writeEntropyBatch2`, the following require condition is added.
`require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');`

However, there is no such condition in `writeEntropyBatch3`. So, if `pseudoRandomValue` equals to `999999`, then it will correspond to golden god. However, there will be another slot that will correspond to golden god which is determined by calling `initializeAlphaIndices` by owner. Due to this, the invariant of game of only having one golden god entity per generation may be incorrect.

The probability of 6 consecutive `9` in 78 digit number is `0.0073%`. Since we are generating `258` numbers, the total probability is `1.88%`.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the require condition in `writeEntropyBatch3` also

Invalid Validation

`taxCut` variable in `EntityTrading` and `EntityForging` determines how much percentage of value needs to sent to `nukeFund`. The remaining is set to `seller` in `EntityTrading` and `forger` in `EntityForging`. However, `taxCut` variable can be updated by `owner`. 

The issue arises when `taxCut` is updated by owner. In `EntityTrading`, the holder of the entity would have listed the entity(by calling `listNFTForSale`) for sale considering the current `taxCut`. If the previous `taxCut` was `10%` and  holder wants to get `9 ether` after `tax deduction`, he would list it for `10 ether`. But if `taxCut` is increased to `20%` after listing but before someone buys it, the holder of entity will get only `8 ether`. Due to this, seller will get less price than anticipated. 

The similar issue will arise in `EntityForging`. It's explained in below poc with example.

## Proof of Concept
* `taxCut` = 10
* The seller lists the NFT(tokenId = 100) for forging by calling `listForForging(100, 1 ether)`.
* The seller put the price as 1 ether previously hoping that he will receive 0.9 ether when someone forges with his entity.
* owner updates `taxCut` to 20
* When someone forges with listed NFT of tokenId = 100, seller will receive 0.5 ether and not what he anticipated.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`taxCut` used in deduction should be the same at which the seller or forger lists the entity and not the updated one.


## Assessed type

Other
