# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L87-L90
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L131-L133


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `forgeWithListed` is used to list the entity for forging. The trait named `forgePotential` is used to ensure that entity can't forge more than `forgePotential` in certain time interval(denoted by `oneYearInDays`). The condition is as follows:
```solidity
require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```
Due to above condition, it will be possible to create a listing even if `forgingCounts[tokenId]` is equal to `forgePotential`. And since there isn't any checking on `forgingCounts` during `forge`, it will be possible to forge an entity more than `forgePotential`. 


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the condition as follows:
```solidity
require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The contract is intended to use the Pausable functionality to allow pausing and unpausing of certain operations. However, the required `pause` and `unpause` functions are not exposed, making it impossible to utilize this functionality.

The contract should include and expose the following functions:

pause(): This function should allow the contract owner or an authorized role to pause the contract, halting specified operations.
unpause(): This function should allow the contract owner or an authorized role to unpause the contract, resuming normal operations.



## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add following functions in all contract:
```solidity
function pause() public onlyOwner {
        _pause();
    }

    function unpause() public onlyOwner {
        _unpause();
    }
```

Library

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L206


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Minor loss of funds for the protocol (maximum of 9 NFTs not minted by users) and lack of availability.

A maximum of 9 NFTs will not be available to mint by the users, or the protocol will be blocked. When 10,000 are minted, the protocol will not allow minting any more NFTs because only the owner can increment the generation.

A secondary, more theoretical, risk exists:
If the owner of the protocol uses a script to automatically increment the generation, there is a risk of determinism. A malicious attacker can mint some NFTs to acquire the 999999th NFT just after the script executes.

## Proof of Concept

First Risk, 

Using the following test with an adress different from the owner called alice and  a mint harness to simplify the handle of merkel tree modifier :

     function test_probleme_10002(address user) public{
		uint256 resultat = user.balance;
		vm.startPrank(alice);
		for( int i=0;i<10002;i++){
			traitForgeNft.mintTokenHarness{value: 0.4 ether}();
		}
	
	}
We obtain the following result :

    ├─ [18830] 0xCeF98e10D1e80378A9A74Ce074132B66CDD5e88d::mintTokenHarness{value: 400000000000000000}()
    │   ├─ [2665] 0x0a6dA0C3010c30cBBbA9dFaF6868583D180818e7::initializeAlphaIndices()
    │   │   └─ ← [Revert] revert: Ownable: caller is not the owner
    │   └─ ← [Revert] revert: Ownable: caller is not the owner
    └─ ← [Revert] revert: Ownable: caller is not the owner

The initializeAlphaIndices is only callable by the owner. As so, the owner need to call _mintNewEntity to unlock the protocol. An NFT will be minted by the owner and not an user.

Second Risk:

The function initializeAlphaIndices uses hashValue, which is based on the block.number and block.timestamp. A malicious attacker could determine the number of blocks required for the script to react, determine the right block.number and block.timestamp to get faster the perfect 999999 entity, and try to get it using the mintWithBudget function.

## Tools Used
Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Delete the modifier onlyOwner from the function initializeAlphaIndices() and use a better randomness generator ( chainlink for example).





## Assessed type

Other

```solidity
    // Check forger's breed count increment but do not check forge potential here
    // as it is already checked in listForForging for the forger
    forgingCounts[forgerTokenId]++;
```


Here in the function `forgeWithListed()` , contract is assuming that `forgingCount` value is always less than `forgingPotential` since  there is a check for the current forgingCount of the tokenId when it gets listed in `listForForging()` function. (mentioned in their comments)

Lets go through that check in `listForForging()`, 

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L87-L90
```solidity
    require(
=>      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential, 
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

Means, even if the forgingCounts[tokenId] == forgePotential , we are continuing the execution and listing that tokenId for forging.

So the same  token Id can be used for forging even though it reaches its forgingPotential.

## Tools Used
Manual.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
A check before incrementing the forgingCount

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L61
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L179
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L70
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L41
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `EntityForging`, `EntityTrading` and `DevFund` contracts all inherits `Pausable` contract from Openzeppelin to allow the contracts to be paused in the event of emergencies. To this effect, these aforementioned contracts all implement a `whenNotPaused` modifier on their various functions. 

For example, in `EntityTrading` the functions `listNFTForSale`, `buyNFT` and `cancelListing` all have the `whenNotPaused` modifier. The same is true for `listForForging`, forgeWithlisted` and `cancelListingForForging` functions in `EntityForging` contract as well as `claim` function in `DevFund` contract. 

It is noted that neither of the three contracts have implemented the `pause()` and `unpause ()` functions which means that the contracts can never enter a pause state . There is absolutely no mechanism for the contract to be paused. 

Openzeppelin requires contracts inheriting from `Pausable` contract to implement an external/public `pause` and `unpause` function which would in turn call their internal `_pause` and `_unpause` functions. 

Effectively, if there is any form of emergency, the contracts can never be paused and critical actions such as canceling Listing, buyingNFT, listing NFT for sale are never paused. 

## Proof of Concept
1. https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/DevFund/DevFund.sol#L61
2. https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L179
3. https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L70
4. https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L41
5. https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63


## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider implementing `pause` and `unpause` functionality in the aforementioned contracts. 


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

**Description**
The `transferFrom()` and `_mint()` methods are used instead of `safeTransferFrom()` and `_safeMint()`, presumably to save gas. I however argue that this isn’t recommended because:

[OpenZeppelin’s documentation](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/token/erc721#IERC721-transferFrom-address-address-uint256-) discourages the use of `transferFrom()` and `_mint()`, use `safeTransferFrom()` and `_safeMint()` whenever possible.


If the `to` argument in the [TraitForgeNft::_mintInternal()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280) is a contract address, that does not support ERC721, the NFT will be frozen in the contract.

As per the documentation of EIP-721:
> A wallet/broker/auction application MUST implement the wallet interface if it will accept safe transfers.

**Impact**

Users possibly lose their NFTs

**Recommended mitigation**

Use `safeTransferFrom()` and `_safeMint()` instead of `transferFrom()` and `_mint()`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L75-L77


# Vulnerability details

## Description
There is a `contradictory` element in `NukeFund` which allow the owner to set a max nuke for more than 50% of the NukeFund to be collected by a single nuke which `go against rules` presented to players and seems to warrant `Medium`. 

One of the key invariant of the game and economy is that a `single nuke cannot claim more than 50%` of the NukeFund contract funds. While the variable `maxAllowedClaimDivisor` controlling this is initialized properly, the owner has a way to `set this value to any arbitrary value` later on, which `doesn't look very legetimate` and is error-prone. I understand the flexibility here, and that the owner is a trusted actor, but this seems to cross the line a bit.

```solidity
  uint256 public maxAllowedClaimDivisor = 2;
  
  ...
  
  uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
  uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
  uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size

  ...  
  
  function setMaxAllowedClaimDivisor(uint256 value) external onlyOwner {
    maxAllowedClaimDivisor = value;
  }
 
```

## Impact
Owner is allowed to set the `max nuke to any arbitrary value` using the priviledge setter.

## PoC
No PoC provided as the claimed issue is very obvious.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The owner can keep the flexibility in case he wants to reduce it, but he should at least make sure the setter is always respecting the 50% rule. This increase legetimacy of the game for the players and ensure any input error with this setter cannot cause a disaster.

# Vulnerability details

## Description
There is a bug in `EntityForging::getListedTokenIds` when the player is unlisting a forger NFT which still return the previous id as if the NFT would `still be listed` which is innacurate and seems to warrant `Medium` severity. 

Be aware that this issue is also present in `EntityTrading` but in a more hidden way as there is not official getter, but `EntityTrading::listedTokenIds` is public and will present the same issue as `EntityTrading` is not cleaning it up either.

The root cause is due to the fact that `_cancelListingForForging` is `not reseting listedTokenIds` but only listings state variable when unlisting a forger NFT. This oversight doesn't seems to cause major damage in the moment, but it's not clear either as it will affect anyone that rely on getListedTokenIds function. `TraitForgeNft::_beforeTokenTransfer` use it, but that doesn't seem to cause any issues.

## Impact
`getListedTokenIds` is not returning the proper information when an NFT is being unlisted.

## PoC
Add the following changes `EntityForging.test.ts` and run `yarn test`
We can see that the function still return 1 as if the NFT was listed.

      await entityForging.connect(owner).cancelListingForForging(tokenId);
      const listingId = await entityForging.getListedTokenIds(tokenId);

      expect(listingId).to.equal(0);
    }); 
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L33-L35
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L72
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L146
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L41


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the owner changes the `taxCut` to a number which doesn't return a percentage value when a number gets divided by it then the calculation for nuke fund and dev fee will be incorrect.

## Proof of Concept
According to the docs:
> 10% of Forge Fees and Sales goes into the Nuke Fund

Let's look at how that is implemented in code (`EntityTrading.sol: buyNFT()`):
```solidity
uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;
```
As you can see it doesn't calculate the nuke fund fee as a percentage and instead divides by `taxCut`. 
For the current value `taxCut = 10` the calculation is fine because dividing by 10 gives us 10% of a number. However if we change the `taxCut` to 20 for example it will not calculate 20%. Here is an example if the nft costs 600 wei:
> 600 / 20 = 300 (50% - incorrect)
600 * 20 / 100 = 120 (20% - correct)

You may argue that the nuke fund fee will always be 10% but the function `setTaxCut()` allows the owner to change the value. If he expects it to work as a percentage then the calculation will be incorrect.

This bug also occurs in `NukeFund.sol` and `EntityForging.sol`:
```solidity
uint256 devShare = msg.value / taxCut; // Calculate developer's share (10%)
```
```solidity
uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
-uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;
+uint256 nukeFundContribution = (msg.value * taxCut) / 100;
```
The same fix applies for all instances.


## Assessed type

Error

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
According to the docs and dev, users have to wait 3 days before being able to nuke their NFT:
> After a 3-day maturity period, anyone can nuke their entity (forever burn) to claim a share of the ETH in the Fund

> -Can people nuke their nfts in the first generations?
-Yes but they must wait 3 days after acquiring

However they can nuke whenever they want without waiting 3 days.

## Proof of Concept
The function `NukeFund.sol:canTokenBeNuked()` returns whether a token can be nuked or not. It does so by checking if the 3 day period has passed:
```solidity
  function canTokenBeNuked(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (bool) {
...
    uint256 tokenAgeInSeconds = block.timestamp -
      nftContract.getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp(tokenId);
    // Assuming tokenAgeInSeconds is the age of the token since it's holding the nft, check if it's over minimum days held
    return tokenAgeInSeconds >= minimumDaysHeld;
  }
```
According to the comment it assumes that `tokenAgeInSeconds` is the time that has passed since the current owner of the token acquired it.
The issue here is that it checks how much time has passed since the token was transferred between users. If the owner has only minted the token without transferring it then he will be able to nuke at any time.

`getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp()` returns a mapping `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp[tokenId]`. This mapping is only changed in `_beforeTokenTransfer()` which is called only during transfers and not on mints. 
This means that if the owner hasn't transferred his token then the mapping will return 0. Now if we try to calculate `tokenAgeInSeconds` we will get `block.timestamp - 0` which will always be more than 3 days. This means any user can nuke his token after minting without waiting.

When I messaged the dev about this issue he said that "Minting sets value for getTokenCreationTimeStamp". Perhaps it was intended for `canTokenBeNuked()` to also check for `getTokenCreationTimeStamp` but it does not.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
  function canTokenBeNuked(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (bool) {
...
-    uint256 tokenAgeInSeconds = block.timestamp -
-      nftContract.getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp(tokenId);
...
-    return tokenAgeInSeconds >= minimumDaysHeld;

+    uint256 ageSinceTransfer = block.timestamp -
+      nftContract.getTokenLastTransferredTimestamp(tokenId);

+    uint256 ageSinceBirth = block.timestamp -
+      nftContract.getTokenCreationTimestamp(tokenId);

+    return ageSinceTransfer >= minimumDaysHeld &&
+    ageSinceBirth >= minimumDaysHeld
  }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L215


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`mintWithBudget()` is a function in `TraitForgeNft.sol` that is intended to allow a user to mint as many NFTs as he can using a set budget. The issue is that this function will not work after the first generation.

## Proof of Concept
The problem occurs in the while statement of the function:
```solidity
    while (budgetLeft >= mintPrice && _tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen) {
      _mintInternal(msg.sender, mintPrice);
      amountMinted++;
      budgetLeft -= mintPrice;
      mintPrice = calculateMintPrice();
    }
```
As you can see the second check in the while statement is `_tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen`. This is used to ensure that the mint cap per gen is not exceeded. The issue is that instead of checking that the tokens minted in the current gen don't excceed the cap, it checks that all tokens in TOTAL don't exceed it. This is a problem as `maxTokensPerGen` is set to 10_000 but `_tokenIds` can go beyond 10_000 as it does not reset on gen incrementation. The function will simply revert after the first 10_000 tokens have been minted.

This check is unnecessary as the `_mintInternal()` function will automatically increment the generation after `maxTokensPerGen` has been reached. It will also adjust NFT prices accordingly.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the `_tokenIds < maxTokensPerGen` check.


## Assessed type

Error

function listForForging(

    require(
@-->    forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential, // @audit <= should be <
        'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );

    ...
}
```

2. Alice forges the token.
3. Alice tries to forge the token again, but the contract incorrectly allows it.

Manual Review

Change line [L88] as follows:

```solidity
require(
-   forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
+   forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential,
    'Entity has reached its forging limit'
);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L147
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L128-L131


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `NukeFund::calculateAge()` function is tasked with computing the age of a token, taking into account its `performanceFactor`, which can be maximum value of `9` (entropy being 999999). Additionally, the `ageMultiplier` is currently set to `1`, a value expected to be deprecated following the audit, according to team plans. Documentation states that top-performing tokens (with entropy being 999999) should mature fastest, approximately within 30 days. However, the function’s maximum output is calculated as `30 (days) * 9 (performance factor) * 100,000 (MAX_DENOMINATOR) * 1 (ageMultiplier) / 365 = 73,972`. Subsequently, when the `NukeFund::calculateNukeFactor()` computes the `finalNukeFactor` on [L147](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L147), the result is `((73,972 (adjustedAge) * 250 (defaultNukeFactorIncrease)) / 100,000 (MAX_DENOMINATOR)) + 24,999 (initialNukeFactor = entropy / 40 = 999,999 / 40) = 25,183`. During the `NukeFund::nuke()` process, the `calculateNukeFactor()` is invoked to verify if a token’s nuke factor surpasses the `nukeFactorMaxParam`, which is `MAX_DENOMINATOR / 2 = 50,000`—nearly twice the size of the computed `finalNukeFactor`. This discrepancy suggests that the maturation period for the highest-performing tokens is not the intended 30 days, but closer to 60 days.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider revising the `defaultNukeFactorIncrease` to `500` or not removing `ageMultiplier` being `2` to align the maturation time of top-performing tokens with the documented 30 days.


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L47-L61


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Entropy values are stored in the entropySlot[770] private variable. Although being a private variable, Ethereum is a public blockchain, which means that any value or variable can be searched by looking at a smart contract's storage slots.

Users can look at the current value to be used and decide whether it is worth making an operation which involves getEntropy() or not, if the see a convenient value near. This incentivizes users to wait for the moment until that value comes and then try to get that value for them, which completely breaks the randomness the system is expected to have.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The recommended mitigation for this issue would involve a complete change in the system: if true randomness is required, entropy values should be calculated in real time by using a decentralized oracle like Chainlink.

Other possible and easier to implement solutions are to calculate values in real time the same way it is done in the current version of the contract (even though we should take into account that this is a deterministic way, so we could predict the outcome if we know the value of ```block.number```, which destroys randomess) or use a variable that sets a waiting time for a user why requests an entropy value, although this would make the system much slower.


## Assessed type

DoS

This issue has severe implications:
1. Generation transitions will always revert, effectively halting the entire minting process once the first generation is complete.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L18
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L63-L92
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L81
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L104


# Vulnerability details

The `listNFTForSale()` function transfers the NFT token from the seller to the `EntityTrading` contract using [nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53). It then creates a new listing with the seller's address (`msg.sender`) as the original owner. However, it does not prevent the token from being transferred again externally.

If an external `transferFrom()` call is made to transfer a listed token, the actual ownership of the token will change, but the listing and the `tokenOriginalOwner` mapping will still point to the original seller. This violates the `consistentOriginalOwner` invariant because the original owner in the ghost mapping will no longer match the actual owner of the token.

1. **Line 53**: [nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId);](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53) - transfers the NFT from the seller to the contract when listing an NFT for sale.

2. **Line 81**: [nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId);](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L81) - transfers the NFT from the contract to the buyer when an NFT is purchased.

3. **Line 104**: [nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId);](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L104) - transfers the NFT from the contract back to the seller when a listing is canceled.

## Impact
1. The original seller may no longer have control over the listed token, but the listing will still indicate them as the seller.
2. The new owner of the token may not be able to cancel the listing or receive the proceeds from the sale.

2. The token is transferred to the `EntityTrading` contract, and a new listing is created with Alice as the seller.
3. Alice approves Bob to transfer the token using the NFT contract's `approve()` function.
5. Bob calls the NFT contract's `transferFrom()` function to transfer the token from the `EntityTrading` contract to himself.
6. The token ownership is now changed to Bob, but the listing and the `tokenOriginalOwner` mapping still indicate Alice as the seller.

2. Modifying the NFT contract's `transferFrom()` function to check if the token being transferred is listed in the `EntityTrading` contract.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L94-L109


# Vulnerability details

`cancelListing()` function can mark a listing as inactive without removing the token ID from the `listedTokenIds` mapping. This violates the assumption that listed token IDs should always map to a valid and active listing index invariantly checked, and let's look at the relevant parts of the `cancelListing()` function: [EntityTrading.sol#L94-L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L94-L109)
```solidity
function cancelListing(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {
    Listing storage listing = listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];

    // check if caller is the seller and listing is active
    require(
      listing.seller == msg.sender,
      'Only the seller can cancel the listing.'
    );
    require(listing.isActive, 'Listing is not active.');

    nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer the nft back to seller

    delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]]; // mark the listing as inactive or delete it

    emit ListingCanceled(tokenId, msg.sender);
}
```
As you can see, the function deletes the listing from the `listings` mapping using `delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]]`. However, it does not remove the token ID from the `listedTokenIds` mapping.

This means that after calling `cancelListing()`, the `listedTokenIds` mapping will still contain the token ID, but the corresponding listing will be inactive or deleted. This violates the `validListedTokenIds` invariant, which expects the listing to be active if the token ID is present in `listedTokenIds`.

## Impact
The presence of inactive listings in the `listedTokenIds` mapping can lead to incorrect assumptions and unexpected behavior in other parts of the contract or external systems relying on this mapping. It can cause confusion and inconsistencies when querying or iterating over the listed token IDs.

Moreover, if the `listedTokenIds` mapping is used for any critical decision-making or calculations, the presence of inactive listings could lead to incorrect results or even enable unintended exploitation.

## Proof of Concept
1. User A lists their NFT with token ID 1 using `listNFTForSale()`.
2. The token ID 1 is added to `listedTokenIds`, and a new active `Listing` is created.
3. User A decides to cancel the listing by calling `cancelListing()` for token ID 1.
4. The `isActive` flag for the listing is set to `false`, but the token ID 1 remains in `listedTokenIds`.
5. The `validListedTokenIds` invariant is now violated, as token ID 1 exists in `listedTokenIds` but points to an inactive listing.

While it deletes the listing from the `listings` mapping, it does not remove the corresponding entry from the `listedTokenIds` mapping. This means that after canceling a listing, the `listedTokenIds` mapping will still contain the `tokenId`, but it will point to a non-existent or inactive listing in the `listings` mapping.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
the `cancelListing()` function should also delete the entry from `listedTokenIds` when a listing is canceled, by adding the following line after deleting the listing from `listings`:

```diff
  delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]];
+ delete listedTokenIds[tokenId];
```

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L116


# Vulnerability details

## Impact 
The `setMaxGeneration` function in the `TraitForgeNft.sol` contract only checks if `maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration` but does not check if `maxGeneration_ >= 10`. This means it is possible to set `maxGeneration_` to a value less than 10, which contradicts the whitepaper's statement: ["There are a total of 10 Generations (extended as the game goes on)"](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pihtkKyyxobFWdaNU4YfAy56Q7WIMbFJjSHUAfRm6BA/edit).

## Proof of Concept
The `setMaxGeneration` function in the `TraitForgeNft.sol` contract only checks if `maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration`, but does not check if `maxGeneration_ >= 10`.
[contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol:setMaxGeneration_L116](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L116)
```solidity
  function setMaxGeneration(uint maxGeneration_) external onlyOwner {
    require(
@audit=>      maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration,
      "can't below than current generation"
    );
    maxGeneration = maxGeneration_;
  }

```
This means it is possible to set `maxGeneration_` to a value less than 10, which contradicts the whitepaper's statement: ["There are a total of 10 Generations (extended as the game goes on)"](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pihtkKyyxobFWdaNU4YfAy56Q7WIMbFJjSHUAfRm6BA/edit).
```solidity
Generation 1 Mint
10,000 “Gen 1” entities are available to mint. The first starts at 0.005 ETH and each subsequent one rises linearly by 0.0000245 ETH until the final is 0.25 ETH. In total if all are minted then 1,275 ETH is raised in Generation 1. Each generation’s price increment increases by 0.000005. There are a total of 10 Generations (extended as the game goes on), which can be minted in parallel via a breeding mechanism. In theory, 24,000 ETH could accrue to the central honeypot. 

```


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to add a check for `maxGeneration_ >= 10`.
```solidity
  function setMaxGeneration(uint maxGeneration_) external onlyOwner {
    require(
-              maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration,
+              maxGeneration_ >= currentGeneration && maxGeneration_  >= 10,
      "can't below than current generation"
    );
    maxGeneration = maxGeneration_;
  }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L375-L379


# Vulnerability details

One of the key features of the `TraitForgeNft` contract is tracking the timestamp of the last transfer for each token using the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` mapping.

The [_beforeTokenTransfer()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L367-L396) function is an internal hook that is called before a token transfer occurs. It is responsible for updating the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` and handling the unlisting of tokens from forging if they are being transferred.

However, there is an issue with the logic that updates the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp`. The condition `if (from != to)` is meant to update the timestamp only when the `from` and `to` addresses are different, indicating a genuine transfer. 

The bug lies in the implementation of the timestamp update logic. Even though the condition `if (from != to)` is correct, the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` is not being updated as expected when `from` and `to` are different. [TraitForgeNft.sol#L375-L379](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L375-L379)

```solidity
uint listedId = entityForgingContract.getListedTokenIds(firstTokenId);
/// @dev don't update the transferred timestamp if from and to address are same
if (from != to) {
    // Bug: The lastTokenTransferredTimestamp is not being updated correctly when from and to addresses are different.
    lastTokenTransferredTimestamp[firstTokenId] = block.timestamp;
}
```

The root cause of the issue needs to be investigated further to determine why the timestamp is not being updated correctly within the `if (from != to)` block.

The issue is in the order of operations and the side effects of the `entityForgingContract.getListedTokenIds(firstTokenId)` function call.

   1. The [getListedTokenIds(firstTokenId)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L375) is called before the `if (from != to)` block.
   2. One possible scenario is that the `getListedTokenIds(firstTokenId)` may revert or throw an exception under certain conditions. If this happens, the execution of the `_beforeTokenTransfer()` function will be halted, and the [lastTokenTransferredTimestamp](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L378) will not be updated.
  
## Impact

1. The `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` mapping will not accurately reflect the timestamp of the last transfer for tokens. This can lead to incorrect tracking of token transfer history and any functionality that relies on this timestamp.

4. Any external system or off-chain process that relies on the accuracy of the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` may make incorrect assumptions or decisions based on the outdated timestamp.

## Proof of Concept

A scenario where `from` and `to` are different addresses, but `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` remains unchanged after the token transfer.

1. Alice owns a token with ID 1.

2. Alice transfers the token to Bob using the `transferFrom()` function.

5. The `_beforeTokenTransfer()` function is called as part of the transfer process.

6. Despite Alice's address being different from Bob's, the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` for token ID 1 is not updated correctly.

7. The `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` remains unchanged, even though the token has been transferred from Alice to Bob.

As a result, the `lastTokenTransferredTimestamp` does not accurately reflect the timestamp of the last transfer for the token.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Refactor the timestamp update logic to ensure that it is reliable and accurate.
  - One approach could be to move the `getListedTokenIds(firstTokenId)` call outside the `_beforeTokenTransfer()` function and handle the unlisting of tokens separately.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L72-L73
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L33-L35


# Vulnerability details

## Description
When a user calls `buyNFT()` function with the desired `tokenId` and the correct `msg.value` matching the listing price, the function transfers the NFT from the contract to the buyer and distributes the proceeds between the seller and the `NukeFund`.

However, there is a potential issue in the calculation of the `nukeFundContribution` and `sellerProceeds`. The `buyNFT()` function uses the `taxCut` variable to determine the portion of the sale price that should be allocated to the `NukeFund`. The `nukeFundContribution` is calculated by dividing `msg.value` by `taxCut`: [#Lines 72-73](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L72-L73)

```solidity
uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;
uint256 sellerProceeds = msg.value - nukeFundContribution;
```

The issue arises when `taxCut` is set to zero. If `taxCut` is zero, it will cause a division by zero error when calculating `nukeFundContribution`, leading to the transaction reverting.

The `taxCut` variable is set using the `setTaxCut()` function, which is restricted to the contract owner: [#Lines 33](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L33-L35)

```solidity
function setTaxCut(uint256 _taxCut) external onlyOwner {
    taxCut = _taxCut;
}
```

However, the `setTaxCut()` function does not include any validation to ensure that `_taxCut` is greater than zero. This means that the contract owner can inadvertently or maliciously set `taxCut` to zero, causing the `buyNFT()` function to always revert due to the division by zero error.

## Impact

If the `taxCut` variable is set to zero, any attempt to purchase an NFT using the `buyNFT()` function will result in a division by zero error, causing the transaction to revert. This effectively renders the NFT trading functionality unusable until `taxCut` is set to a non-zero value.

## Proof of Concept

1. The contract owner calls the `setTaxCut()` function with a value of zero:
   ```solidity
   setTaxCut(0);
   ```
2. A user attempts to purchase an NFT by calling the `buyNFT()` function with the correct `tokenId` and `msg.value`.

3. Inside the `buyNFT()` function, the calculation of `nukeFundContribution` is performed: [#Line 72](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L72)
   ```solidity
   uint256 nukeFundContribution = msg.value / taxCut;
   ```
4. Since `taxCut` is zero, a division by zero error occurs, causing the transaction to revert.

5. The user's transaction fails, and they are unable to purchase the NFT.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
add a validation check in the `setTaxCut()` function to ensure that `_taxCut` is always greater than zero:
```solidity
function setTaxCut(uint256 _taxCut) external onlyOwner {
+   require(_taxCut > 0, "Tax cut must be greater than zero");
    taxCut = _taxCut;
}
```

## Description
The `EntityTrading` contract allows users to buy and sell ERC721 tokens (NFTs) through a listing mechanism. When a user buys an NFT using the `buyNFT()` function, the contract transfers the NFT from itself to the buyer using the `transferFrom()` function of the ERC721 token contract: [#Line 81](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L81)

```solidity
nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer NFT to the buyer
```

However, using `transferFrom()` instead of `safeTransferFrom()` can be problematic. The `transferFrom()` function does not ensure that the recipient is capable of receiving ERC721 tokens. If the recipient is a contract that doesn't implement the necessary ERC721 receiver function (`onERC721Received()`), the token transfer will fail silently, and the token may get stuck in the contract.

This issue is not limited to the `buyNFT()` function. The `EntityTrading` contract uses `transferFrom()` in multiple places: [#Line 53](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol#L53)

```solidity
nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId); // transfer NFT to contract
nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer the NFT back to seller
```

If a user accidentally (or maliciously) interacts with the contract using an incompatible contract as the recipient, the NFTs involved in these transactions could be permanently lost.

## Impact

NFTs bought or sold through the `EntityTrading` contract may become permanently stuck if the recipient is a contract that doesn't support ERC721 tokens.

## Proof of Concept

1. Alice lists an NFT for sale on the `EntityTrading` contract.
2. Bob, using a contract that doesn't implement `onERC721Received()`, calls `buyNFT()` to purchase Alice's NFT.
3. The `transferFrom()` call in `buyNFT()` fails silently because Bob's contract can't receive ERC721 tokens.
4. Alice's NFT is now stuck in the `EntityTrading` contract and cannot be recovered.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Replace all instances of `transferFrom()` with `safeTransferFrom()` when transferring ERC721 tokens:

```solidity
- nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId);
+ nftContract.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId);

- nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId);
+ nftContract.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId);
```


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L170-L172


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The claimable nuke fund could exceed the `maxAllowedClaimAmount`, leading to users claiming more than intended rewards.

## Proof of Concept
In the `NukeFund` contract, the `nuke()` function calculates the claimable amount of nuke funds for an NFT based on its `finalNukeFactor`. The issue arises when the `finalNukeFactor <= nukeFactorMaxParam`. In such cases, the claimable amount is set to `potentialClaimAmount`, which can exceed the `maxAllowedClaimAmount`.

If `finalNukeFactor <= nukeFactorMaxParam`, the code assigns `potentialClaimAmount` to `claimAmount` without ensuring that it does not exceed `maxAllowedClaimAmount`:

```solidity
File: NukeFund.sol
166:     uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
167:     uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size
168: 
169:     // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
170:     uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
171:       ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
172:       : potentialClaimAmount;
```

For intance, given

- `finalNukeFactor` = 1000
- `nukeFactorMaxParam` = 1000
- `potentialClaimAmount` = 0.5 ether
- `maxAllowedClaimAmount` = 0.2 ether

As `finalNukeFactor == nukeFactorMaxParam`, the claimable amount is 0.5 ether, which exceeds `maxAllowedClaimAmount`.

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
-    // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
-    uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
-      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
-      : potentialClaimAmount;
+    uint256 claimAmount = potentialClaimAmount > maxAllowedClaimAmount? maxAllowedClaimAmount : potentialClaimAmount;
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L345
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L227-L232


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The NFT pricing structure disincentivizes users from purchasing NFTs when the `currentGenMintCount` nears `maxTokensPerGen`, causing users to wait for the price reset in the next generation. This can lead to a potential bottleneck at the end of each generation.

## Proof of Concept

Given:
```solidity
File: TraitForgeNft.sol
22:   uint256 public maxTokensPerGen = 10000;
23:   uint256 public startPrice = 0.005 ether;
24:   uint256 public priceIncrement = 0.0000245 ether;
25:   uint256 public priceIncrementByGen = 0.000005 ether;
```

The last NFT price of generation 1 is [startPrice + priceIncrement * currentGenMintCount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L227-L232) = `0.005 ether + 10000 * 0.0000245 ether` = 0.25 ether.

[In the next generation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L351), the NFT price will be set to the `startPrice`, which is 0.005 ether and much cheaper (1/50) than the previous NFT sale price. 

The price of NFTs within a generation increases incrementally [based on the `priceIncrement`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L227). However, once the `maxTokensPerGen` is reached, as the [minted token amount of the new generation is zero](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L351), the price resets to the `startPrice` for the next generation. This significant price discrepancy creates a disincentive for users to purchase NFTs as the `currentGenMintCount` approaches `maxTokensPerGen`, leading to potential stagnation in sales at the end of each generation.

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update `startPrice` to the last NFT sales price in the [_incrementGeneration()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L345) function. 

















## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The age of NFT could constantly being zero, results in smaller nuke factor and nuke less funds.

## Proof of Concept
The NFT age could be constantly zero, as the `perfomanceFactor` in `calculateAge()` function is zero if last digit of token entropy is zero:

```solidity
File: contracts\NukeFund\NukeFund.sol
118:   function calculateAge(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (uint256) {
     ...
126:     uint256 perfomanceFactor = nftContract.getTokenEntropy(tokenId) % 10; // <= perfomanceFactor could be zero
127: 
128:     uint256 age = (daysOld *
129:       perfomanceFactor *
130:       MAX_DENOMINATOR *
131:       ageMultiplier) / 365; // add 5 digits for decimals
132:     return age;
133:   }
```

The `perfomanceFactor` is derived from the last digit of the token entropy, which can be zero. This results in the `age` being calculated as zero, regardless of how long the user holds NFT.

Therefore, the calculated nuke factor is smaller than intended because it can not be adjusted [based on the NFT age](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L147-L148).

As the claimable funds is calculated [based on the nuke factor](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L166-L167), users receive less funds.

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
     uint256 perfomanceFactor = nftContract.getTokenEntropy(tokenId) % 10;
+    perfomanceFactor = perfomanceFactor == 0? 1 : perfomanceFactor;
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L182
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntityForging/EntityForging.sol#L86


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The forge NFT's ability to be used for forging is determined by `forgePotential`. This value is extracted from the last second digit of entropy and dictates how many times the NFT can be used in the forging process. However, due to the `EntropyGenerator::getEntropy()` function right-pads the entropy value with zeros, many NFTs are prone to having a `forgePotential` of zero, rendering them unusable for forging.

## Proof of Concept
The `EntropyGenerator::getEntropy()` function right-pads the entropy value with zeros, which increases the likelihood that the last second digit of the entropy will be zero:

```solidity
182:     uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));
```

In `EntityForging::listForForging()` function, the `forgePotential` is extracted by taking the last second digit from the entropy:

```solidity
86:     uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
```

Due to the padding of entropy values, the last second digit is often zero, leading to a significant number of NFTs with a `forgePotential` of zero.

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
-    uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
+    uint8 forgePotential = uint8((entropy / 10000) % 10); // Extract the 5th digit from the entropy
```






## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Missing slippage check when a user calls the `nuke` function in the `NukeFund` contract.

Every user who holds an NFT and passes all requirements for claiming a portion of the fund in the `NukeFund` contract can call the `nuke` function. The maximum reward a user can claim is 50% of the received fund in the contract.

When a user sends their transaction to claim 50% of the funds, he can easily be front-run as another user can claim 50% or less of the held funds in the contract. This can result in the user receiving less ethers than expected.

Attack vector: For the example below `fund = 10 eth`:
1. Bob calls the `nuke` function to claim `50%` of the funds.
2. Alice front-runs Bob's transaction and claims `40%` of the funds.
3. As a result, Alice will receive `4` eth, and Bob will receive `3` eth, as he expected to receive at least `5` eth.

The current economics of the protocol incentivize users to wait until the funds held in the contract are as large as possible so they can claim as much ether as possible. Therefore, if a user or MEV bot detects that a new transaction is in the mempool, which will claim a larger portion of the funds, the MEV bot can easily front-run the transaction.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/main/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L153

## Tools Used
Mannual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add an input parameter `minAmountOut` to the `nuke` function so users can set the minimum amount they expect to receive. If the amount is less than this, the transaction should revert.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Vulnerability details

The following contracts: TraitForgeNft, NukeFund, EntityTrading, EntityForging, EntropyGenerator and DevFund are supposed to be pausable (as they all inherit from Pausable), but they don't implement the `external pause/unpause` functionalities which means it will never be possible to pause them.

Impact
- Inability to Respond to Emergencies:
- Lack of Control Over Operations

## Proof of Concept
All the following contracts TraitForgeNft, NukeFund, EntityTrading, EntityForging, EntropyGenerator and DevFund inherit from the openzeppelin Pausable extension which means that they contain internal functions _pause and _unpause.

Because those functions are internal, the contract must implement two other public/external pause and unpause functions to allow the `manager/owner` to pause and unpause the contracts when necessary. None of the aforementioned contracts implement those functions, which means even if those contracts are supposed to be pausable (and have the pause/unpause functionalities), none of them can be paused.


## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add public/external pause and unpause functions in the aforementioned contracts to allow them to be pausable, this can be done as in the TraitForgeNft contract. For example:

```solidity
function pause() external onlyOwner {
    _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
    _unpause();
}
```

  function calculateAge(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (uint256) {

    uint256 perfomanceFactor = nftContract.getTokenEntropy(tokenId) % 10;

      perfomanceFactor *
      MAX_DENOMINATOR *
      ageMultiplier) / 365; // add 5 digits for decimals
    return age;
  }
```

8639.6667 minutes / 60 = 143.99445 hours
143.99445 hours / 24 = 5.99977 days, but daysOld = 5 days 

let ageMultiplier = 1000
performanceFactor = 9
age = 5 * 9 * 100000 * 1000 /365 = 12328767
correct age = 5.99977 * 9 * 100000 * 1000 /365 = 14793953

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L171-L175
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L72-L78
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L52-L58


# Vulnerability details


## Impact
In the whitepaper, it is stated:

"**There is a certain entropy, “999999” which is referred to as “the Golden God”, since it has perfect parameters and will exceed all other entities if played correctly. The Golden God is scanned for and is kept out of the first 2 passes, but is deliberately set in the final pass (at some random point). The Golden God should be the most valuable entity**".

The constraint inferred from this is that there should be no `999999` returned as entropy in the first two batches, and this `lucky Golden God` is set in the final pass at a random point (`usually only 1 point`).

However, the current check require(`pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.'`) cannot guarantee this constraint. As a result, `999999` could appear in the first two batches, and there could be multiple `999999` returned as `entropy` which contradicts the team’s design. 

## Proof of Concept

In the functions `writeEntropyBatch1` and `writeEntropyBatch2`, it is required that the `pseudoRandomValue` stored in `entropySlots` should not be `999999`:

```solidity
        require(pseudoRandomValue != 999999, 'Invalid value, retry.');
```

The problem is that the `entropySlots` do not store the `entropy` directly. Instead, it is further processed in `getEntropy`:

```solidity
    uint256 slotValue = entropySlots[slotIndex]; // slice the required [art of the entropy value
    uint256 entropy = (slotValue / (10 ** (72 - position))) % 1000000; // adjust the entropy value based on the number of digits
    uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));

    return paddedEntropy; // return the caculated entropy value
```

Currently, the scope of slotValue is within `uint256`, due to the following computation:
```solidity
        uint256 pseudoRandomValue = uint256(
          keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))
        ) % uint256(10) ** 78;
        ...
        entropySlots[i] = pseudoRandomValue;
```
Since `10 ** 78 > 2 ** 256`, the mod operation here doesn’t take effect. Thus, the scope of entropySlots is `uint256 (or 78 digits)`.

So in `getEntropy`, we have:
```
    uint256 position = numberIndex * 6; // calculate the position for slicing the entropy value
    require(position <= 72, 'Position calculation error');

    uint256 slotValue = entropySlots[slotIndex]; // slice the required [art of the entropy value
    uint256 entropy = (slotValue / (10 ** (72 - position))) % 1000000; // adjust the entropy value based on the number of digits
    uint256 paddedEntropy = entropy * (10 ** (6 - numberOfDigits(entropy)));
```

There are multiple cases when the `entropy` could be `999999`:
- `slotValue=YYYYYYYYY999999XXXXXX` and `position = 66` (`numberIndex = 11`)
- `slotValue=YYYYYYYYY999999XXXXXXXXXXXX` and `position = 60` (`numberIndex = 10`)
- ...

This clearly breaks the intention of the protocol. If there are `multiple Golden God entities`, the game mechanism is greatly influenced.
## Tools Used

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this issue:
• Add a more comprehensive check to ensure the `entropy=999999` does not occur in the first two batches. 





## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The current `nuke` process in the `NukeFund` contract does not have slippage protection, which can result in users receiving less `ETH` if they call the `nuke` function later than others. Since the `fund` decreases after each nuke but the percentage (`finalNukeFactor`) remains unchanged, users calling the function subsequently might receive a significantly lower claim amount than expected, leading to potential losses.

## Proof of Concept

In the `nuke` function, the claim amount received by the msg.sender is determined by the `fund` and `finalNukeFactor`:
```solidity
	    uint256 finalNukeFactor = calculateNukeFactor(tokenId); // finalNukeFactor has 5 digits
@=>     uint256 potentialClaimAmount = (fund * finalNukeFactor) / MAX_DENOMINATOR; // Calculate the potential claim amount based on the finalNukeFactor
	    uint256 maxAllowedClaimAmount = fund / maxAllowedClaimDivisor; // Define a maximum allowed claim amount as 50% of the current fund size
	
	    // Directly assign the value to claimAmount based on the condition, removing the redeclaration
	    uint256 claimAmount = finalNukeFactor > nukeFactorMaxParam
	      ? maxAllowedClaimAmount
	      : potentialClaimAmount;
```

The `fund` is reduced by the claim amount after each `nuke`:

```solidity
    fund -= claimAmount; // Deduct the claim amount from the fund
```

Thus, if multiple users call `nuke` consecutively, the first user could receive a larger share of the fund than subsequent users. This situation is exacerbated if the first user claims a large amount, depleting the fund significantly for the following users.

Additionally, the nuke function does not take a `minAmount` parameter to specify a minimum acceptable claim amount, which could help prevent losses due to slippage.

```solidity
  function nuke(uint256 tokenId) public whenNotPaused nonReentrant {...} // <= No `minAmount`
```

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The refund mechanism in the `mintToken` and `mintWithBudget` functions, which sends excess funds back to the `msg.sender`, can be exploited by malicious users. Specifically, users can intentionally trigger the `refund` process and revert the transaction within the `receive/fallback` function if the generated entropy does not meet their desired criteria. This creates an unfair advantage and can be used to manipulate the minting process.

## Proof of Concept
The refund mechanism in the `mintToken` and `mintWithBudget` functions sends excess funds back to `msg.sender`:

```solidity
    if (excessPayment > 0) {
      (bool refundSuccess, ) = msg.sender.call{ value: excessPayment }('');
      require(refundSuccess, 'Refund of excess payment failed.');
    }
```

A malicious user can exploit this mechanism by:
1. Deploying a contract.
2. Calling `mintToken` or `mintWithBudget` through the contract, sending slightly more than the `mintPrice` to trigger the refund.
3. In the `receive/fallback` function of their contract, checking the generated entropy.
4. Reverting the transaction if the entropy is not favorable.

This allows the user to repeatedly attempt minting until they achieve the desired entropy, giving them an unfair advantage.
## Tools Used

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Ensure that only externally owned accounts (EOAs) can call the minting functions and receive refunds. This can be done by `require(tx.origin == msg.sender, "Caller must be an EOA");`


## Assessed type

Payable

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The check `forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential` in the `forgeWithListed` function is incorrect. As `forgingCounts` will increase by 1 without any further check for `forgerTokenId`, this will cause `forgingCounts[tokenId] > forgePotential`, which breaks the game invariant.

## Proof of Concept

In the `forgeWithListed` function, the `forgingCounts` for the `forgeTokenId` is checked as follows:

```solidity
    require(
      forgePotential > 0 && forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential,
      'Entity has reached its forging limit'
    );
```

The issue arises due to the use of the `<= operator`. The check will still pass when `forgingCounts[tokenId] == forgePotential`. Later in the function `forgeWithListed`, the forgingCounts[forgeTokenId] is directly increased:


```solidity
    // Check forger's breed count increment but do not check forge potential here
    // as it is already checked in listForForging for the forger
    forgingCounts[forgerTokenId]++;
```

This is incorrect since it can result in `forgingCounts[tokenId] > forgePotential`, breaking the game invariant.
## Tools Used

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change the operator from `forgingCounts[tokenId] <= forgePotential` to `forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential`.

**Description:** 
The following contracts: `DevFund`, `EntityForging`, `EntityTrading`, `EntropyGenerator`, `NukeFund` and `TraitForgeNft` contracts are supposed to be pausable (as they all inherit from Pausable contract), but they don't implement the external pause/unpause functionalities which means it will never be possible to pause them.

**Proof of Concept:**
All the following contracts  `DevFund`, `EntityForging`, `EntityTrading`, `EntropyGenerator`, `NukeFund` and `TraitForgeNft` from the openzeppelin `Pausable` extension which means that they contain internal functions _pause and _unpause.

Because those functions are internal, the contract must implement two other public/external pause and unpause functions to allow the owner to pause and unpause the contracts when necessary. None of the contracts implement those functions, which means even if those contracts are supposed to be pausable (and have the pause/unpause functionalities), none of them can be paused.

**Impact:** 
The impact will be when owner wants to pause the contract for some reason, the owner will be not able to do it.

**Recommended Mitigation:** 
Add public/external pause and unpause functions in the contracts to allow them to be pausable, this can be done as in the `DedFund` contract. For example:
```solidity
/**
 * @dev Triggers stopped state.
 * Contract must not be paused
 */
function pause() external onlyOwner {
    _pause();
}

/**
 * @dev Returns to normal state.
 * Contract must be paused
 */
function unpause() external onlyOwner {
    _unpause();
}

# Vulnerability details


 ### Impact: 

    In the traitForgeNft::_incrementGeneration() functions is responsible for incrementing the generation when the time is right now inside this internal function there is this perticular line entropyGenerator.initializeAlphaIndices();  this is a function from EntropyGenerator.sol in this function it is set that it can only be called by onlyOwner and the sponsors plan was for their multisig wallet to be the owner of EntropyGenerator.sol so when this happens then TraitForge.sol won't be able to call that function because is not the owner of the contract
    protocol will be unable to start next generation after the first generation is done



### Proof of Concept:
**Follow this scenario:**
The protocol deploys `EntropyGenerator.sol` using their Multisig wallet.
The mintToken() function is called for the first time. This triggers a chain of function calls:

`mintToken()` calls `_mintInternal()`
`_mintInternal()` calls `_incrementGeneration()`
`_incrementGeneration()` calls `initializeAlphaIndices()`


For the first few times this sequence of functions is called, nothing significant will happen. This is due to a check inside _mintInternal().
```javascript
if (generationMintCounts[currentGeneration] >= maxTokensPerGen) {
    _incrementGeneration();
```

* Once this check passes and `_incrementGeneration()` is called, the function will revert.
The reversion occurs because `_incrementGeneration()` calls a function in another contract that is restricted to onlyOwner.
The issue arises because the owner of `EntropyGenerator` is not set to `TraitForge.sol`.


### Recommended Mitigation:
To resolve this issue, ensure that `TraitForge.sol` is set as the owner of `EntropyGenerator` when deploying. This will allow `TraitForge.sol` to call the necessary functions when required, preventing the reversion in `_incrementGeneration()`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the EntityForging contract, the devFee is calculated during the forging process as follows:
```js
uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
```
Here, forgingFee is essentially the _forgerListingInfo.fee. There is no validation check applied on the setter function for taxCut, which is a crucial parameter in the contract. If the admin mistakenly sets taxCut to a value greater than minimumListFee (in terms of ether), it will cause the devFee calculation to produce 0 due to integer division, effectively bypassing the devFee.

## Proof of Concept
1. The admin mistakenly sets taxCut to a value greater than minimumListFee.
2. When forgeWithListed() is called, the devFee calculation results in 0.
3. The protocol’s revenue collection via devFee is bypassed, the nukeAddress receives 0 ether.

## Tools Used
Manual Code Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Add Validation to Setter Functions:
```js
function setTaxCut(uint256 _taxCut) external onlyOwner {
    require(_taxCut > 0, "Tax cut must be greater than 0");
    require(_taxCut <= minimumListFee, "Tax cut must be less than or equal to minimum listing fee");
    taxCut = _taxCut;
}
```
2. Add Validation to Minimum Listing Fee:
```js
function setMinimumListingFee(uint256 _fee) external onlyOwner {
    require(_fee > 0, "Listing fee must be greater than 0");
    minimumListFee = _fee;
}
```
3. Update the forgeWithlisted() function to include the following logic
```js
uint256 devFee = forgingFee / taxCut;
require(devFee > 0, "Dev fee calculation resulted in 0");
```

In the EntityForging contract, there are multiple scenarios where a listed forger can potentially cause a Denial of Service (DoS) attack against a merger during the forging process. The forger can exploit several vectors to prevent the forging process from completing, such as:
1. Reverting When Funds are Sent: If the forger’s address is a contract with a fallback function that reverts when receiving funds, it can cause the transaction to fail.
2. Canceling Beforehand: The forger can monitor the blockchain for a merger’s transaction and cancel the listing before it completes.
3. Burning the Token: The forger can burn their token, which will cancel the listing.
4. Transferring the Token: The forger can transfer their token to another address, which automatically cancels the listing.

## Proof of Concept
1. The forger lists a token for forging.
2. A merger initiates the forging process by calling forgeWithListed.
3. The forger can use one of the aforementioned methods to cause the transaction to fail, leading to a denial of service for the merger.

Manual Code Review

function claimFees() external nonReentrant {
    uint256 amount = pendingFees[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "No fees to claim");

    pendingWithdrawals[msg.sender] = 0;

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{ value: amount }("");
    require(success, "Claim failed");

    emit FeesClaimed(msg.sender, amount);
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The following contracts: DevFund.sol,EntityTrading.sol,NukeFund.sol and TraitForgeNft.sol are supposed to be pausable (as they all inherit from Pausable), but they don't implement the external pause/unpause functionalities which means it will never be possible to pause them.

## Proof of Concept
DevFund.sol,EntityTrading.sol,NukeFund.sol and TraitForgeNft.sol inherits pausable and implements the whenNotPaused modifier on some function, but doesn't implement any method to actually pause or unpause the contract. Pausable.sol only implements internal functions, which requires external or public functions to be implemented to wrap them. Since nothing like this has been implemented, the entire pausing system is rendered useless and cannot be paused as is intended.

## Tool used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add public/external pause and unpause functions in the aforementioned contracts to allow them to be pausable.

```solidity
function pause() external onlyOwner {
    _pause();
}

function unpause() external onlyOwner {
    _unpause();
}

```

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L39-L61


# Vulnerability details

## Description 
The fallback `receive` function in the `NukeFund` contract is designed to receive ETH and update the `fund` balance. However, it does not restrict or validate the source of the funds being sent. This lack of restriction means that any user can send ETH directly to the contract, thereby altering the `fund` variable. This  variable is used in critical calculations, such as determining the `finalNukeFactor` and claim amounts during a nuke action. This functionality deviates from the intended behavior, which is to only accept funds from project-related activities such as minting, nuking, or forging. The ability for unauthorized users to send ETH directly could result in manipulation of the contract’s financial parameters, potentially leading to unfair advantages or exploitation.

## Impact
The ability for unauthorized users to send ETH directly to the `NukeFund` contract presents a high risk by:
- Compromising Financial Integrity: Altering the fund balance can distort calculations related to `finalNukeFactor` and claim amounts, leading to financial losses or exploitation.
- Undermining Fairness: It disrupts the intended financial mechanisms and fairness of the main process, allowing external manipulation of contract parameters.

## Proof of Concept
To illustrate this issue:
1. Deploy the `NukeFund` Contract: Set up the `NukeFund` contract on a test network.
2. Send ETH Directly: Use a wallet or an external contract to send ETH directly to the `NukeFund` contract.
3. Observe the Impact: Check how the direct ETH transfer affects the `fund` balance and observe any changes in the calculations related to `finalNukeFactor` and claim amounts.
This proof of concept demonstrates how unauthorized ETH transfers can alter the contract's financial parameters and disrupt its intended functionality.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Create a specific payable function in the `NukeFund` contract that is callable only by authorized project contracts for actions such as minting, nuking, or forging. Move the logic from the `receive()` function into this designated function.
2. Remove the `receive()` function to prevent unauthorized ETH transfers directly to the contract.
3. Ensure that the new payable function is protected by access control mechanisms to restrict who can call it.

By implementing these changes, the contract will only accept ETH through controlled and intended channels, ensuring accurate tracking of funds and maintaining the integrity of financial operations.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L10

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L280-L294


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The `EntropyGenerator` contract uses a three-stage process to initialize entropy values stored in the `entropySlots` array. The entropy values are generated using pseudo-random numbers based on the block number and slot index, then stored in the contract. This process results in predictable entropy values since the array is accessible on the blockchain. Users can leverage this predictability to time their minting actions to obtain NFTs with desirable traits.

## Impact
The predictability of entropy values has significant implications:
1. Minting Exploitation: Users can predict future entropy values based on the current index and slot, allowing them to mint NFTs when the entropy value aligns with their desired traits.
2. Unfair Advantage: This predictability undermines the fairness of the minting process, as users can only mint NFTs when the entropy values are favorable, giving them an undue advantage.
3. Integrity of Entropy: The method of generating entropy values may lead to predictable outcomes, impacting the randomness and uniqueness of NFTs.

## Proof of Concept
The entropy values are generated using `(uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.number, i))) % 10^78)`, and the entropy values are stored in the `entropySlots` array. Anyone can retrieve the entropy value for each index, calculate the current and future entropy values, and predict when favorable traits will be available for minting.

Users can track the current entropy index and predict the values for future slots, allowing them to strategically mint NFTs with desired traits when the entropy is advantageous (for example : entropy with high `ForgePotential` and `performanceFactor` values).

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Generate Random Entropy on Minting: Instead of using a predictable process, generate a new random entropy value during each mint action. This ensures that entropy values cannot be predicted in advance.
2. Store Entropy in a Mapping: Implement a mapping in the `TraitForgeNFT` contract to store entropy values associated with each token ID. This mapping should be updated with the randomly generated entropy value at the time of minting.
3. Remove Predictable Logic: Eliminate the current method of generating entropy in predictable batches. Ensure that the entropy values are securely generated and stored, making it impossible for users to anticipate future values.


## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `listNFTForSale()`, `buyNFT()` and `cancelListing()` functions in the `EntityTrading` contract do not check the return value of the `transferFrom` function. In the mentioned function, the contract transfers the NFT from the user to the contract address but does not verify if the transfer was successful. This can lead to scenarios where the NFT remains with the user/contract while the contract assumes it has been transferred. This can lead to scenarios where the NFT remains with the contract while the contract assumes it has been transferred back to the user.

According to OpenZeppelin, ["Usage of this method is discouraged, use safeTransferFrom() whenever possible"](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/api/token/erc721#IERC721-transferFrom-address-address-uint256-). The safeTransferFrom method provides safety checks that ensure the transfer is successful and mitigates the risk of losing NFTs. 


## Proof of Concept
Following scenario is for listing NFT for sale: 

1. Alice calls the `listNFTForSale` function to list her NFT with `tokenId = 1` at a price of `1 ETH`.
2. The `transferFrom` function is called to transfer the NFT from Alice to the contract.
3. Due to an issue (e.g., insufficient gas, etc), the `transferFrom` function fails, but this failure is not checked. The contract assumes the NFT has been transferred to it.
4. Alice's NFT remains in her wallet, but the contract records that the NFT is listed for sale.

The same scenario applies for buying NFT and while canceling NFT for listing

## Tools Used
Manual 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended to replace `transferFrom` with `safeTransferFrom`.

```diff
diff --git a/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol b/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol
index 57a6b07..72abef3 100644
--- a/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol
+++ b/contracts/EntityTrading/EntityTrading.sol


@@ -50,7 +50,7 @@ contract EntityTrading is IEntityTrading, ReentrancyGuard, Ownable, Pausable {
       'Contract must be approved to transfer the NFT.'
     );
 
-    nftContract.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId); // trasnfer NFT to contract
+    nftContract.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId); // trasnfer NFT to contract
 
     ++listingCount;
     listings[listingCount] = Listing(msg.sender, tokenId, price, true);


@@ -78,7 +78,7 @@ contract EntityTrading is IEntityTrading, ReentrancyGuard, Ownable, Pausable {
       ''
     );
     require(success, 'Failed to send to seller');
-    nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer NFT to the buyer
+    nftContract.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer NFT to the buyer
 
     delete listings[listedTokenIds[tokenId]]; // remove listing
 

@@ -101,7 +101,7 @@ contract EntityTrading is IEntityTrading, ReentrancyGuard, Ownable, Pausable {
     );
     require(listing.isActive, 'Listing is not active.');
 
-    nftContract.transferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer the nft back to seller
+    nftContract.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, tokenId); // transfer the nft back to seller
```

Token-Transfer
